core_content.key_takeaway: Two fundamental approaches — linear (sequential, one pass) and iterative (repeatable cycles). Hybrid blends them. Phases exist for three named reasons: grouping activities, better estimates, tracking progress.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Why projects are structured as phases

The syllabus asks for this in so many words, so learn it as three named reasons rather than a vague sense that phases are tidy.

| Reason | What it buys you |
|---|---|
| **Better grouping of activities** | Phases group work by type — analysis, planning, building — so the right people are on the right kind of work at the right time. |
| **More accurate plans and estimates** | Smaller chunks are easier to plan and estimate, which raises both accuracy and confidence. |
| **Tracking and monitoring progress** | Phases create clear break points to measure against checkpoints and milestones, so you can see early whether things are on track. |

Every project passes through the same high-level phases whichever life cycle is used. The life cycle decides *how* you move through them, not whether they exist.

## The two fundamental approaches

There are only two at the top level. Everything else blends them.

**Linear** — distinct, sequential phases in a single pass. You move on only once the current phase is complete.

**Iterative** — repeatable phases. You create an initial output, then build on it with further deliveries of incremental value as the solution evolves.

**Hybrid** — a deliberate blend, because most real environments are messy enough that neither pure approach fits end to end.

## Linear: the phases, and the control they buy

Because each phase finishes before the next begins, linear gives tight control over progression and a clear framework for scheduling, budgeting, resourcing and risk.

The boundaries matter as much as the phases. They create clear **gateways** — which is where milestones, governance and reviews live. No gateway, nowhere to put the decision.

| Phase | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Concept** | An idea — exploiting an opportunity or solving a problem — is analysed for viability and fit with organisational objectives. Research, high-level requirements, often an outline business case. |
| **Definition** | How to make it real is planned: detailed analysis, estimation, planning and a fuller statement of requirements, ending in the sponsor's approval to proceed. |
| **Deployment** | Plans are implemented. Testing and assurance monitor performance to keep intended outcomes and benefits on track. |
| **Transition** | Outputs are accepted and transitioned into use — handover, then formal closure. |

Naming and phasing vary by organisation, shaped by its nature, purpose, environment and governance culture. Smaller projects often use a shorter cycle.

**Fits best:** clearly defined or high-risk projects, where time, cost and risk can flex to protect agreed scope and quality — and projects with a **high cost of change**, where extra rigour up front pays for itself.

## Iterative: how it actually works

Iterative rests on continuous improvement and evolutionary development: the solution evolves as learning takes place and new information emerges.

You start with a high-level vision. Detail is defined and built inside each cycle. Because specification and design run in parallel, deployment is fast-tracked and users get value earlier — which produces rapid feedback you can act on.

A common structure comes from the dynamic systems development method (DSDM):

| Phase | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Pre-project and feasibility** | The idea is established — aligned to objectives, cost effective, technically possible, with a clear measurable goal. |
| **Foundations** | Planning and design: a high-level delivery plan and a technical design. |
| **Evolutionary development and deployment** | Repeatable cycles of detailed design, development, testing and deployment. Early cycles produce an initial output; later ones add value as learning emerges. |
| **Realisation** | Embed the outputs and evolve the next iteration. |

Many iterative life cycles use **sprints** — timeboxed iterations with a fixed end date — typically producing a **minimum viable product** first, with further scope assessed, prioritised and planned into later iterations. A daily **scrum** keeps the team synchronised.

**Fits best:** new or innovative work without detailed up-front knowledge, prototypes and pioneering technology, and situations with a **low cost of change** so the project can pivot quickly.

**What it demands:** collaboration and co-creation. It runs on engagement and regular feedback from end users, and works best with co-located teams, which keeps communication barriers down.

## Hybrid: blending the two

There is no one-size-fits-all life cycle. A hybrid takes the useful parts of each for a specific project.

The common pattern: **iterative through concept and definition** to work through early uncertainty, then **linear for deployment and transition** once there is clarity. Stakeholders get certainty on scope; the project gets structure for controlling schedule, budget, quality and risk.

You are not locked in. Many successful projects adapt as they go.

What makes hybrid work or fail is alignment with the organisation's wider governance — reporting, change control, roles and responsibilities, and dependencies on other initiatives. Blend the life cycles without aligning governance and you get two systems of working arguing with each other.
core_content.outcome_title: Linear, iterative and hybrid life cycles

diagrams.heading: Where each one stops

core_content.key_takeaway: A standard life cycle ends at transition. An extended one adds adoption and benefits realisation, which run in parallel, and keeps the project team accountable until benefits appear.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Where each one stops

A standard project life cycle ends once the agreed outputs are deployed and handed over. An **extended** life cycle adds two phases on the end.

| Added phase | What it covers |
|---|---|
| **Adoption** | Communications, training, knowledge sharing and change management, so operational teams actually use the outputs correctly. |
| **Benefits realisation** | Measuring business performance to confirm adoption is producing the intended outcomes and the anticipated benefits. |

They typically **run in parallel**, not one after the other. As adoption rises, outcomes improve, and benefits follow.

## The chain that makes it make sense

> A new software tool is delivered (**output**) → customer usage increases (**outcome**) → service delivery costs fall (**benefit**).

Delivering the output guarantees none of the rest. That is the entire argument for extending.

## How benefits actually get measured

Worth knowing, because it is what the extra phases *do*:

- The groundwork is laid in **benefits planning**, not at the end — activities and resources for transition into use, testing schedules, acceptance criteria, quality assurance thresholds.
- **Benefit owners and change managers** stay active for the project's whole duration, readying the business to take the outputs.
- Measurement varies by benefit type: **quantitative** for operational and financial benefits, **qualitative** (such as user feedback) for non-financial ones.
- The **project sponsor is ultimately accountable** for the measurement process being robust, usually through formal benefits realisation reviews.
- If benefits are not landing, there are two honest moves: **drive adoption harder, or reset the target**.

## Timing differs by life cycle

This one is directly examinable and easy to miss:

- **Linear** — benefits are usually realised at the end, once all outputs are delivered.
- **Iterative** — benefits are realised incrementally, as the project progresses.

## When to extend

Programmes normally include adoption and benefits realisation as standard. For a **standalone project** it is a real trade-off:

| For extending | Against extending |
|---|---|
| Higher adoption rates | The organisation pays for project professionals' time on those activities |
| Better chance the benefits are realised — often what stakeholders judge success on | Operational teams could manage it instead |
| The project team learns how their work actually lands in the business | |

A project inside a larger programme may only need to deliver outputs, because the programme handles adoption and benefits.

**Timing matters.** If you are going to extend, plan for it in the **early phases** — the requirements, work, resources and risks of the extra phases all belong in the project management plan from the start.
core_content.outcome_title: Project life cycle vs extended life cycle

core_content.key_takeaway: Four factors set the approach: risk appetite, cost of change, business agility, decision-making autonomy. Then project type (how well you know the what and the how) and organisational culture push you towards linear or iterative.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Four factors that set the project approach

Before choosing a life cycle, teams agree a **project approach** — the values, principles and behaviours the project works to. Four factors shape it, and they are the most reliable thing to reason from in a scenario question.

| Factor | The question it asks |
|---|---|
| **Risk appetite** | How much risk is the project willing to take? Usually inherited from the organisation and its industry. |
| **Cost of change** | How easy is it to pivot mid-deployment? Rewriting software code is cheap. Demolishing and rebuilding a football stadium is not. |
| **Business agility** | Is the organisation flexible, resilient and adaptable, or rigid and bureaucratic? |
| **Decision-making autonomy** | Is the team empowered to decide, or does everything need layers of approval? |

**The pattern worth memorising:**

- High risk appetite + low cost of change + team autonomy + strong business agility → fast progress, learning by trial and error → **iterative**.
- Low risk appetite + high cost of change + low autonomy + low agility → the team cannot afford mistakes → controlled, cautious, methodical → **linear**.

A project's approach is not black and white. It moves along a spectrum of agility, risk taking and autonomy as the project progresses.

## Project type: how well do you know the what and the how?

Turner and Cochrane's goals-and-methods matrix asks two questions — how well do we know **what** we are doing, and how well do we know **how** we will do it?

| Type | Goals | Methods | Example | What to do about it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 — earth** | Clear | Clear | Large engineering | Keep concept and planning brief; deliver quickly |
| **2 — water** | Clear | Unclear | Product development | Focus early effort on the 'what' via a clear business case |
| **3 — fire** | Unclear | Clear | Software development | Move fast through concept; experiment between definition and deployment |
| **4 — air** | Unclear | Unclear | Organisational development | Spend longer in concept and definition to gain information and confidence |

Type 4 is the exam-useful row: **high uncertainty justifies more time in concept and definition** — a concrete reason you can point at in a scenario answer.

## Organisational culture

Culture is the unwritten set of rules shaping behaviour and attitudes. Cameron and Quinn's model splits it on two competing pairs — stability vs flexibility, and inward vs outward looking.

| Culture | Character | Life cycle implication |
|---|---|---|
| **Clan** (inward/flexible) | Collaborative, nurturing, family feel, coaching leadership | Supports collaboration and co-creation |
| **Adhocracy** (outward/flexible) | Energetic, entrepreneurial, innovation and risk taking welcome | Iterative projects often have a strong element of adhocracy culture |
| **Hierarchy** (inward/stable) | Rigid, strong order and control, consistency over creativity | Suits projects under strict governance — points to linear |
| **Market** (outward/stable) | Results-orientated, competitive, focused on profit and market share | Creates rivalry between project teams |

Culture also varies *within* an organisation — regional offices, functions, departments and project teams develop their own subcultures.

## Adapting the life cycle

Adaptation is normal, not a planning failure.

- **Phasing and naming change by organisation**, shaped by its nature, purpose, environment and governance culture. Smaller projects often use a shorter cycle.
- **The approach can change mid-project.** Projects move in and out of stability, uncertainty and risk, and the approach should adapt with the environment and stakeholders' needs.
- **Blending scales upwards** to programmes and portfolios — iterative deployment lets a programme realise benefits earlier through rapid user feedback.

**The constraint on all of it:** whatever you adapt must stay aligned with organisational governance — reporting, change control, clear roles, and visible dependencies on other initiatives.
core_content.outcome_title: How context and culture drive the choice

core_content.key_takeaway: Every strength has a matching cost. Linear buys control and pays in flexibility; iterative buys adaptability and pays in certainty; hybrid buys fit and pays in complexity.
core_content.body_markdown:
## The grid

| Life cycle | Strengths | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| **Linear** | Tight control of progression; clear framework for scheduling, budgeting, resourcing and risk; clear gateways for milestones, governance and reviews; suits a high cost of change | Assumes a lot of knowledge up front; poor fit for developing or changeable environments; users wait longer for value; limited scope for major change once delivery is complete |
| **Iterative** | Value delivered earlier; rapid user feedback; adapts as learning emerges; suits innovation, prototypes and pioneering technology; suits a low cost of change | Depends on sustained user engagement and regular feedback; works best with co-located teams; less up-front certainty on total scope, time and cost |
| **Hybrid** | Pragmatic mix tailored to the project; resolves early uncertainty while keeping later control; can adapt as the project progresses | Needs greater skill and clarity to run two ways of working; must be aligned to organisational governance or reporting and change control break down |
| **Extended** | Higher adoption rates; better chance benefits are realised — often what stakeholders judge success on; the team learns how its work lands | Additional cost for project professionals' time; must be planned from the early phases, not bolted on |

## The trade-off in one line each

- **Linear** buys control and pays for it in flexibility.
- **Iterative** buys adaptability and pays for it in certainty.
- **Hybrid** buys fit and pays for it in complexity.
- **Extended** buys benefits and pays for it in cost.

If you can state the cost as fluently as the strength, you understand the life cycle.
core_content.outcome_title: Strengths and limitations

misconceptions.right: Neither is better. Each suits different conditions — cost of change, information available up front, risk appetite, and how much the project depends on user feedback.
misconceptions.wrong: Iterative is the modern approach and is therefore better.

misconceptions.right: They handle change through formal change control. What they handle badly is continuously evolving scope, especially once delivery is well advanced.
misconceptions.wrong: Linear projects cannot handle change.

misconceptions.right: It means two specific phases were added — adoption and benefits realisation — and the project team stayed accountable through them.
misconceptions.wrong: An extended life cycle just means a longer project.

misconceptions.right: The approach can change as the project progresses, and often should. Projects move in and out of stability, uncertainty and risk.
misconceptions.wrong: Once you have chosen a life cycle you are committed to it.

misconceptions.right: Hybrid demands more skill, because two ways of working must be reconciled with one set of governance, reporting and change control.
misconceptions.wrong: Hybrid is the easy option because you can do whatever you like.

misconceptions.right: Outputs do not automatically generate benefit. Adoption creates outcomes, and outcomes generate benefits. Each step has to actually happen.
misconceptions.wrong: Delivering the output means the project delivered its benefits.

misconceptions.right: The Body of Knowledge itself notes that linear life cycles are often referred to as waterfall. 'Linear' is the primary term and the safer one to lead with, but the word is not forbidden.
misconceptions.wrong: You must never use the word 'waterfall'.

key_definitions.plain_english: The set of stages a project moves through from first idea to finished output. It is the skeleton everything else hangs on.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A framework comprising a series of distinct phases required to transform an idea into reality in an orderly and efficient manner.

key_definitions.plain_english: One pass, in order, finish each phase before starting the next. Sometimes called 'waterfall'.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A life cycle that takes the project through a set of distinct, sequential phases in a single pass, only progressing from phase to phase once all the work on the current phase is completed.

key_definitions.plain_english: Build a first working version, then keep improving it in repeated cycles as you learn more.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A life cycle that takes the project through a set of repeatable phases to create an initial output, which is then built upon with further deliveries of incremental value.

key_definitions.plain_english: Mix and match. Commonly iterative early where uncertainty is high, linear later once scope is settled.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A life cycle that blends the philosophies, principles, tools and techniques of both linear and iterative life cycles to suit a particular project.

key_definitions.plain_english: The project does not stop at handover. The team stays accountable until the change is embedded and the benefits show up.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A life cycle that adds adoption and benefits realisation phases to the end of a standard project life cycle.

key_definitions.plain_english: Checking the value actually arrived, rather than assuming it did because the thing got built.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The process of ensuring that benefits are derived from delivered outputs and outcomes.

key_definitions.plain_english: How the team agrees to operate — agreed before picking frameworks or tools, not after.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The overarching values, principles and behaviours the project works to throughout its delivery.

key_definitions.plain_english: A short, fixed-length work cycle. The end date does not move; the scope inside it does.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A timeboxed iteration with a fixed end date.

key_definitions.plain_english: The smallest useful thing you can put in front of users to start learning from them.
key_definitions.apm_definition: An initial output delivered rapidly, with additional scope items assessed, prioritised and planned for in future iterations.

key_definitions.plain_english: Output = the thing you built. Outcome = what changes because people use it. Benefit = the measurable value that change creates.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Adoption and use of outputs creates improved business outcomes, with those outcomes going on to generate the anticipated business benefit.

body.where_this_fits: The life cycle is the first structural decision on a project, and nearly everything else inherits from it. Choose linear and you get gated phases, fixed scope and formal change control. Choose iterative and you get evolving scope, rapid feedback and a different risk process entirely. That single choice reaches into governance, reviews, benefits, resourcing, risk and change control — several of which ask you directly how a process differs between linear and iterative. Get life cycles solid here and you are part-way through four other learning objectives.
learning_outcomes: 1a) Understand the distinctive features of linear, iterative and hybrid life cycles (including why projects are structured as phases in linear life cycles) and know when each is applicable.
1b) Knowledge of the differences between a project life cycle and an extended life cycle.
1c) Understand how the context and culture of an organisation, and the needs of a specific project, influence the choice of life cycle and any adaptations that may be needed to the life cycle.
1d) Knowledge of the strengths and limitations of different life cycles.
progress_checkpoint: I can give the three reasons projects are structured as phases — grouping activities, more accurate estimates, tracking progress.
I can name the two fundamental approaches, linear and iterative, explain how hybrid relates to them, and list the four linear phases in order.
I can explain what phase boundaries are for: they create the gateways where milestones, governance and reviews sit.
I can describe the iterative cycle and explain what sprints and an MVP are for.
I can state the two phases an extended life cycle adds, and explain why adoption and benefits realisation run in parallel.
I can distinguish output, outcome and benefit with an example, and explain how benefits timing differs between linear and iterative.

I can name the four factors that set a project's approach — risk appetite, cost of change, business agility, decision-making autonomy — and explain how organisational culture pushes the choice either way.
I can state one strength and one limitation for each of linear, iterative and hybrid, and justify a life cycle choice using specific details from a scenario.

memory_aids.expansion: The one-line definition of governance. If a question is really asking about authority, accountability or escalation, it is a governance question.
The two purposes of governance. Right things = serving the investing organisation. Right way = complying with good practice, ethics, policy, regulation and legislation.
Sponsor is accountable for the project being worth doing (business case, benefits). Project manager is responsible for it getting done (outputs, delivery).
Who does the person report to? Functional = their function only. Matrix = both function and project manager. Project = the project manager only. Name the structure by naming the reporting line.

core_content.key_takeaway: Governance is a framework of authority and accountability that must sit inside corporate governance. Projects run temporary structures inside a permanent one — functional, matrix or project — and the organisation's governance approach constrains what the project can choose.
core_content.body_markdown:
## What governance is actually for

Governance is a framework of **authority and of accountability**. It is the mechanism through which the organisation funding the work keeps oversight of it — setting and controlling what the project produces, what changes as a result, and what value the organisation gets back.

The cleanest one-line version, and the one worth carrying into the exam: **governance decides who gets to decide what.**

It exists to make sure projects:

- **do the right things** — serving the investing organisation's objectives
- **in the right way** — complying with good practice, ethical standards, policies, procedures, regulation and legislation

Those two halves are worth memorising as a pair, because scenario questions usually break on one or the other. A project delivering something nobody needs fails the first. A project delivering the right thing by cutting regulatory corners fails the second.

## Three levels, one system

Project governance does not stand alone. It overlaps with the rest of the organisation's governance.

| Level | What it governs |
|---|---|
| **Corporate governance** | Vision, mission, strategy — the whole organisation |
| **Business-as-usual governance** | Operations, the ongoing work |
| **Business change governance** | Projects, programmes and portfolios |

Project governance principles must **integrate with wider corporate governance**, and must also be shaped by what the initiative actually is — how big it is, how complicated, how far its effects reach, and which life cycle it runs on. Governance that ignores either half breaks: too detached from corporate and it gets overruled; too generic and it does not fit the project.

Governance is also **fractal** — the same mechanisms apply at each level, with each level governing the one below and feeding information back to the one above. Direction, goals and objectives flow down; feedback, information and KPIs flow up.

## Two levels of control

A useful distinction for structuring an answer:

| Control | At project level it means |
|---|---|
| **Control of direction** | Determining the problem to be solved, defining the outcomes and benefits, and assuring the project's goals stay aligned with organisational strategy |
| **Control of implementation** | Managing alignment of delivery to the agreed outcomes, overseeing key milestones and deliverables, monitoring progress and taking corrective action |

## Delegation is the point, not a compromise

Not every decision can be taken by one person, so governance has to allow **delegation of decision-making within parameters**. The general principle is to delegate to the **lowest level possible** while still keeping control of direction and oversight of progress.

That is why governance both **empowers and constrains**. It empowers project professionals by giving them defined limits of authority to act within, and constrains leaders, who must themselves decide through the process governance lays down rather than around it. Governance is not a brake bolted onto delivery; without it nobody below the sponsor could decide anything at all.

For delegation to work, roles and responsibilities across the team and the governance tiers have to be clearly defined — which is exactly what a **responsibility assignment matrix** does, by clarifying who is accountable and responsible, who must be consulted, and who must be informed.

## Permanent versus temporary organisations

Organisational structures are fundamentally about **power and information**: who holds roles, responsibilities and power, and how information flows between levels of management.

- The **permanent organisation** is the stable backdrop: decisions get made and information travels along routes that stay put. It is built around functional departments — finance, IT, product development, HR — which hold the resources, processes and technologies that do the work.
- **Projects and programmes are temporary endeavours with temporary structures**, designed to manage activities and resources to deliver specific objectives within predetermined timeframes.

Those two do not typically match, but they must be coordinated. Project professionals work across both, and how hard that is depends on how well the two structures align.

**Where the friction shows up:** competing priorities. Pulling skilled people out of the permanent organisation affects operational performance. The **sponsor** manages this interface — negotiating access to the right people, managing the tensions across the boundary, and easing the transition from delivery back into operations.

## The three temporary structures

This table is high-yield. Learn the trade-off, not just the label.

| Structure | Who they report to | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Functional** | Their functional lead only (e.g. the finance director), while working solely on project work | Builds expert domain knowledge | People can feel isolated — a lone project worker in a business-as-usual team |
| **Matrix** | Split between functional lead **and** project manager | Keeps the project visible inside the operation | People struggle with conflicting priorities and two bosses |
| **Project** | The project lead only; fully dedicated | Complete focus on project objectives | The project can become disconnected from the operation |

Authority moves in opposite directions across that list: **line manager authority is highest in a functional structure and lowest in a project structure; project manager authority is the reverse.** Matrix sits deliberately in the middle, which is why it produces the most conflict — nobody has clear primacy.

Choosing a structure creates the **organisational breakdown structure (OBS)**. Combine the OBS with the work breakdown structure and you get the **responsibility assignment matrix (RAM)**, showing every item of work, who has been put on it, and what part each of them plays.

## Why the organisation's governance approach constrains the project's

This is the second half of 2a and easy to skip.

The project does not get a free choice. Its governance arrangements have to reflect the organisation's permanent structure and existing practice — reporting lines, approval thresholds, change control, the standards it already applies. A project inside a rigid, hierarchical organisation with tight approval limits cannot simply declare itself self-governing because the team prefers it.

The practical consequence, and a good scenario answer: if the project's chosen life cycle and the organisation's governance approach pull in different directions, that gap is a **risk to be managed and made visible**, not something to quietly ignore. It usually shows up as decisions taking longer than the delivery approach assumed.
core_content.outcome_title: Governance structures, permanent and temporary organisations

core_content.key_takeaway: Roles are distinct so that accountability is unambiguous and decisions sit at the right level. The sponsor owns the business case and the benefits; the project manager owns delivery of the outputs. The sponsor's involvement starts before and ends after the project manager's.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Why distinct roles exist at all

Because governance is a framework of accountability, and accountability that is shared is accountability that is absent. Distinct roles exist to:

- put each decision at the **level with the right authority and the right information**
- make it unambiguous **who answers** for the business case, for delivery and for benefits
- create a **working escalation route**, so an issue beyond one role's limits has somewhere to go
- let people be **empowered inside clear boundaries** rather than waiting on permission for everything

## The roles the syllabus names

| Role | Core responsibility |
|---|---|
| **Sponsor** | Accountable for good governance and for the work meeting its objectives and the organisation's needs. Owns the vision and business case, secures funding, is accountable for benefits, and is the project manager's first point of escalation. |
| **Project manager** | Responsible for day-to-day delivery of the agreed outputs — planning, managing the work, the team and the resources, controlling progress, and escalating what exceeds their delegated authority. |
| **Project steering group / board** | Oversees performance and makes the decisions above the project manager's authority. Represents financial, provider and user interests. |
| **Project team members** | Deliver the work packages assigned to them, to the agreed quality, and report progress and problems honestly and early. |
| **Users** | Represent the operational reality the outputs must work in. Specify and validate requirements, take part in testing and acceptance, and ultimately accept the deliverables at transition. |
| **Product owner** | Used in iterative life cycles. Represents the user, prioritises what gets built next, and accepts outputs on the user's behalf. |

Two cautions worth carrying:

- **The product owner is an iterative-life-cycle role.** If a scenario describes sprints, a backlog and incremental delivery, a product owner belongs there. In a linear project, sign-off is usually the sponsor's or client's.
- **Users are not the same as the sponsor.** The sponsor represents the *investment*; users represent the *operational use*. A project can satisfy one and fail the other, and that failure mode is a common exam scenario.

## What the governance board actually does

The board discharges its responsibility by:

- watching progress, and checking the work still **lines up with organisational strategy**
- keeping an eye on whether the **benefits** are actually going to land
- keeping an eye on **risk**
- tracking performance through reports, assurance and audit, and testing it against **objective metrics** rather than reassurance
- signing off **corrective action** where performance has drifted, and approving any **major departure from the plan**
- **deciding change requests**, and passing them up the chain when they exceed its own authority
- making sure the project stays inside **policy, regulation, statutory duty and professional and ethical standards**
- taking the formal **go/no-go call at each decision gate**

Its responsibilities and authority are set out in **terms of reference**, usually written by the sponsor, which also define escalation routes for decisions beyond the board's authority.

**Two common models** — know both, because a scenario will describe one of them:

1. **The board is the primary governance body.** Authority is delegated to the board itself, and the sponsor sits on it as one member among several.
2. **The sponsor is the primary source of governance.** Authority is delegated to the sponsor personally, and the board exists to advise them.

Where a project needs so many experts that the board becomes unwieldy, the answer is a **small decision-making board supported by a wider steering group in an advisory role only**.

## Sponsor versus project manager, across the life cycle

This is the sharpest, most frequently examined comparison in the LO. The clean split: **the sponsor is accountable for the project being worth doing; the project manager is responsible for it being done.**

| Phase | Sponsor | Project manager |
|---|---|---|
| **Before / concept** | Identifies needs and requirements, establishes the business case, secures funding, and often selects and appoints the project manager | Frequently not yet appointed |
| **Definition** | Approves the plan and confirms the business case still stands | Plans the work — estimating, scheduling, resourcing, risk |
| **Deployment** | Leads day-to-day governance: oversight, decisions, interfacing between organisation and project. First point of escalation | Manages delivery, the team and the plan; controls progress; escalates beyond delegated limits |
| **Transition** | Ensures the work is properly closed out, oversees handover to operations | Completes handover, closes the project, captures lessons |
| **After** | Remains accountable for **benefits realisation**, during and after delivery | Role has normally ended |

**Two facts that carry marks:**

- The sponsor's role **starts before and continues after** the project manager's.
- The sponsor's engagement **fluctuates, peaking at the initial and final stages** — heavy at the start setting the project up, lighter in the middle, heavy again at closure and benefits.

## What makes a sponsor effective

Beyond the governance duties, sponsorship is a leadership, management, communications and coaching role — supporting the project manager, motivating the wider team through difficult periods, and engaging influential and senior stakeholders.

An effective sponsor is a decision-maker who can work across organisational boundaries, carries enough authority to commit the organisation funding the work, is a genuine advocate for the change, commits enough time to the role, understands project practice well enough to challenge the project manager intelligently, and is aware enough of their own gaps to bring in expertise where needed.

That last point is the one candidates forget: **a sponsor who cannot challenge the project manager competently is a governance weakness**, not a harmless one.

core_content.key_takeaway: Policies, processes, procedures and delegated responsibilities exist to make decisions consistent, compliant, auditable and fast enough. The life cycle decides where control points sit: decision gates between phases in linear, an end-of-iteration review in iterative.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Why each mechanism exists

The syllabus lists the mechanisms; the marks are in saying what each one is *for*. Learn the purpose column, not the list.

| Mechanism | Why it is required |
|---|---|
| **Policies** | Set the organisation's non-negotiable positions, so every project applies the same standard without renegotiating it each time |
| **Regulations and statutory obligations** | Compliance is not optional. A project that ignores them exposes the organisation to legal, financial and reputational harm regardless of how well it delivers |
| **Functions** | Give the project access to specialist capability — finance, legal, HR, assurance — rather than each project improvising it |
| **Processes** | Make outcomes repeatable and comparable across projects, so performance can be measured against something |
| **Procedures** | Turn a process into consistent day-to-day practice, so results do not depend on who happens to be doing the work |
| **Delegated responsibilities** | Push decisions to the lowest level that can properly take them, so the project moves at pace without losing control |

Behind all six sits one common thread: **governance records underpin internal and external audit**. Accurate, well-organised and accessible records are essential — a decision nobody can evidence is, for audit purposes, a decision that was never properly made.

## What good governance depends on

Governance runs on **good and timely information** and **fully engaged people**. Sponsors, boards and senior stakeholders can only make informed decisions from robust reporting and good-quality information.

Where work has **multiple owners** — co-owned or co-funded projects — the structure has to hand each stakeholder a share of influence that matches what they have put in, where they sit and what they know — plus somewhere to take a disagreement. Equal say for unequal stakes is a governance design fault.

## Limits of financial authority

Authority is not binary; it is bounded. Governance sets **delegated limits of authority**, and names in advance where anything exceeding them has to go — whether that is an issue, a decision or a change request.

In financial terms this produces a ladder. Each level can commit spend or approve change up to its threshold, and anything beyond it escalates:

| Level | Typically decides |
|---|---|
| **Project manager** | Spend and change within the agreed budget tolerance |
| **Sponsor** | Beyond the project manager's limit; also holds **top-level contingency (management reserve)** |
| **Governance board** | Beyond the sponsor's limit; determines change requests and agrees major departures from plan |
| **Corporate / higher authority** | Beyond the board's terms of reference — the board escalates |

Two things to be precise about in an answer:

- The **sponsor secures funding and top-level contingency**. Management reserve is not the project manager's to spend.
- **Escalation is a designed route, not an admission of failure.** Working within your limit and escalating past it is the system operating correctly.

## How the life cycle changes the governance framework

Governance arrangements have to fit the life cycle chosen — and the structures, standards and levels of rigour should be proportionate to the work. Rigour scaled to a large infrastructure programme, applied to a small internal project, buys nothing and slows everything.

The **principle common to every life cycle**: nothing moves forward until whatever the previous phase was supposed to deliver has actually been delivered. What changes is *where the control point sits* and *how often it happens*.

| | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| **Control point** | Decision gates between life cycle phases | Formal review at the end of each iteration |
| **Frequency** | Few, at fixed phase boundaries | Many, at the end of every cycle |
| **The decision being made** | Go / no-go to enter the next phase | Whether to draw down work for the next cycle |
| **Test applied** | Assurance of the work done, plus integrated plans for the work to come | Whether the **value proposition remains positive** |
| **Consequence** | Change is handled through formal change control between gates | Direction can change every cycle without a change request |

**"The value proposition remains positive"** is the phrase to remember for iterative governance. It captures the real difference: an iterative project is re-justified continuously, and can be stopped at the end of any cycle when it stops being worth continuing. A linear project is justified at gates, and between them the machinery is change control.

This also explains why iterative governance is not lighter, only differently placed. Reviewing every cycle is more frequent oversight, not less — it is just faster and closer to the work.
core_content.outcome_title: Why governance mechanisms are required, and how the life cycle changes them

core_content.key_takeaway: Projects exist to implement strategy. Senior leaders must be able to show how each one contributes to strategic intent, and where a project does not align, its relevance should be questioned — including cancelling it.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Projects are how strategy actually happens

Strategy that stays on a slide changes nothing. Projects, programmes and portfolios flow out of strategic decisions and are the mechanism that turns them into capability, process, technology and, eventually, benefit. Strategy implementation is widely regarded as the hardest part of the strategy process, and it is precisely the domain project professionals work in.

The hierarchy worth being able to sketch:

**Strategic intent** — the constant, long-run direction of travel → **strategy formulation** — how the organisation intends to get there → **strategy implementation** — the projects and programmes that do it.

## Why the link has to be explicit

Senior leaders need to be able to **demonstrate how each project or programme they fund contributes to the overall strategy** and delivers the strategic intent. The corollary is the sharp bit, and it is examinable: **where projects do not align with organisational strategy, executives must question their relevance.**

Read that as intended — a misaligned project is a candidate for cancellation, not for a communications plan. Organisational resources spent on it are resources not spent on something that does advance the strategy.

## What alignment buys, concretely

| Benefit of a clear link | What goes wrong without it |
|---|---|
| Justifies the investment and keeps the business case credible | The project competes for funding on personality and volume, not merit |
| Gives the project a basis for prioritisation against other work | Resource conflicts get settled by whoever escalates loudest |
| Provides a decision rule when scope, cost or schedule must be traded | Trade-offs get made on local convenience |
| Focuses the project on **benefits and value**, not just outputs | The team optimises for delivering the thing, not for the value it was meant to create |
| Lets governance actually govern — the board can review alignment with strategy | The board can only review progress against plan, which says nothing about whether the plan is still worth following |

That last row connects 2d straight back to 2b: checking that the work still serves the organisation's strategy and its strategic intent is a stated duty of the governance board. Without an explicit link, the board cannot perform one of its core duties.

## Not every project is a direct strategic play

A nuance that protects you from over-simplifying in a scenario. Project work may also be an enabler that:

- **creates capabilities or assets** needed for later change initiatives
- **maintains existing capabilities or assets**
- ensures **compliance with new legislation or regulation**
- satisfies **professional, ethical or social imperatives**

A compliance project may show a weak direct return and still be entirely correct to fund. The link to organisational objectives is real; it just runs through licence to operate rather than through growth.

## Who keeps the link alive

Alignment is not a one-off check at approval:

- The **sponsor** ensures the **continuing validity of the business case** — continuing, not initial.
- The **governance board** reviews alignment with strategy as a standing responsibility.
- **Portfolio management** maintains alignment between project work and strategic objectives across the whole set of initiatives, and balances them.
- **Control of direction**, one of the two levels of governance control, exists precisely to assure that the project's goals stay aligned with organisational strategy as the environment shifts.

Strategies evolve as opportunities and threats emerge. A project that was well aligned at approval can drift out of alignment without changing at all — because the strategy moved. That is why the check is periodic, and why 'we got approval' is not an answer to 'is this still worth doing?'
core_content.outcome_title: Linking projects to organisational objectives

misconceptions.right: Governance both empowers and constrains. It defines delegated limits of authority so people can decide without asking permission every time, and gives a clear escalation route when a decision exceeds them. Without it, every decision would have to travel to the top.
misconceptions.wrong: Governance is bureaucracy that slows the project down.

misconceptions.right: They are different accountabilities. The sponsor is accountable for the business case and the benefits — whether the project is worth doing. The project manager is responsible for delivering the agreed outputs — whether it gets done.
misconceptions.wrong: The sponsor and the project manager are basically the same job at different seniorities.

misconceptions.right: The sponsor remains accountable for benefits realisation, during and after delivery. The project manager delivers the outputs that make benefits possible. The sponsor's role continues after the project manager's has ended.
misconceptions.wrong: The project manager is accountable for delivering the benefits.

misconceptions.right: Iterative governance is more frequent, not lighter — a formal review at the end of every iteration rather than a gate at each phase boundary. What changes is where the control point sits and what it tests, not how much oversight there is.
misconceptions.wrong: Iterative projects have lighter governance than linear ones.

misconceptions.right: Matrix is the structure most likely to produce conflicting priorities, because people report to a functional lead and a project manager at the same time. It buys visibility inside the operation and pays for it in split loyalty.
misconceptions.wrong: A matrix structure is the balanced compromise, so it is the safest choice.

misconceptions.right: Boards oversee work in a way consistent with its size and complexity. In one common model the sponsor is the primary source of governance and any board only advises them. Governance rigour should be proportionate to the work.
misconceptions.wrong: Every project needs a governance board.

misconceptions.right: Where the number of experts would make a board unwieldy, a small board makes the decisions and a wider steering group supports it in an advisory role only. The terms overlap in general use, so read the scenario for which function is described.
misconceptions.wrong: A steering group and a decision-making board are the same thing.

misconceptions.right: Project work may instead create or maintain capabilities, ensure compliance with legislation, or satisfy professional, ethical or social imperatives. The link to organisational objectives is still required — it just may run through licence to operate rather than growth.
misconceptions.wrong: Every project must show a direct financial contribution to strategy or it should be cancelled.

misconceptions.right: The sponsor ensures the continuing validity of the business case and the board reviews alignment as a standing duty. Strategy evolves, so a project can drift out of alignment without changing at all.
misconceptions.wrong: Once the business case is approved, strategic alignment is settled.

key_definitions.plain_english: Who is allowed to decide what, who answers for the result, and how decisions get escalated when they exceed someone's authority.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The system by which the organisation and its portfolio, programme and projects are directed and controlled. It is a framework of authority and accountability.

key_definitions.plain_english: The organisation's own rulebook. Project governance has to fit inside it, not compete with it.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The governance of the organisation as a whole, covering vision, mission and strategy, within which business-as-usual governance and business change governance both sit.

key_definitions.plain_english: The business leader who owns the investment. Accountable for the business case and the benefits, before, during and after delivery.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The individual accountable for good governance and for ensuring the work meets its objectives and the organisation's needs. Sometimes known as the senior responsible owner.

key_definitions.plain_english: The group the sponsor usually chairs, representing financial, provider and user interests, that makes the decisions too big for the project manager.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A body that oversees a project, programme or portfolio, reviewing performance and making decisions consistent with the size and complexity of the work. Also called a project board, programme board, steering group or steering committee.

key_definitions.plain_english: The board's job description and its ceiling — what it can decide, and where it has to pass the decision upwards.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The document setting out a governance board's responsibilities and authority, usually developed by the sponsor. It may define specific member roles and escalation routes for decisions beyond the board's authority.

key_definitions.plain_english: How far you can go before you have to ask. Exceed your limit and it becomes someone else's decision, not a judgement call.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The boundaries within which a role may decide, defined by governance, together with a clear escalation route for issues, decisions and change requests that exceed them.

key_definitions.plain_english: The project's own org chart. It exists for the life of the project and then dissolves.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The organisational structure created to manage the activities and resources of a project or programme, delivering specific objectives within predetermined timeframes. It does not typically match the permanent organisation's structure but must be coordinated with it.

key_definitions.plain_english: Three answers to 'who does this person actually work for while the project runs?' — their department, both, or the project.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The three most common temporary structures for projects, each distributing resources differently: functional (resources stay in and report to their function), matrix (resources split reporting between functional lead and project manager), project (resources dedicated to and reporting only to the project).

key_definitions.plain_english: The project org chart in breakdown form. Combined with the WBS it produces the responsibility assignment matrix.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A hierarchical structure created by the choice of organisational structure, visualising the project hierarchy and enabling identification of resource requirements.

key_definitions.plain_english: The grid that stops 'I thought you were doing that'. Often seen as RACI.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A matrix formed by combining the work breakdown structure and the organisational breakdown structure, clarifying which roles are accountable and responsible for activities and decisions, which must be consulted, and which need to be informed.

key_definitions.plain_english: The single voice for what the users want, so an iterative team gets one prioritised list instead of twenty competing opinions.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A role used in iterative life cycles that represents the user, prioritises what is built next, and accepts outputs on the user's behalf.

key_definitions.plain_english: The long-run goal projects are supposed to serve. Strategy changes; strategic intent mostly does not.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The driver to achieve an important outcome, encapsulating the broad direction of travel for the organisation and staying constant over a reasonable period while the ways of achieving it may change.

body.where_this_fits: Governance answers one question: who is allowed to decide what. Everything you learn later that involves a decision — approving a business case, passing a decision gate, accepting a change request, signing off quality, escalating a risk — is really a governance question wearing a different hat. LO1 decided the shape of the project; LO2 decides who controls it. The two are directly linked, and the syllabus says so: the life cycle you chose changes the governance framework you need. Reviews, assurance, change control and business case all sit downstream of this LO, so time spent here pays back four or five times over.
learning_outcomes: 2a) Knowledge of different types of permanent and temporary organisation structures and their features (including functional, matrix, and project), and know that an organisation's governance approach will inform the approach used for a project.

2b) Understand why there are distinct roles within project management and know the responsibilities of each role (including users, project team members, the project manager, the project steering group/board and the product owner), and understand the differences in responsibilities of the project manager and project sponsor throughout the project.

2c) Understand why aspects of project management governance are required (such as the use of policies, regulations, functions, processes, procedures and delegated responsibilities), and understand the impact of a project's life cycle on its governance framework and the limits of financial authority.
2d) Understand the importance of linking projects to an organisation's objectives.
progress_checkpoint: I can define governance as a framework of authority and accountability, and state its two purposes — the right things, done the right way.
I can explain why governance both empowers and constrains, using delegated limits of authority and escalation routes.
I can describe functional, matrix and project structures with one strength and one weakness each, and say how authority shifts across the three.
I can explain why tensions arise between the permanent and temporary organisations, and what the sponsor does about them.
I can name the responsibilities of the sponsor, project manager, governance board, project team members, users and product owner.
I can compare sponsor and project manager responsibilities across the life cycle, including that the sponsor starts earlier, finishes later, and peaks at the start and end.
I can say why policies, regulations, processes, procedures and delegated responsibilities are each required, and explain limits of financial authority as an escalation ladder.

I can contrast decision gates in a linear life cycle with end-of-iteration reviews in an iterative one, including what each one tests, and explain why a project must stay linked to organisational objectives.

core_content.key_takeaway: A business case justifies investment by comparing options on time, cost, risk and benefit across five dimensions — strategic, economic, commercial, financial, management. PESTLE, SWOT and VUCA are the named techniques for identifying the external and internal factors that shape it.
core_content.body_markdown:
## What a business case is for

Every project costs money, so anyone proposing one has to show that the cost, effort and benefit add up to good value for the organisation. The business case is where that argument is made: options evaluated on **time, cost, risks and benefit**, then one recommended.

**Accountability versus the work.** The sponsor is accountable for the business case. In practice, preparing it is usually delegated to project professionals working alongside subject-matter experts. That delegation is treated as good practice rather than a shortcut — it brings the project team into the shaping of the initiative and builds shared understanding early.

## The five dimensions

High-yield. Learn the question each one answers, because scenario questions usually attack one specific dimension.

| Dimension | The question it answers |
|---|---|
| **Strategic** | Is there a compelling case for change, and does it align with the organisation's strategic objectives and other initiatives? |
| **Economic** | Does the return justify the investment — time, cost and resources set against organisational, societal and environmental benefits? |
| **Commercial** | How will it be paid for and how will resources be sourced? Is the deal achievable and attractive in the market? |
| **Financial** | Can the organisation afford it **now**, in the timescales proposed — or should it wait? |
| **Management** | How will the project actually be run — team roles, governance, choice of life cycle, ways of working? |

The distinction candidates most often blur is **economic versus financial**. Economic asks *is it worth it*. Financial asks *can we pay for it now*. A project can be excellent value and still unaffordable this year.

## Business cases are storytelling documents

An unusual point in the source, and worth using because it sounds like judgement and is actually examinable content: the strongest business cases put the technical investment appraisal alongside a **narrative backed by evidence** — how this team, working this way, is going to make it succeed.

The reason is competitive. Most organisations have more problems and opportunities than funding, so decision makers are making trade-offs between viable initiatives. The case has to persuade, not merely calculate.

**Without a clear business case**, decision makers risk funding unsound work — leading to financial losses, reduced productivity, environmental harm and damaged stakeholder confidence.

## How a business case gets created

1. **Define the business need.** Work with the sponsor to state the problem being solved or opportunity being exploited, and link it back to organisational strategy.
2. **Analyse the options.** With subject-matter experts, gather high-level estimates of the work and duration, resources and costs, the risks, and the societal, environmental and sustainability impacts.
3. **Handle the uncertainty.** The case is written early, when detail is thin. Counter that with proven estimating techniques, risk-based contingency planning and third-party assurance.
4. **Agree a recommendation.** Project professionals and sponsor review the options together and put one forward, showing how the work will be achieved — governance approach, chosen life cycle, how sustainability will be managed.
5. **Seek approval.** The sponsor submits it to a defined governance forum — an executive board or investment committee. Approval formally starts the project.

**Rigour scales to the life cycle.** Linear projects tend towards detailed up-front analysis. Iterative approaches use a lighter business case, because the detail arrives as the project progresses. Ties straight back to LO1 and LO2 — and a scenario describing an iterative project buried under a 90-page business case is describing a mismatch.

## The three named techniques

The syllabus names PESTLE, SWOT and VUCA specifically. Each does a different job.

**One line each, before the detail:**

- **PESTLE** — what is going on *outside* that could affect this project?
- **SWOT** — what are we good and bad at, set against what the world is offering and threatening?
- **VUCA** — how predictable are conditions, and therefore how firmly can we plan?

These are general management techniques rather than APM-specific ones. The Body of Knowledge does not set them out as business case tools, so learn them as standard practice the syllabus expects you to know — not as APM doctrine you could quote back.

### PESTLE — scanning the external environment

Six categories of external pressure an organisation must respond to:

| Letter | Factor | Example impact on a business case |
|---|---|---|
| **P** | Political | Change of government policy alters funding or priority |
| **E** | Economic | Interest rates or inflation change cost and affordability |
| **S** | Societal | Shifting public expectations change what counts as an acceptable solution |
| **T** | Technological | A new technology reduces the benefit of the proposed option |
| **L** | Legal | New legislation makes an option non-compliant, or mandatory |
| **E** | Environmental | Emissions targets or environmental regulation reshape the options |

Use it to populate the **strategic and economic cases**, and to surface risks and assumptions early.

**Spelling.** You may see **PESTEL** — identical six factors, letters in a different order. Both are correct. Longer variants exist (STEEPLE adds ethics; PESTLIED adds international and demographic), but PESTLE is what the syllabus names, so use it.

**Using it in an answer:** do not list all six and stop. Pick the two or three the scenario actually turns on and say what each does to the case — 'new emissions legislation (legal, environmental) rules out option B, so the recommendation changes'.

### SWOT — internal capability against external conditions

Four boxes on two axes: internal versus external, helpful versus harmful.

| | Helpful | Harmful |
|---|---|---|
| **Internal** | **Strengths** — capability, skills, assets the organisation already has | **Weaknesses** — gaps, constraints, things done badly |
| **External** | **Opportunities** — conditions the organisation could exploit | **Threats** — conditions that could damage it |

The axis pair is the thing to remember: **strengths and weaknesses are yours; opportunities and threats belong to the world.** Candidates routinely file a competitor as a weakness rather than a threat.

Use it to test whether the recommended option is one the organisation is actually equipped to deliver — which feeds the **management case**.

**Spelling.** SWOT, not SWAT. Four letters, four boxes.

**Using it in an answer:** the value is in the pairings, not the four lists. A strength that lets you seize a named opportunity is a reason to proceed. A weakness that leaves you exposed to a named threat is a risk the business case has to answer.

### VUCA — naming the conditions you are planning under

| Letter | Condition |
|---|---|
| **V** | Volatility |
| **U** | Uncertainty |
| **C** | Complexity |
| **A** | Ambiguity |

Coined by the US military to describe an increasingly vulnerable and unpredictable world. **The key implication: inherent uncertainty makes it difficult to predict and plan with great accuracy.**

The consequence for a business case is direct. Expecting full and perfect knowledge is unattainable in turbulent conditions, and forcing detailed planning and fixed-price contracting onto an uncertain future can be counterproductive and damaging. So under VUCA conditions the sensible responses are flexible plans, iterations, prototyping, options evaluation and scenario planning — and a business case that expects to be revisited.

**Spelling.** VUCA, not VOCA. And the four terms are conditions, not actions.

**Using it in an answer:** name which of the four the scenario shows, then say what it does to the plan. High volatility and ambiguity justify a lighter business case, shorter commitment horizons and iteration — the opposite of a fixed-price contract signed on a detailed up-front specification.

**How the three fit together:** PESTLE finds the external factors, SWOT weighs them against internal capability, VUCA tells you how much confidence to place in either. PESTLE and SWOT populate the case; VUCA sets how firmly you are entitled to write it.

## Investment appraisal — how the economic case gets tested

Investment decisions are part of governance, so they need robust justification. Decision makers balance:

- **Strategic alignment** — do the outcomes fit organisational goals, policy, regulation and legislation?
- **Affordability** — is there enough money both to carry the risks and to land the benefits?
- **Value delivered** — will it return a decent financial figure, or other measurable value, across the economic life of the product?
- **Portfolio effect** — how does this sit among everything else the organisation is already doing?

| Measure type | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Simple** | Value ratio, net benefit, return on investment (ROI) |
| **Time-adjusted** — money now is worth more than money later | Internal rate of return (IRR); net present value (NPV), and its social variant NPSV. All three come out of discounted cash flows (DCF) |
| **Comparators** | Weighted average cost of capital (WACC); organisational **hurdle rates** |

**Non-financial factors matter too** — practicality, maturity of definition, and **decision bias**. Private organisations usually decide on financial grounds; public and non-profit organisations weigh value for money, affordability and service.

One governance point worth carrying: independent review and scrutiny of the investment case should allow for **several possible outcomes rather than one** — particularly early in the life cycle, when uncertainty is at its highest.

core_content.key_takeaway: The business case is a living document providing ongoing evidence the project still delivers value for money. It is reassessed at existing control points — change control, project reviews, stage gates — and significant impacts go to the sponsor, who may seek reapproval or accept the project being stopped.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Why it cannot be a one-off document

Projects run in complex environments where internal and external change happens daily. A case approved on day one describes conditions that no longer exist by month six. So the business case is maintained as a **living document**, continuing to show that the money is still being well spent.

The framing to carry into the exam: the business case does not justify **starting** the project, it justifies **continuing** it, and it has to keep doing that.

## What can undermine a business case

Learn these as five recognisable scenario triggers — a question will describe one of them and ask what you do.

| Event | Effect on the case |
|---|---|
| **New stakeholder requirements** | Additional work and cost |
| **Economic instability** | Changes the cost and availability of resources |
| **Technological advances** | Reduce the benefit of the proposed solution — the option chosen is no longer the best one |
| **Organisational restructuring** | Creates additional risk and uncertainty |
| **Project team changes** | Delays, additional cost, changes in approach |

The technological one is the least intuitive and the most examinable: **the project can be running perfectly and the business case can still collapse**, because something better appeared elsewhere.

## When to review it — use the control points you already have

A project professional cannot spend their time continuously re-examining the business case. Good practice is to reassess viability at governance and control points that already exist:

| Control point | What it tests |
|---|---|
| **Change control** | The impact of requested changes assessed against the project's baseline |
| **Project reviews** | Schedule, resources, scope and budget performance against forecast |
| **Phase / stage-gate reviews** | Whether the project is approved to proceed into the next phase |

That is an efficiency argument, and it is the reason 4b exists as a distinct sub-outcome. Continuous re-justification is not affordable; **piggy-backing the check onto existing decision points is**.

## What happens when something significant lands

1. The project professional brings it to the **sponsor's** attention. This is not a decision to take alone.
2. If the impact is significant, the sponsor may need to update the business case, or return to decision makers for **renewed approval**.
3. Decision makers decide whether the project should **continue or not**.

The hard-edged point, and one that separates a strong answer from an average one: a project may be **asked to pause even when its business case still delivers benefits**, if other initiatives competing for the same resources are considered better value for money. Being worthwhile is not the same as being the best use of constrained resources.

## The business case as baseline

The syllabus asks you to know that the business case forms the baseline for the project. What that means in practice:

- It records the **approved** position — the expected time, cost, risks and benefits at the point of approval.
- Change control assesses proposed changes **against that baseline**, so the case is the reference point for whether a change is acceptable.
- Variance is measured against it. Reviews compare where the project actually is with what was approved.
- In extended life cycles it becomes the yardstick for **benefits realisation** — whether the anticipated benefits actually appeared.

A useful precision, because the exam distinguishes these: the business case baselines **why the project is worth doing and what it will return**. The project management plan baselines **how it will be delivered**. Both are baselines; they answer different questions.

## Feeding lessons back

Where benefits over- or under-perform against the case, the variance is reviewed with the sponsor and the business case updated. Project professionals should then **share lessons learned**, so the next business case rests on better assumptions and sharper estimates.

That closes a loop worth naming in an answer: business cases are written under uncertainty, so the only way they get more accurate as an organisational capability is by feeding real outcomes back into the next one.
core_content.outcome_title: Reviewing the business case, and its role as the project's baseline

misconceptions.right: It is a living document. It provides ongoing evidence that the project still represents value for money, and is reassessed at change control, project reviews and stage gates throughout the life cycle.
misconceptions.wrong: The business case is written once to get approval, then filed.

misconceptions.right: The sponsor is accountable for it. Preparing and maintaining it is often delegated to project professionals, which is considered good practice, but accountability does not move.
misconceptions.wrong: The project manager owns the business case.

misconceptions.right: The economic case asks whether the return justifies the investment. The financial case asks whether the organisation can afford it now, in the timescales proposed. A project can be good value and still unaffordable this year.
misconceptions.wrong: The economic case and the financial case are the same thing.

misconceptions.right: External change can undermine it while delivery is flawless. A technological advance can reduce the benefit of the chosen solution, making a perfectly run project no longer the best use of the money.
misconceptions.wrong: If the project is delivering to plan, the business case is safe.

misconceptions.right: Where several initiatives compete for the same resources, a project may be paused even though its business case still delivers benefits, because others are judged better value for money.
misconceptions.wrong: A project with a positive business case will not be stopped.

misconceptions.right: The rigour depends on organisational culture and the chosen life cycle. Linear projects tend towards detailed up-front analysis; iterative approaches use a lighter case because detail emerges as the project progresses.

misconceptions.right: Its specific implication is that inherent uncertainty makes accurate prediction and planning difficult, which is why detailed planning and fixed-price contracting against an uncertain future can be counterproductive.

key_definitions.plain_english: The argument for spending the money — options weighed, one recommended, and the reasoning left visible so it can be re-tested later.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The justification for undertaking a particular project, programme or portfolio. It evaluates the time, cost, risks and benefit of different options before recommending the best solution to achieve the desired outcome.

key_definitions.plain_english: Five different questions a business case has to survive — is it worth doing, does it pay back, can we buy it, can we afford it now, and can we run it.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The five dimensions a well-rounded business case typically covers: strategic, economic, commercial, financial and management.

key_definitions.plain_english: Approval is not the end of it. The case has to keep being true, and gets rewritten when the facts move.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A business case maintained and updated throughout the life cycle to provide ongoing evidence that the project still delivers value for money, rather than a one-off approval artefact.

key_definitions.plain_english: The financial arithmetic behind the recommendation. Simple measures ignore timing; the sophisticated ones account for money being worth more today than later.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The evaluation of an investment decision using measures such as value ratio, net benefit and return on investment, or time-value measures including net present value, internal rate of return and discounted cash flow.

key_definitions.plain_english: The bar an investment has to clear before it is worth doing at all. Below it, the money is better used elsewhere.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The minimum target return an organisation defines for its investments.

key_definitions.plain_english: A checklist for scanning the outside world. Six headings so you notice the threat that is not in your industry's usual line of sight.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Political, economic, societal, technological, legal and environmental — the categories of external pressure an organisation must respond to.

key_definitions.plain_english: Two internal boxes, two external. What we are good and bad at, set against what the world is offering and threatening.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats — an analysis pairing internal capability against external conditions.

key_definitions.plain_english: A label for conditions where confident forecasting is not available. Naming it stops you writing plans that assume knowledge you do not have.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity — a term coined by the US military to describe conditions in an increasingly vulnerable and unpredictable world. Its key implication is that inherent uncertainty makes it difficult to predict and plan with great accuracy.

key_definitions.plain_english: The numbers may be wrong because someone wanted them to be, or because nobody noticed what they were assuming.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The risk that estimates are unfair, shaped by agendas or prejudices, or that psychological biases and blind spots are influencing decision-making.

key_definitions.plain_english: When the facts move far enough, the original approval no longer covers what the project has become. Someone has to say yes again.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The process by which a sponsor returns to decision makers for a renewed decision when changes significantly impact the timeframe, cost, risk or benefits of the initiative.
