core_content.source_ref: BoK 8e 4.4 (p201), 4.4.1 (p202-203), 3.6.3 (p164); team role and type models from general management theory — see source_confidence
core_content.key_takeaway: A group becomes a team through five stages, and the leader's role changes at each. Individuality has to be allowed to emerge in stage two rather than suppressed — and the reintegration stage at the end is the one most projects skip.
core_content.body_markdown:
## The starting position

**A team that is ready to go almost never turns up.** The job is to **take whoever you were given and make them cohere** — and that phrasing matters, because it acknowledges the constraint: **you rarely get full say over who ends up on it.**

What does help is reputation. **A project professional's reputation strongly influences who wants to come and work for them**, and since the right skills are often hard to get, **the team is frequently developed on the project** — creating future capability and, in turn, enhancing that reputation for next time.

**Treat them as individuals.** Everyone arrives with **different capabilities, different preferences, different cultural expectations**. What team development should produce is **a working culture positive enough to sustain high performance**.

## The five stages

The leader's **role and priorities change as the group matures**. This is the core content of 13a.

| Stage | The team | What the leader does |
|---|---|---|
| **1 — Unstructured group** | Not yet a team | Set out goals and objectives plainly, build an environment nobody is excluded from, and get people working |
| **2 — People assert their individuality** | Differences surface | **Allow differences to emerge**, support open discussion, **resolve conflicts positively** |
| **3 — Team starts to get on** | Settling | Supply structure, process and clarity about who does what — but **let the team settle its own behavioural norms** |
| **4 — Effective team** | Performing | Promote open, honest and trusting relationships. The team collaborates, so the leader **focuses on supporting its work** |
| **5 — Reintegration** | Work complete | **Help team members transition into their next roles** |

**Stage 2 is the one that gets handled badly.** The instruction is to *allow* differences to emerge — not to suppress them in the name of harmony. That is the LO11 argument arriving inside team development: a team that never surfaces its differences goes into stage 3 with them intact and unspoken.

**Stage 5 is the one that gets forgotten.** Reintegration links directly to LO8's administrative closure — new skills recorded, learning put to use elsewhere, HR involved where roles no longer exist.

## As the team matures, management reduces

As a team performs, **there is less to manage and the leader's role gets quieter**. It turns into **servant leadership — supplying whatever the team needs to keep going**.

This is the direct link to LO12's situational leadership. The four styles map onto the maturity of the team, and stage 4 is where **trusting** applies.

## Factors that influence the stages

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Who you get** | Little control over team membership; skills often developed on the project rather than recruited |
| **Individual differences** | Capabilities, preferences, cultural norms and expectations all differ |
| **Whether conflict is allowed to surface** | Stage 2 depends on differences emerging and conflicts being resolved positively |
| **Role fit** | Assigning people to roles that **suit them, match their strengths, or offer development** |
| **Variety in the work** | Some project tasks are **dull and teach nobody anything**, so roles have to be built with variety and learning in them |
| **Support provided** | **Training, coaching and mentoring** |
| **Co-located or dispersed** | Changes how relationships and trust form — see 13c |
| **Multi-organisation membership** | Consultants, suppliers, partners and client staff bring different loyalties and norms |
| **Temporary nature** | People **return to business-as-usual roles** afterwards, which shapes their engagement throughout |
| **Pressure and wellbeing** | Motivating pressure can **become unbearable, and overload leads to damaging stress** |

## Building resilience through role design

A practical technique worth knowing: distinguish **process** work from **technical** work. **It is easy to train someone into a process role with little technical content** — the example given is a business analyst working on requirements capture taking on a risk analysis role.

The payoff is threefold: **role variety**, **skills built**, and **team resilience** — and it gives people **a feel for what the rest of the team actually does**.

## The models the syllabus names

**Read this before learning them.** The syllabus names six models for 13a. **Four of them do not appear in the Body of Knowledge at all** — Belbin, Margerison McCann, Myers-Briggs, and Katzenbach and Smith all return zero occurrences. **Tuckman appears only as a figure attribution**, and **Hackman only in a recommended-reading title**. Treat all of them as general management theory the exam expects, not as APM doctrine.

### Tuckman — stages of group development

The five stages above are explicitly **inspired by Tuckman's model**, so the mapping is worth holding:

| Tuckman | BoK stage | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Forming** | 1 — Unstructured group | Polite, uncertain, dependent on the leader |
| **Storming** | 2 — Asserting individuality | Differences and conflict surface |
| **Norming** | 3 — Starting to get on | Norms and roles settle |
| **Performing** | 4 — Effective team | Collaborative, largely self-managing |
| **Adjourning** | 5 — Reintegration | The team disbands and members move on |

Teams can **move back down** as well as up — a change of membership or objective can push a performing team back into storming.

### Belbin — team roles

Nine roles a person tends towards, grouped in three:

| Group | Roles |
|---|---|
| **Thinking** | Plant, Monitor Evaluator, Specialist |
| **Action** | Shaper, Implementer, Completer Finisher |
| **People** | Coordinator, Teamworker, Resource Investigator |

**The usable idea:** an effective team needs a spread of roles, not nine copies of the same one. It echoes LO12's point that a leader assembles people whose strengths cover their own weak spots.

### Margerison McCann — team management profile

Maps preferences around a wheel of work functions — advising, innovating, promoting, developing, organising, producing, inspecting, maintaining, with linking at the centre. **The usable idea:** teams often over-invest in the work they enjoy and leave a gap elsewhere on the wheel.

### Myers-Briggs — personality type preferences

Four preference pairs — extraversion/introversion, sensing/intuition, thinking/feeling, judging/perceiving. **The usable idea:** differences in how people take in information and reach decisions are preferences, not deficiencies. Directly relevant to LO12's warning that people **view others through their own lens**.

### Katzenbach and Smith — team performance curve

Distinguishes a **working group** from a **real team**, and plots a curve from working group → pseudo-team → potential team → real team → high-performing team. **The usable idea:** a **pseudo-team performs worse than a working group**, because it has the coordination overhead of a team without the shared commitment. Calling a group a team does not make it one.

### Hackman — enabling conditions

Focuses on the conditions that let a team succeed — a real team with clear boundaries, a compelling direction, an enabling structure, a supportive context and expert coaching. **The usable idea:** most team performance is decided by set-up, not by intervention once running.
core_content.outcome_title: Stages of team development and the models used to understand it

core_content.key_takeaway: Effective teams collaborate and communicate well, pursue their own development, innovate and challenge one another, are efficient and productive, and become largely self-managing and self-motivating — which is what lets the leader step back.
core_content.body_markdown:
## The five characteristics

A team that is performing tends to show all five of these:

| Characteristic | What it looks like in practice |
|---|---|
| **Collaborate and communicate well** | Information moves without being chased; people work across role boundaries |
| **Pursue their own development** | Learning is not something the leader has to impose |
| **Innovate and challenge one another** | The LO11 link — **positive conflict is present**, so weak ideas get tested |
| **Be efficient and productive** | Output per unit of effort rises as coordination overhead falls |
| **Become largely self-managing and self-motivating** | Direction is needed less often, and motivation does not depend on the leader supplying it |

That third characteristic is the one to notice. **An effective team challenges one another** — which means an absence of challenge is a symptom, not a sign of health. A team where nobody argues is displaying the groupthink failure state from LO11.

## The benefits

| Benefit | Why it follows |
|---|---|
| **The need for team management reduces** | The leader's role becomes **more subtle — a servant leadership role providing resources** |
| **The leader's time is freed** | For stakeholder engagement, decisions, and developing the team further |
| **Better decisions** | Diversity of thinking plus challenge produces better group decisions than individuals reach alone |
| **Resilience** | Where people have skills that **can cover for colleagues**, absence and turnover hurt less |
| **Future organisational capability** | People **leave with enhanced skills and experience**, taking that capability into their next role |
| **Reputation** | A team developed well **enhances the leader's reputation for future projects**, which influences who wants to join next time |
| **Wellbeing** | A team that looks out for one another spots overload earlier |

## What makes a team effective

Drawing the conditions together from across the source:

- **Clear goals and objectives** established from stage 1, and an **inclusive environment**.
- **Structure, process and clear roles and responsibilities** provided at stage 3 — but with the team **developing its own behavioural norms** rather than having them imposed.
- **Open, honest and trusting relationships** promoted at stage 4.
- **Roles that suit people** — matching strengths or offering development — with **variety and opportunities to learn**, because some project work is neither exciting nor developmental.
- **Support through training, coaching and mentoring.**
- **Differences allowed to emerge and conflicts resolved positively**, rather than suppressed.
- **Attention to wellbeing**, because pressure that was motivating can **become unbearable**.

## The temporary-team dimension

Project teams are **temporary, formed for a specific purpose**, and **their transitory nature brings different challenges from business-as-usual teams.**

Two consequences for effectiveness:

- **There is less time.** A permanent team can take a year to reach stage 4; a project team may not have one. That is an argument for deliberate team development rather than waiting for it to happen.
- **People are thinking about what comes next.** Members **return to business-as-usual roles** when the work finishes, and should **ideally leave with enhanced skills and experience, without losing out in terms of advancement.** Where an organisation cannot place people at closure, LO8's warning applies — talent leaves, and people start exiting projects early to stay employed.

## Wellbeing as an effectiveness issue

**Project work can be genuinely exciting — fast, pressured, delivering good work against the time and money available.** But **the same pressure that was energising can tip into something people cannot carry, and that overload does real damage.**

**Looking after the team, and yourself, is a duty rather than a nicety** — which means being able to **spot workplace stress, reduce it, and handle it when it appears**.

Worth treating as a performance factor rather than a welfare footnote — a team under sustained overload will not display any of the five characteristics above.
core_content.outcome_title: Characteristics and benefits of effective teams

core_content.key_takeaway: Distance removes what co-location supplies for free — trust, informal conversation, visible signs of conflict and of distress. Virtual leadership starts with style and mindset, then norms, then technology. Technology is an enabler and is not enough by itself.
core_content.body_markdown:
## What co-location gives you

Worth stating first, because the challenges are all consequences of losing it. Where teams share a place, you get **one room where the plans and the progress are up on the wall**, and **relationships that grow close through proximity**.

**A dispersed team is one split across places, and often across time zones too** — virtual or remote are the other names for it. **The technology has made this both more common and less painful**, and **home working rose in many organisations after the COVID-19 pandemic.**

## The hybrid rule

A specific and highly examinable instruction: **run it as a dispersed team even if most of the people happen to sit together.** Doing so hands **the same access and the same opportunities to everyone, as nearly as that can be managed.**

That is the answer to a hybrid-team scenario. Running the meeting in the room and dialling the remote people in creates two classes of membership. Treating everyone as remote levels it.

## The seven challenges

| Challenge | What is lost |
|---|---|
| **Trust and relationships** | **Depth and trust are harder to build through a screen than face to face** |
| **Communication** | Degrades, taking **understanding and empathy** down with it |
| **Spotting and resolving conflict** | Harder to see conflict developing, and harder to resolve it |
| **Less positive conflict** | The result is **less constructive challenge** — the LO11 failure state, arriving by default rather than by culture |
| **Informal conversation** | The **unplanned talk that happens around a kettle or a corridor** disappears, and with it goes some **connection and sense of shared responsibility** |
| **Development, productivity and wellbeing** | Personal and professional development and productivity can suffer; **being isolated and lonely through the working day harms wellbeing**, and **those problems are much harder to notice and address at a distance** |
| **Diversity and practicalities** | **Differences in culture and language, generational differences**, and the practical problem of **different time zones** |

The fourth row is the one worth carrying into an answer, because it is not obvious: distance does not only reduce communication, it specifically reduces the *productive disagreement* a team needs. Silence on a call reads as consent far more easily than silence in a room.

The response the source gives: **hearing out every individual, and understanding how they see it, matters more here than it would in a room.**

## Why the leadership approach must differ

**Tools enable this; they do not deliver it.** Virtual leadership is built from the middle outward, and **what sits in the middle is leadership style and a virtual mindset**:

| Layer | What it requires |
|---|---|
| **1. Style and mindset** | **Facilitating rather than directing** when working with remote colleagues and stakeholders. Knowing **what people prefer and what they can do**, and **how trust gets built and kept** |
| **2. Team norms** | Agreement on how the team will **communicate, collaborate and challenge** — reached with **everyone's preferences in the room** |
| **3. Technology** | Only then can technology **implement team processes** |

The ordering is the answer to 13c. A leader who starts with tool selection has begun at layer three and skipped the two that decide whether it works.

**A facilitative approach specifically** — which connects to LO10's facilitation content. Remaining neutral, drawing out contributions, ensuring everyone can contribute and be heard. Those skills are optional in a room where people interrupt naturally; they are load-bearing on a call.

## What technology has to be evaluated for

| Area | What it must support |
|---|---|
| **Virtual meetings** | Talking, facilitating, sharing information, reaching consensus, capturing notes |
| **Workload management** | Identifying tasks, allocating them, tracking them |
| **Collaboration** | Working on things together, holding a dialogue, getting at documents |

**A social element, a clear process and a facilitative approach all improve a virtual meeting.** The social element is deliberate, not decoration — it is the replacement for the informal conversation that distance removed.

## The organising principle

The source states it plainly, and it is the best single line to end a 13c answer on: **much of leading a dispersed team consists of rebuilding, by other means, whatever people would have got for free from sharing a room.**

Everything else follows from that. Trust that would have formed naturally has to be built deliberately. Challenge that would have happened over a desk has to be invited explicitly. Distress that would have been visible has to be asked about.
core_content.outcome_title: Leading virtual and hybrid teams

core_content.source_ref: BoK 8e 4.5 (p209), 4.5.1 (p210); protected characteristics from the Equality Act 2010 — see source_confidence
core_content.key_takeaway: Diversity is the full range of human difference, wider than any legal list. The syllabus names characteristics from UK equality law — those define the legal floor, and project professionals are expected to go beyond it to inclusion and belonging.
core_content.body_markdown:
## What diversity means here

**Diversity is about spanning the widest possible range of people.** The dimensions the source names:

- ethnicity and race
- social class
- age
- gender, and gender identity
- sexual orientation
- the languages people speak
- mental health
- faith or religion
- ability, both physical and mental
- neurodivergence

Note how wide that is. **Class, language and neurodivergence** all appear, and none of them is a legally protected characteristic in the UK. Diversity as a concept is broader than the law's list.

## The five terms to keep separate

The source introduces five, and the exam can test the distinctions between them.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Diversity** | Having the broadest range of different people |
| **Inclusion** | Creating an environment where everyone feels welcome |
| **Belonging** | Everyone feeling the environment is *theirs*, not somewhere they were let into |
| **Advocacy** | Using your voice on behalf of a group being marginalised or discriminated against |
| **Allyship** | Backing people from marginalised groups |

The progression from diversity → inclusion → belonging is the one to hold. Each is a step further, and each is harder.

## The characteristics named in the syllabus

The syllabus lists characteristics **which may cause a person to be treated less favourably**:

| Characteristic |
|---|
| **Age** |
| **Disability** |
| **Marriage and civil partnership** |
| **Pregnancy and maternity** |
| **Race** |
| **Religion or belief** |
| **Sex** |
| **Sexual orientation** |

These are protected characteristics under the **Equality Act 2010**, which is where the framing comes from — not from the Body of Knowledge.

**Two things worth knowing precisely:**

1. **The Act protects nine characteristics; the syllabus list names eight.** The one not listed is **gender reassignment**. The syllabus says 'such as', so the list is illustrative rather than complete — learn all nine, because the ninth is equally protected in law.
2. **This is the legal floor, not the goal.** **Plenty of countries make discrimination unlawful — the expectation on a project professional runs past that, into owning inclusion and belonging.** Compliance with the Act stops you being unlawful. It does not produce a team where people can contribute.

## Why the legal frame is not enough on its own

The source's position is that **teams are stronger for their differences**, and that they **do best where people are valued for their capabilities instead of being run down for their weak spots.**

That is a performance argument rather than a compliance one — and it is the argument the exam is more interested in. LO14b and 14c both build on it.

## The jurisdiction point

Worth carrying, because scenarios can be set anywhere: **some jurisdictions require diversity, inclusion and cultural-difference training by law**, and **in many places certain expressions of conscious bias are themselves unlawful** — putting both the individual and the organisation **at risk of prosecution**.

The source's own instruction where that arises: **if unsure, project professionals should always seek advice.** That is the correct answer in any scenario where the legal position is uncertain — not a guess about what the law requires.
core_content.outcome_title: What diversity covers, and the characteristics that attract less favourable treatment

core_content.key_takeaway: Different people interpret situations through different filters, which produces more perspectives, broader skills, better problem-solving, more creativity and more robust decisions. But diversity only pays out where inclusion lets those perspectives be heard.
core_content.body_markdown:
## The mechanism

**The benefits of diversity are proven** — but knowing *why* is what earns marks. The mechanism is this: **people genuinely perceive the world differently, and read the same situation through unlike filters.** The result is **a different angle on every part of a project, programme or portfolio.**

Everything else follows from that single fact.

## The benefits

| Benefit | How it arises |
|---|---|
| **More perspectives** | Different backgrounds and cultures bring different experiences to bear on the same problem |
| **Broader skills** | **Irrelevant-seeming capabilities find useful applications** in project work, making the team more adaptable |
| **More effective problem-solving** | More approaches available to any given problem |
| **Greater creative thinking and innovation** | The direct answer to the second half of 14b |
| **More robust decision-making** | Options get tested from more angles before being chosen |
| **Deeper empathy with end users** | **The more a team resembles the community it is building for**, the better it designs and delivers something those users actually need |
| **Strong community** | An inclusive environment produces a **stronger sense of community within the team** |
| **Greater adaptability and resilience** | A broader range of personalities, experiences and skills lets a team **tolerate and support one another and thrive under stress**, and **absorb a shock through fresh thinking, moving fast, and backing each other** |

## 'From team members to customers'

The syllabus phrase matters. Diversity is not only an internal staffing question — the **deeper empathy with end users** benefit is about the *output*, not the working environment.

A team that resembles the people it is building for understands them better. A team that does not will make confident assumptions about users it has never met, and those assumptions end up in the product. That is a delivery risk, not only an ethical one.

## The equation that organises the whole LO

The source is unusually direct here, and this is the highest-value thing in 14b:

| Combination | Result |
|---|---|
| **Diversity without inclusion** | Leaders **cannot get the best from people** — the perspectives are present but cannot be heard |
| **Inclusion without diversity** | **Comfortable, short on new ideas, short on challenge, and poorly attuned to the society the project exists to serve** |
| **Diversity with inclusion** | **Enhanced team performance and better results** |

That middle row is the one candidates never think of. A warm, welcoming, entirely homogeneous team is not the safe option — it is the groupthink condition from LO11 with better manners.

## Why project professionals specifically can do this

A point some candidates dismiss: it is easy to assume a project manager has no real purchase on organisational culture. The source rejects that.

**A project team gets built with a culture of its own**, which puts **its wellbeing in the project professional's hands** — and **assembling a diverse team is frequently a choice available to them**, with enough control to make that team an inclusive one.

A temporary team is built from scratch. That is an opportunity a line manager inheriting a permanent department does not get.

## Building an inclusive environment

**Start at the entry point.** **Inclusion starts with ensuring there are no barriers to entry**, which probably means **measuring who applies, who gets appointed, and who stays — particularly from underrepresented groups**. Retention as well as appointment — hiring people into an environment they then leave is not inclusion.

**At hiring:**

- **capability-based requirements** set for each role
- **open recruitment** wherever possible
- **blinded CVs** where possible — names, genders, ages and other personal identifiers removed before review
- a deliberate call on whether you are **recruiting the strongest individuals or assembling the strongest team**, with perspectives balanced across it

That last one is a genuine judgement call and a good scenario answer: the strongest individuals do not automatically compose the strongest team.

**Once the team exists:**

| Action | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Training** in diversity, inclusion and cultural differences | Mandatory in some jurisdictions, good practice everywhere |
| **Periodic surveys** | Feedback on how the team actually feels, rather than how you assume they feel |
| **Meeting structure and facilitation** | So everyone can contribute **and people listen** |
| **Echo and attribute** | **Where a contribution is not acknowledged, repeat the point and attribute it to the speaker** |
| **Recognition and celebration** | Give recognition for collaboration and celebrate wins together |
| **Mentoring and sponsorship** | Gives people a route through the culture and someone to raise difficulties with. **Not everyone finds it easy to promote themselves**, and a sponsor can make sure their achievements get aired |
| **Advocacy** | Speaking up for someone being denied due respect — though **it can strip power from the person, however kindly meant** |
| **Allyship** | Supporting people **without speaking for them** — helping them secure a platform to speak for themselves. **Check first that support is wanted, and what form it should take** |
| **Speak out** | **If you see prejudice, discrimination or disrespect, say so** |

**The 'echo and attribute' technique is small and specific enough to be worth naming in an answer.** So is the advocacy-versus-allyship distinction: advocacy speaks *for* someone, allyship helps them speak. The source flags that advocacy can disempower, which is why allyship is usually the better default.

**And on leadership:** the job is to **set the standard and call out breaches of it. Everyone needs a line they will hold, and the willingness to challenge whoever steps over it.**

core_content.key_takeaway: Conscious bias is deliberate and sometimes illegal; unconscious bias is subtle, harder to spot and operates without awareness. Three strategies address both. And fairness is not treating everyone the same — it is adapting to each person's needs.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Where bias comes from

**Human beings are most at ease around people who resemble them.** That is the root, and stating it matters — bias is not presented as a moral failing found in bad people, but as a default human tendency that everyone has to work against.

It leads to **discrimination**, whose sources are **prejudice** and **bias**:

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Discrimination** | One person treated more or less favourably than another |
| **Prejudice** | Reaching a view **before the relevant facts are in**, usually off stereotypes or perceptions that have dated |
| **Bias** | Favouring or disfavouring someone, or their ideas, **on something other than the merits** |

**Fairness, respect and wellbeing all suffer from either one.**

## Conscious versus unconscious

| | Conscious (explicit) bias | Unconscious (implicit) bias |
|---|---|---|
| **Awareness** | People **are aware of it and express it deliberately** | Operates **below conscious awareness** — people do not know it is happening |
| **Roots** | Upbringing, social conditioning, experiences, cultural norms | Beliefs, stereotypes and assumptions |
| **How it shows** | People or groups **discriminated against, excluded or harassed** because of who they are | Affects **selection, recognition, working relationships and decision-making** |
| **Legal exposure** | **In many jurisdictions some expressions are illegal**, exposing individuals and organisations to **risk of prosecution** | Harder to identify, and correspondingly harder to police |
| **Difficulty** | Easier to spot, harder to excuse | **More subtle and harder to identify** |

**Handling conscious bias** — three specific actions:

1. **Enforce strict anti-discrimination policies.**
2. **Give people a route to report misconduct.**
3. **Act quickly on anything that raises concern.**

And where the legal position is unclear: **always seek advice.**

## Four common causes of unconscious bias

| Cause | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| **Fear** | Of difference, of competition, or of failure |
| **Shortcuts** | Snap judgements that never get examined |
| **Reluctance** | Unwillingness to learn about people, to unlearn habits, or to change |
| **Perceptions** | Getting it wrong about what is right or what is expected |

## Why bias is a project risk, not only an ethical problem

The source makes this argument explicitly, and it is the strongest framing available for a scenario answer:

- Bias leads to **unfair hiring, opportunities and advancement**.
- That harms individuals **and misses out on access to talent**.
- It makes the workplace **hostile**. **Instances that look trivial still leave people feeling unwelcome and undervalued**, and that costs **morale, productivity and welfare**.
- It **skews choices that affect delivery, drives stakeholders away, and can leave a situation misrepresented**.
- **Projects, programmes and portfolios end up at risk because of it.**

That final sentence is the one to reach for. Bias is a delivery risk with a named mechanism, not a soft topic bolted onto the syllabus.

## The three strategies

This is the directly examinable list for 14c.

| Strategy | What it involves |
|---|---|
| **Awareness and education** | Talking openly about diversity and inclusion, and **bringing in expert training** |
| **Inclusive processes** | Structure in **how decisions get made, how people are hired, how communication is planned** |
| **Constant vigilance** | **Holding a culture of belonging in place through feedback, accountability and individual responsibility** |

The middle one is the most practically useful. Because unconscious bias operates without awareness, **good intentions cannot detect it** — only structured process can. That is why blinded CVs, capability-based role requirements and structured decision-making appear as remedies rather than 'try harder to be fair'.

And 'constant' in the third strategy is doing real work. **Project professionals must constantly apply these strategies** — bias is not addressed once and closed out.

## What fairness actually means

The single most important line in 14c, and the one most likely to be misunderstood:

> **Treating everyone identically is not what fairness means. Fairness means adjusting to what each person needs and prefers.**

Identical treatment is not fair treatment. Someone who needs a written agenda in advance to contribute well, or a different meeting time, or a screen reader, is not being given an advantage when they get it — they are being given the same opportunity to contribute that others already had.

This maps directly onto the syllabus wording for 14c: **adapting behaviours to support individuals' needs and facilitate their contributions.**

## Facilitating contributions in practice

Drawing the specific techniques together:

- **Structure meetings and facilitate** so everyone can contribute — **and so people listen**.
- **Echo an unacknowledged contribution and attribute it to the speaker.**
- **Mentoring and sponsorship**, particularly because **self-promotion is less comfortable for some people**.
- **Allyship over advocacy** where possible — help people speak for themselves rather than speaking for them, and **ask first whether help is wanted and how**.
- **Periodic surveys** to find out how people actually feel.
- **Speak out** when you see prejudice, discrimination or disrespect.
core_content.outcome_title: Conscious and unconscious bias, and treating people fairly

key_definitions.plain_english: The range of difference present in a group. Much wider than the legally protected list.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Having the broadest range of different people. It includes race and ethnicity, class, age, gender and gender identity, sexual orientation, language, mental health, religion, physical and mental ability, and neurodivergence.

key_definitions.plain_english: Making it possible for the people who are there to actually take part.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Creating an environment where everyone feels welcome.

key_definitions.plain_english: One step past inclusion. Not 'you are welcome here' but 'this is yours too'.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Making everyone feel that this is their environment — people do not feel the need to 'fit in', because the team accepts and values their differences.

key_definitions.plain_english: Using your voice for someone who is not being heard — while being aware it can disempower, even when well meant.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Speaking up for a group or individual who is marginalised, discriminated against, or not getting the respect they deserve.

key_definitions.plain_english: Handing over the microphone rather than using it on someone's behalf. Ask first whether help is wanted, and how.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Supporting people from marginalised groups — not by speaking for them, but by helping them secure a platform to speak for themselves.

key_definitions.plain_english: Different treatment for reasons unrelated to what someone can do.
key_definitions.apm_definition: When one person is treated more or less favourably than another. Its sources are prejudice and bias.

core_content.key_takeaway: Requirements are gathered, analysed and validated, prioritised, then baselined — and reviewed regularly thereafter. Success criteria and benefits are different things, and requirements must be SMART, clear and unambiguous to be testable at handover.
core_content.body_markdown:
## What requirements management is for

It means finding out **what stakeholders want and need, working out which of it holds up, and ranking what remains**. Requirements that are both thorough and achievable become **the yardstick the project gets measured against** — they shape **the benefits, the objectives, and the acceptance criteria**.

**Requirements and scope are inseparable.** You cannot describe the work to be done — the scope — without first knowing what the stakeholders are asking the project for. **Neither exists without the other.** That is the direct answer to how requirements management establishes scope.

## Requirements evolve in detail through the life cycle

| Stage | What requirements do |
|---|---|
| **Early life cycle** | **High-level requirements** show how the change aligns with organisational strategy and help define what success looks like. They help sponsoring stakeholders **draw out the benefits, confirming they are realistic, attainable and measurable** — feeding early decision-making and the **business case** |
| **As the project progresses** | **Finer-grained requirements** emerge as project professionals work alongside subject-matter experts, defining **objectives and acceptance criteria** and linking back to the identified benefits and success criteria |

**Rigour varies by life cycle.** **Heavy rigour up front suits some projects; others do better letting requirements evolve** — the same linear-versus-iterative split as everywhere else.

## Success criteria versus benefits

Highly examinable, and a genuine conceptual distinction.

| | Success criteria | Benefits |
|---|---|---|
| **What** | The satisfaction of stakeholder needs, measured against criteria agreed at the start | **Positive and measurable improvements delivered by change**, focused on **strategic intent** |
| **Example** | An office building is refurbished | Maintenance costs fall (**tangible**); staff morale improves (**intangible**) |
| **When known** | At **project handover** | Often only once the product is **adopted and embedded into business as usual** (in a linear life cycle) |
| **Accountable** | The **project manager** | The **project sponsor** |

That accountability split is the single most quotable fact in 16a.

**And the consequence:** **a project can deliver its success criteria and fail to deliver the benefits.** **And the reverse happens too — benefits land, yet the project is remembered as a failure.** The two are measured separately, so they can diverge.

**Stakeholders may have different views of success.** The project professional's role is to:

- **draw out how different people are defining success and benefit**
- **broker a shared position, so far as one is available**

'As far as possible' is doing real work there — total agreement is not always available, and the job is to get as close as the situation allows and make the remaining differences visible.

**Success criteria can change**, but only **subject to formal approval** — change control, per LO24. In an **iterative** environment, shifting success criteria are **easier to absorb**, because steady contact with end users lets the team **learn and adapt as it goes**.

## What makes a good requirement

Project professionals ensure that:

- **benefits, success criteria, objectives and requirements all connect visibly to each other**
- **the objectives are spelled out, and stakeholders have agreed them**
- **each requirement is unambiguous, and put as plainly as it can be**

That chain — benefits → success criteria → objectives → requirements — is worth memorising as a chain. Every requirement should be traceable back up it.

**The test: SMART.**

| Letter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **S** | Specific |
| **M** | Measurable |
| **A** | Achievable |
| **R** | Relevant |
| **T** | Time-based |

**Measures make acceptance possible.** The source's example: a requirement (speed of ship) plus a measure (greater than 12 knots) is what lets a deliverable **actually be accepted when it transfers to users**. A requirement without a measure cannot be accepted or rejected — it can only be argued about.

**But not everything measures easily.** A benefit the sponsor wants **can generate a requirement that resists easy measurement** — the example given being **delivering the work in an environmentally sustainable way**. Acknowledging that difficulty is better than pretending a soft requirement is hard.

## The four-step process

The process **first establishes a requirements baseline, then regularly reviews it**.

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1. Identify stakeholders and gather requirements** | Work out who the stakeholders are by **looking at which parts of the business gain from the change or are hit by it**. Settle how you will capture requirements — **workshops, surveys** — then go and get their first view |
| **2. Analyse, validate and align** | **A proposed requirement is not automatically accepted.** Analyse thoroughly for **dependencies, risks and constraints**; validate each one; check it **aligns with project objectives and contributes to broader organisational aims** |
| **3. Prioritise** | **The list almost always exceeds what can actually be built.** Use **MoSCoW**, ranking on **value, benefit, cost, risk and size**. Stakeholders agree the prioritisation, and **the initial baseline is set** |
| **4. Review and reprioritise regularly** | As more information emerges, review and reprioritise. **New requirements follow the same analysis, validation and alignment** before being consolidated into an updated baseline |

The syllabus phrases this as **gather, analysis, justifying requirements and baseline needs** — the same four steps under different labels. 'Justifying' is step 2's validation: proving a requirement earns its place.

**Step 2 is the one that carries the marks.** Stakeholders propose; the project analyses and validates. A requirements process that simply records what people asked for has skipped its most valuable step.

## MoSCoW

| Category | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Must have** | Non-negotiable — the project fails without it |
| **Should have** | Important but not vital; there is a workaround |
| **Could have** | Desirable; included if capacity allows |
| **Won't have** | Explicitly excluded **this time** |

The fourth category is the useful one. **Won't have is a decision that was taken and recorded**, not a requirement that got lost — which prevents it reappearing later as an assumed inclusion.

## When reviews happen

**Frequency should be project-specific**, though in practice they cluster around **the moments that already matter — a stage gate, the end of an iteration** — reusing existing control points, exactly as LO4 and LO6 recommend.

**It runs for the whole life cycle**, absorbing **information that surfaces later and needs that shift as it goes.**

And the handover to 16b: when requirements change or new ones are introduced, they have to be **brought into line with the configuration management and change management processes**, so **governance, control and the decision itself all happen properly.**

## Requirements and acceptance: the V model

Defining a requirement and designing the test that will judge it are the same act viewed from two ends. The **'V' depiction** of the life cycle shows this: requirements descend the left-hand side from user requirements through system requirements to design and build; testing ascends the right-hand side, with each test level **verifying or validating** its counterpart on the left.

**Why the rigour matters commercially:** the level of rigour **mitigates the risk of a later dispute about acceptance and transition of deliverables into use**. For projects **delivered under a commercial contract this is particularly important, safeguarding both the investing and supplier organisations** — the LO5 link. It is **more achievable when the project is well understood and the commercial setting is steady**, which is precisely why uncertain projects need a different approach.

## Requirements in iterative life cycles

**Requirements get surfaced, then sharpened through analysis** until everyone agrees what is meant. Some methods write them as **user stories** — **a feature a stakeholder has asked for, written in ordinary language**, carrying **only enough detail to size the development effort roughly**.

That last phrase is the point of a user story. It is deliberately not a specification; it carries enough to estimate and to start a conversation.
core_content.outcome_title: Establishing scope through requirements management

core_content.key_takeaway: Configuration management keeps an accurate, traceable record of what the deliverable currently is. Five steps: plan, identify, control, status accounting, verification audit. It is version control at its simplest and asset control at its most complex.
core_content.body_markdown:
## What configuration management does

It is the **technical and administrative work of creating, maintaining, controlling changes to, and quality-checking the project's technical configuration.**

Done well, it delivers two things: **accuracy and alignment of the latest configuration**, and **clear traceability between versions**.

**Why it exists:** on a technical project, **what change control approves lands straight in the specification of what gets built**. Once a change is agreed it must be **written into the project's configuration**, so that any change to the **functional and physical characteristics** of a deliverable is **documented and communicated to the entire team**.

Without it, a change is approved and half the team keeps building to the old specification.

## It scales with complexity

| Complexity | What configuration management looks like |
|---|---|
| **Simplest** | **Version control of documents and information**, keeping changes and knowledge up to date — the LO6 information management link |
| **More complex** | Designs that are **many-sided, pull in several technical disciplines, and cover a spread of different assets** |
| **Most complex** | **Asset control** — keeping every asset's configuration **within organisational and regulatory standards** |

**Business information modelling (BIM)** sits alongside it: **digital representations of physical assets, created and maintained**. Those models **make a complicated configuration visible** and **let people decide about a technical asset — a building, an aircraft**.

## The five steps

The syllabus names these explicitly — planning, identification, control, status accounting, verification audit. Learn what each actually does.

| Step | What it involves |
|---|---|
| **1. Configuration management planning** | A **configuration management plan** describing the project-specific procedures, **how they are applied and who completes them** — the worked example being how a construction project's technical designs get updated and issued |
| **2. Configuration identification** | Break the project into **configuration items**, giving each a **unique number or reference**. That becomes **the first baseline, and the one place the truth lives** |
| **3. Configuration control** | Once **change control has approved something**, this is what gets it **into the current configuration version** — including **updating any dependencies between configuration items** that the change disturbs |
| **4. Configuration status accounting** | **Regular reporting on the configuration's status**, so everyone has **the most up-to-date information**, and keeping **each configuration item traceable across its whole development** |
| **5. Configuration verification audits** | **Check the deliverable actually matches the configuration on record.** Usually run **as a phase closes, once a deliverable is complete, or as the output passes into use** |

**Step 3 is where the two processes meet.** Configuration control does not approve changes — **change control does that** (LO24). Configuration control makes sure an approved change actually lands in the record. Getting that division right is the difference between a good answer and a confused one.

**Step 3 also carries an easily-missed detail:** interrelationships between configuration items get updated too. Changing one component can invalidate another that depended on it.

## How the two processes divide the work

The cleanest way to hold 16a and 16b together:

| | Requirements management | Configuration management |
|---|---|---|
| **Job** | **Establishes** scope | **Manages and controls** scope |
| **Question it answers** | What are we building, and why? | What exactly is it right now, and how did it get that way? |
| **Output** | An agreed, prioritised **requirements baseline** | An accurate, traceable **configuration** |
| **When** | Heaviest early, continuing throughout | Throughout delivery, into transition |

## Where verification audits sit

The timing of step 5 connects to three other LOs at once:

- **At the end of a life cycle phase** — alongside the decision gates of LO6.
- **When a deliverable is finished** — supporting the quality and acceptance work of LO18.
- **As the output passes into use** — the acceptance sequence of LO8, where deliverables are tested against **acceptance criteria** before the sponsor signs off.

That last one closes the loop opened in 16a. Requirements defined a measure; the V model designed a test against it; configuration management recorded what was actually built; and the verification audit confirms the built thing matches the documented configuration before it is handed over.

## Governance applies to requirement changes

From 16a, restated because it is the bridge: a changed or newly-arrived requirement has to be **run through configuration management and change management**, so that **governance, control and the decision itself all happen properly**.

A new requirement is not simply added to a list. It goes through analysis, validation and alignment; it is prioritised against everything already there; it goes through change control if it affects an approved baseline; and it lands in the configuration record.
core_content.outcome_title: Managing scope through configuration management

misconceptions.right: Success criteria and benefits are different. A project can deliver its agreed success criteria and fail to deliver the benefits, and it can deliver benefits and still be perceived as a failure.
misconceptions.wrong: Delivering the success criteria means the project succeeded.

misconceptions.right: Whether the success criteria were met is known at handover, and that sits with the project manager. Benefits usually only arrive once the output is adopted into business as usual, and the sponsor answers for those.
misconceptions.wrong: The project manager is accountable for the project's benefits.

misconceptions.right: Just because a stakeholder proposes something does not mean it should be accepted. It must be analysed for dependencies, risks and constraints, validated, and checked for alignment with project objectives and organisational aims.
misconceptions.wrong: A requirement proposed by a stakeholder should be captured as a requirement.

misconceptions.right: The process establishes a baseline and then reviews it regularly, most commonly at stage gates or iteration cycles, continuing throughout the life cycle as new information emerges and stakeholder needs evolve.
misconceptions.wrong: Requirements are captured once at the start of the project.

misconceptions.right: It is an explicit, recorded decision to exclude something this time. Recording it prevents it reappearing later as an assumed inclusion.
misconceptions.wrong: 'Won't have' in MoSCoW means a requirement was left out.

misconceptions.right: It needs a measure. A requirement plus its measure — speed of ship, greater than 12 knots — is what makes acceptance of the deliverable possible at transition.
misconceptions.wrong: A requirement is complete once it is written down clearly.

misconceptions.right: Change control approves changes. Configuration control ensures an approved change is reflected in the latest configuration version, and that interrelationships between configuration items are updated.
misconceptions.wrong: Configuration management approves changes to the deliverable.

misconceptions.right: That is its simplest form. It becomes more complex where designs are multifaceted and span technical disciplines, and can extend to asset control ensuring all assets comply with organisational and regulatory standards.
misconceptions.wrong: Configuration management is document version control.

misconceptions.right: Requirements management establishes scope — what are we building and why. Configuration management controls it — what exactly is it now, and how did it get that way.
misconceptions.wrong: Requirements management and configuration management are two names for the same activity.

misconceptions.right: Some are easier to measure than others. Benefits desired by a sponsor may produce requirements that cannot easily be measured, such as work being delivered in an environmentally sustainable way.
misconceptions.wrong: Every requirement can be made measurable if written well enough.

key_definitions.plain_english: Did we deliver what we agreed to deliver, judged against criteria set before we started.

key_definitions.plain_english: What it does, and how well it has to do it. Both need stating; the second is the one people forget.

key_definitions.plain_english: Four buckets for requirements. The fourth one — won't have — is a decision, not an omission.

key_definitions.plain_english: The agreed line in the sand. Everything afterwards is measured as a change against it.

key_definitions.plain_english: One tracked part of the deliverable, with an identifier so everyone knows which version they mean.

key_definitions.apm_definition: The creation and management of digital representations of physical assets, related to configuration management. Business information models aid visibility of complex configurations and enable decision-making for a technical asset such as a building or aircraft.

body.where_this_fits: LO16 opens the delivery half of the course, and it is where the abstract becomes concrete: benefits and success criteria from LO4 and LO9 turn into requirements you can build against and test. Two processes, cleanly split — requirements management *establishes* scope, configuration management *controls* it once established. The distinction the exam most wants: success criteria and benefits are not the same thing, and a project can hit one while missing the other.

core_content.key_takeaway: Generate options before choosing one, evaluate them against criteria agreed with stakeholders in advance, then document the decision. Linear life cycles fix scope at approval; iterative ones hold a prioritised backlog and fix scope in stages.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Where solutions development starts

Requirements management dealt with **what stakeholders need or want to be able to do**. Solutions development explores **how to meet them** — determining the optimal solution to satisfy the agreed requirements.

It begins by **getting clear on what problem is actually being solved** — which forces you to **rank the competing requirements different stakeholders brought**. From there the team **produces several options and works through them** before settling on one, and that choice then goes through **refinement and change control**.

**It mixes two modes of thinking:** finding options needs **creative thinking, good facilitation and technical expertise**; choosing between them needs **rigorous analysis** to find the option offering greatest value.

## Solutions must meet both kinds of requirement

| Type | What it covers |
|---|---|
| **Functional** | The things it has to be **able to do** |
| **Non-functional** | The **qualities** it must have — how it looks, how long it lasts, how sustainable, reliable, secure and safe it is, how it performs, how it is maintained |

Non-functional requirements are the ones that get under-specified and then become acceptance disputes. A solution that does everything asked of it but cannot be maintained has failed a real requirement.

## Build in time to explore options

**Carve out time at the start purely for producing options and alternatives.** The source is blunt about why: **too often there is a rush to solutions.**

On a larger, more complex project, **dedicating a phase to option generation demonstrates good governance** and **improves transparency — clarifying to others why the eventual approach was taken.**

That is a strong scenario answer: the value of an options phase is not only a better solution, it is a defensible decision.

## Framing determines what options exist

The single most useful idea in LO17, and worth learning with the source's own example:

| Framing | Options it permits |
|---|---|
| **'Build a bridge between A and B'** | Location and type of bridge |
| **'Facilitate the movement of people between A and B'** | Bridge, tunnel, ferry, relocating the destination, removing the need to travel |

**Frame it as the problem needing solved**, and the outcomes you want and the benefits behind them follow naturally from there. Frame it as a solution and you have chosen before you started.

## The dimensions options should cover

| Dimension | The question |
|---|---|
| **Doing nothing** | What happens if we do not proceed? Always an option |
| **Minimum viable solution to complete solution** | How much of the possible scope do we build? |
| **Single-phased or multi-phased** | Do we do it in one pass or several? |
| **Level of technology maturity** | How proven does the technology need to be? |

**On minimum viable solution:** it **should always be considered** as an option. It is **the cheapest and quickest to deliver**, and makes designers work out **the least that has to be true for the project to have succeeded at all.** But stakeholders **may want to go further and add features for greater benefits in the longer term** — so MVP is a benchmark to reason from, not automatically the recommendation.

**On phasing:** a simple short project can be single-phase. More complicated ones need thought — **should there be a pilot for proof of concept? Should it be trialled in one area, evaluated, and rolled out once the lessons are in?** Or does **the clock, or a need to show commitment across the board, force it all into one phase?** And where the details are not known at the outset, **a discovery phase may be needed to reach full clarity** — after which the project is **either terminated or replanned in light of what was learned.**

**On technology maturity:** most stakeholders **dislike depending on ageing technology**, but **anything not yet properly proven, or whose standards are still unsettled, deserves an argument before it is adopted.** Different options carry different risks.

**On the strategic dimension:** starting a project **cuts off other options and future opportunities**. Some options **allow a wider variety of future opportunities; others take the organisation down a tightly defined path.** So projects must be **considered in line with the organisation's broader strategic direction, not evaluated in isolation** — the LO4 and LO9 link.

## How options get evaluated

**Working every option up into a full solution is not realistic**, but each should at least be **named and roughly assessed**, leaving **a shortlist worth pursuing**. Assess on:

- **what the project is for** — the problem being solved
- **what it does for the organisation's future**
- **the risk it carries, and how likely it is to succeed or fail**
- **whether we can actually deliver it**
- **cost, time and quality, as always**

**The critical sequencing point:** the assessment **holds up best when the criteria were settled with stakeholders before anyone listed an option.** Criteria written after the options are on the table can be shaped, consciously or not, to favour a preferred answer.

Criteria might take in **a cost-benefit analysis tied back to the business case**, plus impacts that are **commercial, operational, technical, environmental and strategic.**

## The six-component process

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1. Identify options** | **More options increase the likelihood of project success.** Engage the team to research and think creatively. Every option has to **speak to what stakeholders have prioritised** and be **able to return value to the organisation funding it** |
| **2. Evaluate options** | Against criteria agreed with stakeholders beforehand |
| **3. Select** | The best option to meet requirements and deliver value |
| **4. Governance framework** | Wraps the whole process — **document the option selected, the decision process followed, and the specification for the solution**, and **communicate the choice to stakeholders** |
| **5. Monitoring** | A monitoring and control cycle during delivery, including **quality assurance and quality control**. Run **plan-do-check-act — the Shewhart cycle** — to adjust the process and tighten efficiency. Decide **what data to collect** to understand progress and anticipate issues |
| **6. Change control** | Ensures **all requests for change to features or functionality get a robust assessment**. Once approved, **record the new solution configuration in full** and **tell stakeholders what changed** |

It ends with **sign-off ahead of handover** — the final piece of governance in the process.

## Turning the solution into scope

With a solution chosen, **develop a scope that articulates its parts**, aiming to **maximise clarity and minimise ambiguity**.

**In scope and out of scope both get stated.** Recording **assumptions and exclusions** is **crucial for mitigating the risk of scope creep**. The source's examples of exclusions: **transition resources drawn from BAU rather than funded by the project; customised reporting in a software implementation; ground-source heating left out of a building refurbishment.**

Stating both sides **cuts the risk of misunderstanding** and **gives you something to judge change requests against**. **Scope defined badly is a well-known route to delay, cost overrun and benefits that never arrive.**

**Interfaces matter too.** Understanding interfaces with other work is **critical to avoid duplication, conflicts or omission** — whether that is inside a programme or portfolio, across to other standalone projects, or against BAU work.

## The four breakdown structures

In linear life cycles, **breakdown structures formally define scope**:

| Structure | Defines |
|---|---|
| **PBS** — product breakdown structure | **Things to create** |
| **WBS** — work breakdown structure | **Activities to complete** |
| **OBS** — organisation breakdown structure | **Allocation of people** |
| **CBS** — cost breakdown structure | **Project budget** |

A **work package** is the part of a WBS allocated to a team member. Combining the WBS and OBS produces the **responsibility assignment matrix** — the LO2 link.

## Linear versus iterative

This is the second half of 17a, and the distinction the exam wants.

| | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| **When scope is fixed** | **Approval of the scope definition fixes it.** Planning then optimises time, cost and quality | **Solutions selected and scope fixed later, and in stages** |
| **How scope is held** | Breakdown structures | A **product backlog** of potential scope elements, often as **user stories** |
| **How scope changes** | **Only through formal change control** | The team **draws down the highest-priority items each iteration** |
| **When it stops** | At the agreed scope | **Iterations keep adding until the next increment of benefit costs more than it returns** |

**Iterative approaches identify options in much the same way** — the difference is when they commit. Deferring the commitment **suits situations where committing early would be a mistake**:

- requirements that keep moving
- technology still under development
- a build process you expect to learn from

**Stop when the next increment costs more than it returns.** That is the phrase worth memorising — the iterative equivalent of a scope boundary, an economic rule rather than a fixed list.

## MVP and MMP

The syllabus names both. They answer different questions.

| | Minimum viable product (MVP) | Minimum marketable product (MMP) |
|---|---|---|
| **Question** | What is the smallest thing that works and lets us learn? | What is the smallest thing customers would actually accept or pay for? |
| **Purpose** | Validate assumptions, gather feedback, reduce wasted build | Reach the market, or reach real users, with the least scope necessary |
| **Audience** | Often internal or a limited user group | The market or the full user base |
| **Risk it addresses** | Building the wrong thing | Building more than the market needed before earning anything back |

**How they work together in an iterative life cycle:** early iterations produce an **MVP** to test whether the solution is right at all. Later iterations build towards an **MMP** — the point at which the output is good enough to release and start generating outcomes and benefits. Iterations carry on past that point, adding value **right up until the next increment stops paying for itself**.

This connects straight to LO1 and LO9: **iterative projects realise benefits incrementally**, and the MMP is the point where that realisation can begin.

**Note on sourcing:** MVP is covered in the Body of Knowledge. **MMP is not** — it is standard iterative practice named by the syllabus, and is presented here as such rather than as APM content.

core_content.key_takeaway: Quality planning sets acceptance criteria — the quality indicators — and decides how the project will assure and verify against them. Those criteria must reconcile with the business case's quality statements, and QA and QC both cost time and money that has to be scheduled.
core_content.body_markdown:
## What quality means here

APM's definition: quality is **being fit for the purpose intended, or how closely a process's outputs — or the process itself — conform to what was required.**

Note that the definition covers **the process as well as the output**. That is why QA exists at all: a sound process is part of what quality means, not merely a route to it.

**And the scope boundary worth fixing early:** assurance and audit (LO7) look at **the overall governance and management** of the work. **Quality planning looks at how the outputs meet the customer's standards.** Different targets.

## Whose job it is

**Anyone leading project work owns quality**, and their task is to **build a culture where the team owns it too.**

That framing matters for scenario answers: quality is not delegated to a quality function. It is led.

## What quality planning determines

Five things, and this list answers 18a directly:

| Determination | What it settles |
|---|---|
| **The organisation's attitude to quality** | How much conformance is expected, and at what cost |
| **The acceptance criteria** — the **quality indicators** — against which quality will be assessed | The pass mark |
| **How the project will ensure output quality meets the criteria** | The **QA** approach |
| **How the project will verify output quality meets the criteria** | The **QC** approach |
| **How the project will communicate with stakeholders about quality** | Reporting and confidence |

**The acceptance criteria, and the plan for hitting them, are what a quality plan is really about.**

## Quality indicators and the business case

The syllabus asks specifically how quality indicators relate to the business case, and the source answers it in one line: acceptance criteria have to **square with whatever the business case said about quality.**

The logic runs both ways:

- **Downwards.** The business case promised a certain standard of output in order to justify the investment. Acceptance criteria have to deliver on that promise, or the case was overstated.
- **Upwards.** QA and QC **eat time and resource, and both have to be scheduled and priced**, so the quality regime feeds back into the cost side of the business case. Higher conformance is not free.

That second point is the more examinable one. **Quality is a cost decision, not only a standards decision** — which is why 'the organisation's attitude to quality' is the first thing quality planning determines.

**Timing:** acceptance criteria are set **after scope definition and before further planning**. After scope, because you cannot write criteria for deliverables you have not defined. Before further planning, because the QA and QC activity has to be scheduled and resourced like any other work.

## What the acceptance criteria reference

| Source | Why it constrains quality |
|---|---|
| **Customer requirements** | The primary input |
| **Legislation, regulations and standards** applicable to the products | Non-negotiable — the LO15 link |
| **Values and policies of the investing organisation** | Internal expectations above the legal minimum |
| **Quality management standards and methodologies** | How the organisation does quality |
| **Testing and assurance methodologies and toolsets** | What verification is practically available |

And the **external constraints** the team must understand: **industry standards, regulatory or legal requirements, organisational policies.**

## What the quality plan documents

A high-yield list, because it is concrete:

- **a pass/fail line for every output**
- **the QA process itself**
- **how conformance to specification will be verified**
- **test scripts**
- **how often testing, checking or auditing happens**
- **how much gets sampled, and at what percentage**
- **how much failure is tolerable**
- **what it needs** — outside facilities, test kit, people
- **the governance around it** — formal sign-off, stakeholder approval

**'Levels of failure the project can tolerate' is the one candidates skip.** Deciding in advance how much non-conformance is acceptable is what makes a QC result actionable rather than arguable.

**Handover goes far more smoothly where stakeholders already agree, and planning for that agreement is itself a success factor** — the LO8 link.

## QA: preventing defects

**QA is what keeps the quality plan's procedures and standards being applied consistently**, so that people can be **confident the relevant standards will actually be met.**

**A regular cycle of reviewing project work** assesses conformance to:

- the product specification, and the quality standards set for it
- the project's own procedures and processes
- organisational policy, procedure and values
- industry standards, and anything required by law or regulator

**QA covers the work's outputs and the processes that produced them alike.** After evaluations, **a lessons-learned review identifies actions to remedy issues and strengthen project processes.**

**What effective QA actually needs.** The source is unusually direct: a good QA team is indispensable and **clear roles and responsibilities are necessary**, **but attitudes are more important.** Where quality is genuinely valued you get **more awareness, more problem solving, more knowledge shared, and steady improvement** — and **everyone comes to expect their work to be looked at properly.**

That last phrase is the practical test of a quality culture: nobody is surprised or offended by being checked.

**QA versus project assurance.** An important boundary. **QA is a project or programme activity**, whereas **project assurance and audit are imposed on the project by the organisation** (LO7). Doing QA well **reduces the risk of external scrutiny uncovering issues.**

## Life cycle differences

| | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| **Scope and acceptance criteria** | **Documented and signed off before project planning** | Evolve with the backlog |
| **QA** | Throughout delivery | **Throughout each iteration** |
| **QC** | At defined test points | **At the end of each iteration** |
| **Who signs off** | Usually **the project sponsor or client** | **On behalf of the user** — sponsor, client or **product owner** |

**Sign-off on the quality plan comes from the sponsor or client, together with any governance board above them**, and it then **sits inside the integrated project management plan** — the LO19 link.

**Inside a programme**, the higher-level quality requirements **can be planned and controlled by the programme**, with **individual projects working to programme standards.**
