core_content.key_takeaway: QC verifies outputs against acceptance criteria through inspection, measurement and testing. It needs configuration management, test plans, defect documentation and a remediation process — and the response to non-conformance depends on how much deviation the product can tolerate.
core_content.body_markdown:
## What QC is for

**QC exists to prove that what the project produced actually meets the acceptance criteria set during quality planning** — and it does that by **inspecting, measuring and testing.**

The clean contrast with QA, worth stating exactly:

| | Quality assurance | Quality control |
|---|---|---|
| **Focus** | **Preventing** defects, errors and waste | **Detecting and rectifying** defects |
| **How** | **Puts quality into the delivery itself**, through standard process and procedure backed by training and feedback | **Catches whatever slipped through production before the customer sees it** |
| **Acts on** | The process (and the outputs) | The outputs |
| **Timing** | Throughout | At verification points |

**QA builds it in; QC catches what got through.** If you can only remember one line about this LO, that is the one.

## The four things effective QC needs

| Requirement | Why |
|---|---|
| **Configuration management of specifications** | You cannot verify against a specification you cannot pin down — the LO16 link |
| **Test plans and an inspection regime** | The what and how of checking |
| **Documentation of defects** | Undocumented defects cannot be tracked or trended |
| **An implementation process to remedy defects** | Finding a defect achieves nothing without a route to fix it |

## Test plans

**Test plans carry a lot of weight.** They should cover:

- **how much gets tested** — everything, or a random sample
- **the protocols** — precisely what is tested, and by what method
- **what it takes** — facilities, people, expertise, equipment
- **who runs or watches the test independently** — a regulator, or the operational owner

That last one is the mark-earner. **Independent witnessing** connects QC to the independence principle from LO7: a test the delivering team ran and marked itself is weaker evidence than one a regulator or the operational owner observed.

## QC applies everywhere, not just to technical products

**In many projects, products are complex and technical**, and verifying conformance is a large task where **testing is well understood**. But **every project has to hand over something fit for purpose, so QC never stops mattering.**

**Interim outputs count as much as final ones** — and the source names them: **reports, communication materials and financial models.**

A useful corrective. A change project producing no physical product still has deliverables that can be checked against criteria.

## Deciding what to do about non-conformance

**How closely the customer needs the output to conform is always the central question.** It gets answered during **quality planning**, which sets both **the acceptance criteria** and **what happens when something falls short.**

Two ends of the spectrum, and the exam will use one of them:

| Situation | Response |
|---|---|
| **Safety-critical products** | **A non-compliant item simply cannot be used.** Rework follows, and that **changes the plan** |
| **User acceptance testing of a system** | **Early use can absorb some deviation.** Decision makers may **go live knowing about the issues**, with remedial work after handover as **part of BAU maintenance**. These appear on a **snagging list** |

The reasoning to show in an answer: the right response is not a fixed rule, it follows from **what the product is** and **how much deviation the customer can tolerate** — both of which were decided at planning, not discovered at testing.

**Note the knock-on:** rework **triggers a change to the plan**. A QC failure is not contained within QC; it consumes schedule and budget, and goes through change control (LO24).

## How QC determines whether success criteria are met

This is the exact wording of 18b, so worth answering directly. The chain:

1. **Success criteria** are agreed with stakeholders at the start (LO16).
2. **Quality planning** converts them into **acceptance criteria** — formal, pass/fail statements for each deliverable, reconciled to the business case.
3. Those criteria then **shape which measurements and tests get planned** to check the output against specification.
4. **QC executes those measurements and tests** — inspection, measurement, testing — against the criteria.
5. Results are **assessed and documented**, unacceptable issues **referred for remediation**, and verified products **signed off**.
6. Sign-off against acceptance criteria is what allows **transition into use** (LO8), where the sponsor accepts the deliverables.

So QC is the mechanism that turns 'we think this is finished' into evidence. **Without measurable acceptance criteria, QC has nothing to test against** — which is why LO16's insistence on requirements having measures matters here.

## The QC sequence

The activities, in order:

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Define the requirements and acceptable levels of deviation** | Set at quality planning |
| **Work with stakeholders** | Draw on what they know, and keep them confident in the process |
| **Assess defects and write them down** | The record matters as much as the finding |
| **Refer unacceptable issues for remediation** | The route out for anything beyond tolerance |
| **Sign off verification of products** | The formal outcome |

With **continuous improvement** running alongside throughout.

## Continuous improvement

**A standing effort to make products, services or processes better.** The gains can arrive **gradually, or as a single large step change.** The Japanese term is **kaizen**.

| Goal | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Immediate** | Improve **efficiency and reliability**, and **reduce waste** |
| **Ultimate** | Deliver **greater value by increasing benefits and reducing cost** |

**The loop:** gather performance data (quantitative and qualitative) → analyse it → identify opportunities for improvement → implement changes → evaluate the outcomes.

**It operates at two levels:** on **organisational project, programme or portfolio management processes**, and on **how the project professional runs this project, and how this team works together on it.**

### The Shewhart cycle

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Plan** | Set the standards, put procedures in place, assign the resource |
| **Do** | Run the processes and watch what comes out |
| **Check** | Measure how the project performed against those standards |
| **Act** | Take the lessons on board and correct what needs correcting |

### The tools

- **performance indicators** — quality standards, KPIs, or objectives and key results (OKRs)
- **prototyping and piloting** anything innovative
- **numbers** — gathering data and analysing it
- **judgement** — surveys, interviews, watching how things go
- **the team looking at itself** — lessons-learned reviews, retrospectives

Wider frameworks drawn from manufacturing: **total quality management (TQM), Lean and Six Sigma.**

### What makes it work

**Both iterative and linear approaches can adopt continuous improvement equally**, though it **turns up most naturally in iterative work** — indeed **some argue that working iteratively simply is continuous improvement.**

**Where it works, it is systematic and leadership treats it as a priority** — and that combination **signals a mature project management capability.**

It is **a choice about culture**, and it **thrives where curiosity, ongoing learning and developing people are valued** — and where **problems get solved and learned from instead of pinned on someone.**

That closes a circle running through LO11, LO12 and LO14: a blame culture suppresses the information every one of those processes depends on.

misconceptions.right: QA prevents defects by ensuring the process follows the quality plan. QC detects and rectifies defects that got through, by inspection, measurement and testing. QA builds it in; QC catches what escaped.
misconceptions.wrong: Quality assurance and quality control are two names for checking the output.

misconceptions.right: Assurance and audit look at overall governance and management, and are imposed on the project by the organisation. Quality management looks at whether the outputs meet the customer's standards, and is a project activity.
misconceptions.wrong: Quality management is the same as project assurance.

misconceptions.right: Quality planning starts by determining the organisation's attitude to quality. QA and QC take time and consume resources that must be scheduled and costed, so the quality regime feeds back into the business case.
misconceptions.wrong: Higher quality is always the right answer.

core_content.key_takeaway: The PMP collects and aligns the constituent plans into one holistic document — scope, schedule, cost, resources, risk, success criteria and benefits. Format varies with complexity, organisational process and stakeholder preference, but it must summarise succinctly enough to be used at a governance board.
core_content.body_markdown:
## What integrated planning is

**Gathering the separate plans, making them consistent with one another, and keeping them that way — so what emerges is a single whole-project plan.**

Three verbs, and each matters. **Collecting** gathers the separate plans. **Aligning** makes them consistent with each other. **Managing** keeps them that way as things change.

**The aim:** get every component of the project pointing the same way, so **stakeholders can believe the business case is deliverable.** Note where that points — back to LO4. The PMP exists to make the business case credible.

## Typical contents

The component parts named directly:

| Component | Covered in |
|---|---|
| **Scope** | LO16, LO17 |
| **Time and schedule** | LO20 |
| **Cost** | LO22 |
| **Resources** | LO21 |
| **Risks and issues** | LO23 |
| **Success and completion criteria** | LO16, LO18 |
| **Benefits** | LO9 |

Other elements named elsewhere in the syllabus that sit inside the PMP: the **procurement management plan** (LO5), the **quality plan** (LO18), the **benefits realisation plan** (LO9), and the **information management** approach including data security (LO6).

**That list is the answer to 19a's 'typical contents'** — and the more useful way to hold it is that the PMP is the container for every other plan the course teaches.

## Format

**Format is not fixed.** It follows:

- how complex the project is
- what the organisation's own processes demand
- what the key stakeholders want to see

Most of the time, though, it will **pull the important information into a short enough summary that a steering committee or governance board can work from it.**

**'Succinctly' is doing real work there.** The PMP is not a repository of every plan in full — it is a summary fit for the people who have to make decisions from it. A document nobody on the board can get through is not fit for its stated purpose.

## How the life cycle changes it

| | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| **Assumption** | **You can pin the work down up front**, giving a **detailed baseline** to run against | Flexibility and agility are assumed instead |
| **Baseline** | Detailed and fixed early | **Still required, but much less defined** |
| **How detail arrives** | Up front | **Component parts, and so the plan itself, gain detail as the project progresses** |

**The point the source makes about linear**, which is worth quoting in a scenario: **things will go wrong in delivery regardless — and that is no argument for planning any less carefully before work begins.** 'The plan will change anyway' is not an argument against planning.

## The three things that make an initial PMP possible

**Building the first integrated plan is genuinely difficult, and it takes input from a lot of people.** Three things carry you through it:

1. **robust estimation**
2. **dependency management processes**
3. **risk identification**

Between them they give stakeholders enough confidence to **sign the thing off and let the project start.**

### Estimation

**Working out how much time, resource and money the agreed scope will need at the agreed quality.** It serves four purposes:

- inform **investment appraisals and option selection** for the business case
- input to the **resource plan and project schedule**
- enable **budget setting and assessment of affordability**
- the point from which **risk analysis and contingency planning** begin

| Approach | Method | How it works |
|---|---|---|
| **Top-down** | **Parametric** | Historical data compared with known project variables. *1 litre of paint covers 5 square metres; a 550 square metre wall needs 110 litres* |
| **Top-down** | **Analogous** (also called comparative) | Like-for-like comparison against historical projects. *2,000 bricks built that house; the same specification needs 2,000 again* |
| **Bottom-up** | **Analytical** | Break the project into parts, estimate each in detail using internal and external data. *Cost each component of a computer against an external benchmark* |
| **Bottom-up** | **Delphi** | Break into parts, then reach **consensus among subject-matter experts**. *A group of engineers agree how long each build task takes* |

**Top-down suits the early life cycle**, when detailed information is not available. **Bottom-up is often used to validate top-down estimates** once more detail exists — and **combining techniques builds confidence**.

**Three-point estimates** determine a range, from which you give **an informed opinion on the most likely estimate**, **noting any estimating assumptions**. Those assumptions matter beyond the estimate: **they go on to support risk analysis and contingency planning.**

**Estimating is not a one-off activity for the business case.** It **runs continuously, sharpening as information arrives**, and **revised estimates go through change control, which then adjusts the integrated plan.**

**Both life cycles need the same estimation data, documentation and rigour** — they just approach it differently, linear estimating in more detail early, iterative building detail as it goes.

### Dependency management

**A dependency is how one activity or resource relates to another** — where whether a task can start, or finish, hangs on something else being done.

**Why it matters:** **dependencies left unmanaged are a standard route to a project stopping, replanning, costing more and delivering its benefits later.**

| Type | Definition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Logical / hard** | Work that **cannot** begin until something else has begun or finished | You cannot paint a wall that has not been built |
| **Preferential / soft** | Work that **should not** begin until something else has — **usually a governance, process or quality-control decision** | A communication should not go out until peer review is complete |
| **Resource** | Activities that cannot start until another completes **because they use the same resource** | One developer, so the product page waits for the homepage |

**Cannot versus should not** is the distinction that separates hard from soft. A hard dependency is physics; a soft one is a decision — which is why it can be removed.

**The three link types** in scheduling: **finish-to-start** (task 2 starts only when task 1 finishes), **start-to-start** (task 4 starts only when task 3 has started), **finish-to-finish** (task 6 finishes only when task 5 has finished).

**Managing them:** identification often happens naturally during scoping — for instance when defining a **work breakdown structure** — but bring in **the experts to settle how the tasks actually relate to each other**. Feed dependencies into planning so **the sequence is agreed and impacts are planned for**, using **critical path** and **critical chain** (LO20), which consider dependencies through activities and resources respectively.

**And a genuinely useful risk point:** **the more dependencies a project carries, the riskier it is by construction.** The response is to **strip out preferential and resource dependencies wherever you can** — weighing what that does to cost, benefit and quality. You cannot remove a hard dependency; you can often remove a soft one.

### Risk identification

Risks must be described clearly, **separating three parts**:

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Cause** | Something in the environment that introduces uncertainty |
| **Event** | Something that might happen, inside the project or around it |
| **Impact** | What that would do to one or more of the project's objectives |

**The worked example:** a general election on the horizon (**cause**), inflation rising as a result (**event**), and the project's resources costing more (**impact**).

**Group workshops** are common, usually early in the life cycle. Describing risks in this structure helps **align differing stakeholder opinions and address group bias** — the LO12 link.

**Every risk gets a risk owner** — **the individual or group best placed to assess and manage it** — and is **documented in the risk register**, ready for analysis under LO23.

**Risk identification is not finished when the workshop ends.** Adopt **a risk-based mindset throughout**, because further risks emerge as the project evolves, stakeholders join, and information arrives.

### Contingency planning

**Setting aside resources solely reserved for responding to risks and uncertainty.** It **bridges the gap that risk creates**, It covers **risks you have named, risks you have not, and the plain uncertainty in early estimates.**

That third category is easy to miss: contingency covers **estimating uncertainty** as well as identified risks.

## The deployment baseline

**All the planning work results in a deployment baseline** — the plan for executing the project, **supporting the integrated PMP**. It sets out baseline plans for:

- **scope**
- **timeline**
- **quality**
- **budget**

**Both the deployment baseline and the PMP are approved at the decision gate before the deployment phase.**

| | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| **Scope at approval** | **Fixed** — changes in deployment go through **change control** | More evolutionary, given greater uncertainty |
| **What drives** | **Scope and quality drive; cost and time are calculated from the scope** | Resources committed over **timeboxes** with fixed end dates |
| **Baseline may include** | Scope, timeline, quality, budget | **Number of iterations, necessary functionality, baseline resources and schedule** |
| **Variation** | Managed by exception | **Scope and quality may vary as new knowledge emerges**; the team may have authority to reprioritise. **Work not achieved in a timebox returns to the backlog** |

**Approving the deployment baseline is a good moment to reconfirm the project's boundaries:** what falls inside the scope and what does not, where it touches **other projects** in a programme or portfolio, and where it touches **BAU**. **Any lack of fit requires the PMP to be reworked before approval** — either by moving the scope, or by **releasing contingency to pay for risk responses the original scope never covered**.

**Two further points worth carrying:**

- Under **critical chain** scheduling, **the buffers get approved and locked into the deployment baseline**, which is what makes performance measurable.
- **Good practice is an integrated baseline review by an independent reviewer** — **a risk-based review giving assurance that the deployment baseline is realistic and achievable within budget and schedule.** The LO7 link, applied to the plan itself.

core_content.key_takeaway: Separate plans that never meet will contradict each other. Integration exists to give stakeholders confidence the business case is achievable, to make change assessable, and to give delivery something coherent to be measured against.
core_content.body_markdown:
## The core argument

**Integrated planning exists to line up every component of the project so that stakeholders can believe the business case will actually be delivered.**

That single sentence answers 19b. Everything below expands it.

## Why integration specifically

The components of a project are not independent. The source makes the point through dependencies, and it generalises:

> **The parts are related. Move one and another moves with it, whether you intended that or not.**

So a project with a schedule plan, a cost plan and a resource plan that were produced separately does not have three plans. It has three claims that have never been tested against each other. Integration is what turns them into one statement about what will happen.

**The plan's job is to get each part arriving at the moment it is needed — which is what gives the project its best chance.**

## What producing one achieves

| Benefit | Why it follows |
|---|---|
| **Confidence the business case is achievable** | The stated aim. The PMP is the evidence that the promise in LO4 can be delivered |
| **Sign-off becomes possible** | Robust estimation, dependency management and risk identification give stakeholders **the initial confidence to sign off and proceed** |
| **A single view for governance** | Everything important, in one summary a steering committee or governance board can actually use — the LO2 link |
| **A baseline for progress monitoring** | The deployment baseline is **the starting point for progress monitoring** |
| **A basis for assessing change** | Change control assesses requests **against the baseline** (LO24). Without an integrated baseline, the impact of a change cannot be traced across components |
| **Control demonstrated during delivery** | Component-level data is **collected and watched, which is how control gets evidenced** |
| **Boundaries reconfirmed** | Approval is when you re-examine what is in scope, what is out, and where the project touches other projects and BAU |
| **Contingency held deliberately** | Resources **solely reserved** for risk response, rather than discovered to be missing later |

## The consequence of not integrating

The source gives one consequence directly, about dependencies, and it stands for the whole:

**Dependencies left unmanaged stop projects, force a replan, push costs up, and push the benefits back.**

Pause, replan, cost more, deliver benefits later. That is the failure mode integration prevents, and it is a better scenario answer than a general appeal to good practice.

## Integration continues after approval

A PMP produced once and filed is not integrated planning — it is a document. The source is clear that the work continues:

- **As things move and information arrives, keep watching the plan** through data on each component.
- **The agreed governance forums** are where **progress gets reported and contingency gets released** when things slip.
- **Estimating is continuous**, and **updated estimates feed into change control, driving adjustments to the integrated plan.**
- **Dependencies are managed through regular review and replanning.**
- **Risk identification continues throughout**, as the project evolves and new stakeholders arrive.

Notice the pattern: every constituent process feeds back into the integrated plan. That is what makes it integrated rather than assembled.

## Why it is hard, and what makes it possible

**Producing that first integrated plan is hard, and it needs a lot of people to contribute.** Acknowledging the difficulty is part of a good answer — the three techniques exist precisely because it is hard:

| Technique | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| **Robust estimation** | Numbers stakeholders can believe, with assumptions visible |
| **Dependency management** | A sequence that can actually happen |
| **Risk identification** | Honesty about what could go wrong, and contingency sized for it |

## Assurance on the plan itself

**Good practice is an integrated baseline review completed by an independent reviewer** — **a risk-based check that the deployment baseline is achievable inside the budget and the schedule it claims.**

Worth noticing what that implies. The plan is important enough to warrant independent assurance in its own right, before any delivery has happened. A plan nobody has challenged is a plan whose optimism has not been tested.

## The honest framing

Two things to hold together, because scenario questions often set them against each other:

- **Plans will change.** Issues arise, information emerges, estimates are revised.
- **That does not reduce the need to plan well.** The source says it plainly of linear projects: problems will arise regardless, **and that is no reason to plan any less carefully before starting.**

The integrated plan is not a prediction that must come true. It is the current best statement of how the project delivers its business case — maintained, monitored and revised through governance as reality arrives.

memory_aids.expansion: Float is latest start minus earliest start. An activity with none of it cannot slip at all without moving the project's end date.

memory_aids.acronym: Path counts tasks, chain counts people
memory_aids.expansion: Critical path emphasises activities and ignores resource constraints. Critical chain starts from resources and builds a schedule that respects them.

memory_aids.acronym: Safety in every task, or safety at the end
memory_aids.expansion: Critical path leaves padding inside each estimate. Critical chain strips it out and pools it in one buffer, which is why the buffer goes further.

memory_aids.acronym: Compress the critical, and nothing else

core_content.key_takeaway: Scope covers outputs, outcomes and benefits, plus the work to produce them. Breakdown structures turn that into something schedulable: PBS for what gets created, WBS for the activities, CBS for the budget, OBS for the people.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Scope covers three things, not one

From LO17, restated because 20a depends on it: **scope covers the whole of what the project produces — outputs, outcomes and benefits — together with the work needed to produce it.**

| Element | What it is | Who it belongs to |
|---|---|---|
| **Output** | The thing the project creates | Project manager delivers it |
| **Outcome** | What changes because the output is used | Arrives through adoption |
| **Benefit** | The measurable improvement that change produces | Sponsor is accountable |

A schedule built only around outputs will finish at handover and leave the outcomes and benefits unscheduled — which is exactly the failure LO8 and LO9 describe. Where an extended life cycle is used, adoption and benefits realisation are scheduled work too.

## The breakdown structures

Breakdown structures are what convert scope into something you can put dates against. The syllabus names three for 20a; the fourth completes the set.

| Structure | Defines | Feeds |
|---|---|---|
| **PBS** — product breakdown structure | **The things to create** — scope expressed as products | The WBS |
| **WBS** — work breakdown structure | **The activities to complete** to deliver those products | The schedule and the RAM |
| **CBS** — cost breakdown structure | **The project budget** | LO22 |
| **OBS** — organisation breakdown structure | **The allocation of people** | The RAM, LO21 |

**The sequence matters.** Products first, then the work needed to produce them. Building a WBS without a PBS produces a list of activities nobody can trace to a deliverable.

**A work package** is the slice of the WBS handed to one team member by whoever manages the project or programme. It is the unit that gets estimated, scheduled and tracked.

**WBS + OBS = responsibility assignment matrix**, setting out every item of work, who is on it, and what part each of them plays (LO2, LO21).

## From breakdown to schedule

1. **Decompose scope** into products (PBS), then activities (WBS).
2. **Agree the dependencies** between activities — logical, preferential and resource (LO19).
3. **Estimate durations**, ideally as **three-point estimates — the optimistic case, the pessimistic case, and the point in between judged most likely.**
4. **Build the precedence network** from the dependency logic.
5. **Run critical path analysis** to find the duration, the critical path and the float.
6. **Present it**, usually as a **Gantt chart** showing activities as bars on a timeline.

**Estimates of duration are based on effort** — which is why LO19's estimating methods sit underneath this LO.

## Levels of schedule

**Schedules come at different levels of resolution — anything from a single-page plan up to a full control schedule.** **Big or complicated projects often run several at once**, each covering a different aspect, with **one master schedule pulling them together, coordinating them and tracking them.**

**Rolling wave** is common for linear projects: **near-term activities in detail, later stages at a higher level.** It is an honest response to the fact that distant detail is guesswork.

## What the schedule is for

**The schedule is how you demonstrate that the timeline is actually deliverable.** It **settles what the project team and the customer are each expecting**, and **everything monitored later gets measured against it.**

The resulting timeline **forms an important part of the deployment baseline**, documented in enough detail to **inform the direction of work and the monitoring of progress**.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Dependency types and link types

From LO19, because the schedule is built on them:

| Dependency type | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Logical / hard** | **Cannot** start until another has started or finished |
| **Preferential / soft** | **Should not** start — driven by governance, process or quality control |
| **Resource** | Cannot start because the same resource is in use elsewhere |

**Link types** in the network:

| Link | Constraint |
|---|---|
| **Finish-to-start** | Task 2 starts only when task 1 finishes |
| **Start-to-start** | Task 4 starts only when task 3 has started |
| **Finish-to-finish** | Task 6 finishes only when task 5 finishes |
| **Start-to-finish** | Shown in the source as **generally bad practice** |

Links can carry a **lag** (a deliberate delay after the predecessor) or a **lead** (an overlap, starting before the predecessor completes). **Finish-to-start is the generally acceptable practice**; the source marks start-to-finish as one to avoid.

## Critical path analysis, worked

This is the arithmetic the exam can test. The example below is ours, not from the source — but the method is standard and every figure has been checked.

**A seven-activity project:**

| Activity | Duration (weeks) | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| A — Survey site | 4 | — |
| B — Design | 6 | A |
| C — Procure materials | 5 | A |
| D — Build frame | 7 | B |
| E — Order fittings | 3 | B |
| F — Install services | 4 | C, D |
| G — Inspect and hand over | 2 | E, F |

**Step 1 — forward pass.** Earliest start (ES) = latest EF of all predecessors. Earliest finish (EF) = ES + duration.

**Step 2 — backward pass.** Latest finish (LF) = earliest LS of all successors. Latest start (LS) = LF − duration.

**Step 3 — float** = LS − ES.

| Activity | Dur | ES | EF | LS | LF | Float | Critical? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 4 | 0 | 4 | 0 | 4 | **0** | **Yes** |
| **B** | 6 | 4 | 10 | 4 | 10 | **0** | **Yes** |
| C | 5 | 4 | 9 | 12 | 17 | 8 | No |
| **D** | 7 | 10 | 17 | 10 | 17 | **0** | **Yes** |
| E | 3 | 10 | 13 | 18 | 21 | 8 | No |
| **F** | 4 | 17 | 21 | 17 | 21 | **0** | **Yes** |
| **G** | 2 | 21 | 23 | 21 | 23 | **0** | **Yes** |

**Critical path: A → B → D → F → G. Project duration: 23 weeks.**

**Check it by enumerating every path** — the critical path must be the longest:

| Path | Length |
|---|---|
| **A → B → D → F → G** | **23** |
| A → B → E → G | 15 |
| A → C → F → G | 15 |

23 − 15 = 8, which matches the float on C and E exactly. **If your float figures do not reconcile with your path lengths, one of them is wrong.**

**What float means in practice:** activity C can start up to 8 weeks late, or take 8 weeks longer, without delaying the project. Activity D cannot slip by a single day. **Zero float means critical.**

## Critical path versus critical chain

| | Critical path | Critical chain |
|---|---|---|
| **Emphasis** | **Activities** | **Resources** |
| **Resource constraints** | **Not considered** | Considered, alongside dependencies |
| **Estimates used** | Three-point, usually the most likely | **The most optimistic — the best case** |
| **Where safety time sits** | Inside each activity estimate | **Stripped out and pooled as a buffer at the end of the chain** |
| **What gets monitored** | Start and end dates, EVA, CPI, SPI | **Rate of buffer consumption** |
| **Monitoring frequency** | Monthly may suit many projects | **At least weekly, often daily** |

**Both have the same purpose:** to **enable analysis of the work, determine start and end dates, and use scarce resource efficiently.**

### Why critical chain exists

It targets three specific behaviours that make estimates unreliable:

- **switching between several activities at once**
- **beginning work the moment its earliest start arrives, then holding the time until it is done**
- **opening tasks that are not properly ready**, just to avoid the stop-start of waiting on information, materials or sign-off

**Tasks then run past the estimate** — an estimate that never allowed for any of this.

### What critical chain requires

- **Resources available when an activity is due to start** — so the team and anyone else needing the same resource must be **consulted and reach agreement**.
- **A culture accepting that best-case estimates may not be achieved.** The buffer is the safety net **for the whole project**, not for each task.
- **Focus** — once working on a task, resources concentrate solely on completing it to standard. **Start and end dates stop being the thing watched; what matters is people moving through the work quickly and efficiently.**

**Where time really matters, there is evidence of unusually strong results** — better on-time delivery, better quality, lower cost.

**The buffers get signed off and locked into the deployment baseline**, which is what makes their consumption measurable.

## What else drives the schedule

This is the specific point of 20b, and the syllabus names the factors:

| Factor | How it impacts the schedule |
|---|---|
| **Business-as-usual activities** | BAU staff are often the same people the project needs. Operational peaks, year-end, seasonal demand and BAU incidents all take resource away. Transition into use has to fit around operational readiness |
| **Costs** | Funding release may depend on stage gates or product release, so activity cannot start until the money is drawn down. Cost limits constrain how much resource can be applied to compress a path |
| **Quality** | QA and QC **take time and consume resources that must be scheduled**. Testing, inspection, independent witnessing and rework all sit on the timeline — and rework after a failed test changes the plan |
| **Risks** | Contingency is time as well as money. Risk responses are scheduled activities. A materialising risk consumes buffer or float |
| **Scope** | Every change to scope changes the work, so changes the network. Scope creep lengthens paths silently if it is not controlled |

**Both approaches require input from technical and BAU stakeholders**, because they are the ones who know **what will hit the schedule in time or resource terms.** That is the source's own instruction, and it is the direct answer to 20b: you cannot build a credible schedule from inside the project alone.

**Interfaces cut both ways.** LO17 required understanding where the project touches other work in a programme or portfolio, and **where it touches BAU**, to avoid duplication, conflicts or omission.
core_content.outcome_title: Links and dependencies — and what else drives the schedule

core_content.key_takeaway: Estimates improve as information arrives, so re-estimating is continuous rather than a failure to plan properly. Optimisation compresses or reshapes the schedule, and monitoring against the baseline is what tells you when either is needed.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Why re-estimate at all

A schedule **is never fixed. It gets reviewed continually, so that delivery still lands inside the time the project agreed to.**

The underlying reason comes from LO19: **estimating is not something done once for the business case and then closed. It runs continuously, sharpening as information arrives.** The further the project goes, **the more accurate its estimates get — and the better the decisions stakeholders can make on them.**

So re-estimating is not an admission that the first plan was wrong. It is the plan doing what it was designed to do.

## Reasons to re-estimate

| Trigger | Why the estimate changes |
|---|---|
| **New information emerges** | Early estimates were made with least knowledge. Detail replaces assumption |
| **Actual performance data arrives** | Real durations and costs from completed work are better predictors than forecasts |
| **Scope changes** | Approved changes alter the work, so alter the estimate |
| **Risks materialise or close** | A risk that occurs consumes contingency; one that passes releases it |
| **Resource availability shifts** | People leave, arrive, or get pulled into BAU |
| **Dependencies change** | A removed soft dependency shortens a path; a discovered one lengthens it |
| **Rolling wave moves forward** | The next wave of near-term work gets planned in detail for the first time |
| **An iteration completes** | **Burndown data shows how efficiently the team worked, which sharpens the next estimate** |

That last row is worth noting: in iterative working, re-estimating is built into the rhythm. Each iteration produces velocity data that improves the next forecast.

## Benefits of re-estimating

- **Better-informed decisions** for stakeholders, because the forecast reflects what is now known.
- **Earlier warning.** A revised forecast surfaces a problem while there is still time to respond.
- **Credibility.** A schedule maintained honestly is trusted; one defended past the point of plausibility is not.
- **Improved future estimating.** Comparing estimate to actual is how estimating capability improves — the LO6 lessons-learned link.
- **Contingency managed deliberately** rather than consumed silently.

**And the governance route:** **revised estimates go through change control, which is what then adjusts the integrated plan.** Re-estimating does not mean quietly rewriting the baseline.

## Schedule optimisation

Optimisation means reshaping the schedule to meet a constraint — usually time, sometimes resource.

| Technique | What it does | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| **Reduce preferential or resource dependencies** | Removes an artificial constraint, shortening a path | Requires accepting the governance or quality reason the dependency existed for |
| **Apply more resource to critical activities** | Shortens critical path duration | Costs money, and not all work divides |
| **Overlap activities using leads** | Starts a successor before its predecessor finishes | Increases risk of rework if the predecessor changes |
| **Re-sequence the network** | Finds a shorter arrangement of the same work | Needs the dependency logic re-agreed with experts |
| **Level or smooth resources** | Resolves resource conflicts (LO21) | Levelling may extend the end date; smoothing works within float |
| **Reduce scope** | Removes work from the network entirely | Requires change control, and may cost benefits |

**Where to apply effort:** the critical path. **Compressing a non-critical activity achieves nothing** — it only increases that activity's float. This is the most common practical error, and a good scenario answer names it.

**And a caution:** compress a critical path far enough and a previously non-critical path becomes critical. In the worked example, driving A → B → D → F → G below 15 weeks would make both other paths critical, and further compression would need work on all three.

**In iterative life cycles**, optimisation works differently: **the time and the money are what stay fixed, while scope and quality flex**, so you agree a **timebox** and get through as much of the work as you efficiently can inside it. **It may take a number of iterations before the output is genuinely fit for purpose.** You do not compress the timebox; you change what goes in it.

## What tells you re-estimation is needed

Progress monitoring. **The three elements required for performance measurement:**

1. **something to measure against** — the baseline
2. **what actually happened** — real performance data
3. **a judgement on what that performance means** for the rest of the project

All three are needed. Data without a baseline is a number with nothing to compare it to; both without an assessment is reporting rather than control.

**What gets monitored:**

| Area | Includes |
|---|---|
| **Progress** | Whether planned scope is being delivered to the required quality; what has been committed and how cash is flowing; how contractors are performing |
| **Opportunities and risks** | Shifts in the project's environment; a changing risk profile and what it does to **time buffers or cost contingency**; opportunities spotted, and their effect |
| **Health of the project** | Stakeholder sentiment and engagement effectiveness; motivation and satisfaction of team members; health of supply chain relationships |

That third category is easily dismissed and shouldn't be. **The project manager and team are responsible for monitoring the non-quantifiable areas** — stakeholder engagement, team morale — while **the people doing the work are best placed to track it**, though plenty of organisations hand it to the **PMO**.

**Frequency depends on circumstances and may change through the life cycle.** With EVA or CPI, **monthly may be appropriate for many projects**, though **critical activities may warrant more frequent tracking**. Under **critical chain the data comes in and gets reviewed weekly at minimum, frequently every day.**

**How to report it:** typically quantitatively, with **traffic-light approaches** flagging areas in or out of control, individually or in a **dashboard**. But **any project of real length needs its performance shown graphically, so a trend becomes visible and problems surface early** — a trend is visible long before a threshold is breached. **Iterative approaches use burndown charts.**

**And when recovery is not possible:** **when monitoring surfaces something the project cannot recover from, you replan and establish an amended baseline.** That is the honest end point — not optimisation, but a new baseline through governance.
core_content.outcome_title: Re-estimating and schedule optimisation through the life cycle

misconceptions.right: It is the longest chain of dependent activities — the sequence with zero float. Its length sets the shortest possible project duration. Importance and difficulty have nothing to do with it.
misconceptions.wrong: The critical path is the most important or most difficult work.

misconceptions.right: Critical path places emphasis on activities and does not consider resource constraints. Critical chain is the approach that considers both dependencies and resource constraints.
misconceptions.wrong: Critical path analysis accounts for whether resources are available.

misconceptions.right: Only compressing critical path activities shortens the project. Compressing an activity with float simply increases its float, achieving nothing.
misconceptions.wrong: Speeding up any late activity will pull the project back on track.

misconceptions.right: It uses the most optimistic estimates — the best case of a three-point estimate — and strips the safety time out of each activity, pooling it as a buffer at the end of the chain.
misconceptions.wrong: Critical chain uses the same estimates as critical path.

misconceptions.right: The focus is on rate of buffer consumption — the percentage of buffer used against the percentage of chain completed. Critical chain does not use EVA, CPI or SPI.
misconceptions.wrong: Critical chain projects are monitored by tracking start and end dates.

misconceptions.right: Estimating is a continuous process that evolves as information emerges, and estimates become increasingly accurate as the project progresses. Updated estimates go through change control to adjust the integrated plan.
misconceptions.wrong: Re-estimating means the original estimate was incompetent.

misconceptions.right: Business-as-usual activities, costs, quality, risks and scope all impact it. Both scheduling approaches require input from technical and BAU stakeholders precisely because of this.
misconceptions.wrong: The schedule is determined by the activities and their dependencies.

misconceptions.right: Time and cost are fixed while scope and quality are flexible, so a timebox is agreed instead — a fixed period with determined resources, within which the work is completed as efficiently as possible.
misconceptions.wrong: In an iterative life cycle you estimate how long the work will take.

misconceptions.right: On projects of any length, performance should be reported graphically so trends can be identified and issues detected early. A trend is visible well before a threshold turns red.
misconceptions.wrong: A traffic-light dashboard is sufficient progress reporting.

misconceptions.right: When monitoring surfaces something unrecoverable, you replan and set an amended baseline through governance — rather than compressing a schedule that has already stopped working.
misconceptions.wrong: If the project falls behind, the schedule should be optimised until it fits.

key_definitions.plain_english: Working out when everything happens, and keeping that answer current as things move.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The process of developing and maintaining schedules, identifying when activities are planned to be performed, considering dependencies, for internal and external resources and activities.

key_definitions.plain_english: The longest chain of dependent activities. Its length is the project's shortest possible duration.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A scheduling approach placing emphasis on activities. It identifies the series of tasks that must be completed promptly to ensure the project's timely and successful completion. It does not consider resource constraints.

key_definitions.plain_english: Critical path with the resource problem taken seriously, and safety time pooled into a buffer at the end.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A scheduling approach placing emphasis on resources, considering both task dependencies and external factors such as resource constraints, ensuring limited resource is considered in constructing a realistic schedule.

key_definitions.plain_english: How long an activity can slip without delaying the project. Zero float means it is on the critical path.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The flexibility identified when activities are planned using critical path analysis, indicating whether an activity is time critical or whether there is flexibility in the start date.

key_definitions.plain_english: The map of what depends on what, drawn before any dates are calculated.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A network diagram created by establishing the logic between activities, enabling estimates of duration based on effort to be made and used in a critical path analysis.

key_definitions.plain_english: Contingency pooled at the end rather than hidden inside every task. Shared, so it goes further.
key_definitions.apm_definition: In critical chain, the safety time stripped out of individual activity estimates and held at the end of a chain of activities, monitored by rate of consumption.

key_definitions.plain_english: Fixed time and cost, flexible scope and quality. The opposite of estimating how long something will take.
key_definitions.apm_definition: In an iterative life cycle, a fixed period with determined resources agreed in advance, within which work to fulfil the scope is completed as efficiently as possible.

key_definitions.plain_english: Plan the near future precisely and the far future roughly, because you cannot know the far future yet.
key_definitions.apm_definition: An approach often used for linear projects in which near-term activities are considered in detail, with later stages of the project considered at a higher level.

key_definitions.plain_english: The schedule of schedules.
key_definitions.apm_definition: On large or complex projects, the schedule that combines, coordinates and tracks several subordinate schedules dealing with different aspects of the project.

key_definitions.plain_english: Work remaining, plotted downwards over time. Its slope tells you whether the iteration will finish.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A chart used in iterative approaches to track completion and measure progress, used to calculate the efficiency of the team and improve future estimates.

body.where_this_fits: The schedule is where every other plan gets tested against time. Scope from LO17 becomes activities, dependencies from LO19 become a network, resources from LO21 constrain it, and risk from LO23 buys contingency in it. The distinction the exam wants is critical path versus critical chain — one emphasises activities and ignores resource constraints, the other starts from resources. Learn to calculate float by hand: it is the one piece of arithmetic in this LO that gets tested directly.
learning_outcomes: 20a) Know how to define scope in terms of outputs, outcomes and benefits (including use of product, work and cost breakdown structures).

20b) Understand there are links and dependencies between activities within a project and business-as-usual activities — for example business-as-usual activities, costs, quality, risks and scope can all impact the schedule for the project.
20c) Understand the reasons for and benefits of re-estimating, and schedule optimisation, throughout the project life cycle.

I can name the dependency types and link types, and say which link type the source marks as bad practice.

I can check my float figures against path lengths to verify a critical path calculation.

memory_aids.acronym: Levelling asks when, smoothing asks what
memory_aids.expansion: Levelling asks when the work finishes given the people you actually have. Smoothing asks what resource is needed to hit what was promised. The two questions are the whole distinction.

memory_aids.acronym: Levelling moves the date, smoothing moves the money
memory_aids.expansion: Levelling holds resource constraints fixed and lets the timeline extend. Smoothing holds scope, quality and time and accepts an impact on cost.

memory_aids.acronym: R does it, A owns it
memory_aids.expansion: Responsible conducts the work; Accountable owns it and approves it when complete. Consulted feeds in during decisions; Informed just hears about progress.
The WBS supplies the rows, the OBS supplies the columns, and the RAM is what they make where they meet.
The same specialist skills a linear project concentrates early are needed across every iteration in an iterative one. Life cycle choice changes the demand curve, not just the dates.

core_content.key_takeaway: Requirements identification starts once high-level scope exists, and covers skills, seniority, domain expertise and qualifications. Capacity is then estimated as full-time or part-time effort, and the chosen life cycle changes when those resources are needed.
core_content.body_markdown:
## What resource management covers

**Getting hold of the resources a project needs — internal and external — and putting them to work.** Both halves matter — getting hold of resource, and putting it to work.

**Why it matters:** **get the processes and controls wrong and you invite schedule delay, weaker quality, higher cost and thinner benefits.** All four of the things the project is judged on.

**A resource is anything needed to complete a project**, but the emphasis falls on **people resources and how best to leverage their skills and experience.**

## When requirement identification starts

**Normally once the high-level scope exists**, because that is what makes **the work to be done visible.** You cannot say who you need before you know what is being built — which is why LO17 comes first.

**And no two projects are the same.** Scope, requirements and stakeholder needs all differ, so **the particular skills, experience and competences each project needs differ with them.**

## The four things to identify

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Skills** | **Hard skills** — coding languages, for example — and **soft skills** such as communication |
| **Seniority** | Junior, mid-level or senior, matched to **the project's demands and complexity** |
| **Domain expertise** | Whether previous experience in a particular sector is needed — financial services, construction |
| **Qualifications** | Whether **industry-specific qualifications** are required — CEng, ChPP |

**How to work them out:** ask **subject-matter experts**; look at **what comparable projects resourced and what they learned**; or run **a skills analysis such as job role mapping.**

That middle route is the LO6 link — lessons learned from a comparable project is the cheapest source of a realistic resource profile.

## Estimating capacity

Once skills and competences are established, **estimate the capacity required from each resource**:

- **full-time or part-time requirement**
- **how much effort, in hours or days each week**

**Past data and expert judgement both help here**, together with **top-down and bottom-up estimating used in combination** — the LO19 methods applied to people rather than money.

## Constraints that shape the answer

**As the picture sharpens, weigh what cost, time and quality will each permit.** The factors named:

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Resource availability** | What actually exists to be had |
| **Budget** | What can be afforded |
| **Seniority** | Senior people cost more and are scarcer |
| **Hiring lead times** | How long it takes to get someone who is not already there |
| **Location** | **A key consideration in a hybrid working world** |

Together they settle **whether the resource comes from inside or is brought in** — the make-or-buy question from LO5, applied to people.

## Life cycle changes when resources are needed

A specific and examinable point:

| Life cycle | Resource profile |
|---|---|
| **Linear** | Design and planning specialisms tend to be **concentrated at the front** |
| **Iterative** | **A similar project may require those skills throughout the entire life cycle** |

Same project, same skills, entirely different demand curve. That is the answer to any scenario asking how life cycle choice affects resourcing.

## Working with HR

**Work with human resources experts to understand how resource requirements align with established job roles in the organisation.** This **standardises resource profiles** and gives a foundation for the rest of capacity planning.

## Availability: the wider picture

Resource capacity planning is **typically managed at programme, portfolio or organisational level** and runs in three parts:

1. **Identifying resource requirements** — per project
2. **Assessing total capacity** — setting demand against capacity across programmes and portfolios
3. **Capacity optimisation** — squeezing the most benefit out of what exists

**And the honest constraint:** **demand sometimes exceeds capacity, and something has to give.** What you do then is **lay out clearly what each initiative is worth, how it ranks and what it depends on**, so **stakeholders can choose between them on the facts.**

That is the correct scenario answer when a project cannot get the people it needs: not to escalate for more, but to give decision-makers what they need to choose between initiatives.

**Get resource requests in early — late ones cost you time** — and **go to the resource managers** to start the allocation conversation.
core_content.outcome_title: Determining resource requirements and availability

Show exactly one A per row — the single-accountability rule is the point the diagram should make visually, so a reader scanning a row sees one A and possibly several Rs and Cs.

core_content.key_takeaway: The OBS says who is on the project; the WBS says what work exists. Combine them and you get a RAM, coded with RACI so every work item has exactly one accountable owner.
core_content.body_markdown:
## The two inputs

| Structure | What it defines |
|---|---|
| **OBS** — organisation breakdown structure | The **people** — created by the choice of organisational structure, visualising the project hierarchy |
| **WBS** — work breakdown structure | The **work** — scope broken down into **work packages representing the lowest level of work you intend to manage** |

**The OBS comes from the structural decision.** Choosing functional, matrix or project (LO2) **creates the project's organisational breakdown structure**, which then **enables the identification of resource requirements**.

**The WBS needs enough granularity.** By the end of the breakdown, **every item needs to be defined finely enough that it can be estimated and put on a schedule.** Too coarse and you cannot allocate; too fine and you are managing minutiae.

## Combining them

**Put the WBS and the OBS together and you get a responsibility assignment matrix.** Work down one axis, people across the other.

What it shows: **each separate item of work, who has been put on it, and what part they play.**

## RACI coding

The roles are shown using **RACI coding**:

| Letter | Role | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| **R** | **Responsible** | **Conducting** each piece of work |
| **A** | **Accountable** | **Owns it, and signs it off once done** |
| **C** | **Consulted** | **Brought into the decisions, and supports the work along the way** |
| **I** | **Informed** | **About the work's progress** |

**The distinction that carries the marks: R does it, A owns it and signs it off.** They can be the same person, but the accountability does not move even when the work is delegated — the same principle as sponsor and project manager in LO2, applied at task level.

**One accountable per work item.** Two people accountable for the same thing means nobody is.

## What the RAM is actually for

Three uses, all named in the source:

1. **Allocating resources at the correct times**, in line with the project's schedule.
2. **Setting resources' expectations of what is required** of them.
3. **Tying each person and their piece of work back to what the project is for** — which is the LO12 motivation point: people work better when they can see why their piece matters.

## It is not fixed

**Structure and allocation both shift as the project moves and new information lands.** So **continue to regularly engage with resource managers** to ensure **new or updated allocations are agreed and actioned** — a process that **starts during resource identification** and does not stop there.

**And where a change to resource requirements is needed:** **weigh what it does to things like quality and cost**, then **put a formal change request against the baseline** through **the organisation's change control process**, so that **change requests and impact assessments are reviewed with proper transparency and control** (LO24).

Left — linear: design and planning specialisms spiking early, build resource peaking mid-project, testing late; an uneven profile with distinct humps. Right — iterative: a flatter, sustained profile with the same skill mix present across every timebox, marked with timebox boundaries. The contrast in shape is the argument for why life cycle choice changes resourcing.

core_content.key_takeaway: Resources are categorised by type, by skill and seniority, and by whether they are internal or external. Linear schedules allocate against a fixed plan with front-loaded specialisms; iterative schedules commit resource per timebox and need capabilities available throughout.
core_content.body_markdown:
## How resources get categorised

Pulling the categorisations together from across the source:

| Basis | Categories |
|---|---|
| **Type** | **Labour** — your own people or contracted in; **services** bought in, such as development work or legal advice; **materials and consumables**, whether finished or raw; **assets** like equipment, vehicles and infrastructure, purchased, leased or rented |
| **Skills** | **Hard skills** and **soft skills** |
| **Seniority** | Junior, mid-level, senior |
| **Domain and qualification** | Sector expertise; industry-specific qualifications |
| **Source** | **Internal or external** |
| **Commitment** | **Full-time or part-time**, estimated in hours or days per week |

**A scheduling consequence worth knowing:** **some organisations put every resource into the schedule** — materials and procurement phasing included — while **others schedule labour alone** — with **non-labour costs appearing only in the budget** (LO22). Both are legitimate; the scenario tells you which is in play.

## Allocating in a linear schedule

1. **Define the work** through the WBS into work packages.
2. **Pin down as precisely as you can the start and end of every work package.**
3. **Build the RAM** and use it to **allocate resources at the correct times, in line with the schedule.**
4. **Request allocation** from resource managers, as early as possible.

**The demand profile is front-loaded for specialisms** — design and planning skills concentrated early. Resource conflicts are resolved by levelling or smoothing (21d) before the deployment baseline is set.

**Because the plan is fixed at approval**, a change in resource requirement is a change to the baseline and goes through change control.

## Allocating in an iterative schedule

**Iterative projects commit resources over limited periods — timeboxes.** Within a timebox, **a fixed period with determined resources is agreed**, and the work is completed as efficiently as possible.

| | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| **Commitment horizon** | The whole plan, fixed at approval | **One timebox at a time** |
| **Skill demand curve** | **Front-loaded** design and planning specialisms | **Those skills needed throughout the entire life cycle** |
| **What flexes** | Time and cost flex against fixed scope and quality | **Time and cost are fixed; scope and quality flex** |
| **Team shape** | Specialists arrive and leave as their phase runs | Stable cross-functional team held across iterations |
| **Adjusting resource** | Change request against the baseline | Adjust what enters the next timebox |

**The practical consequence:** an iterative project needs its capabilities available continuously, so a specialist who can only be released for four weeks is a genuine constraint on the approach — not merely a scheduling inconvenience.

## Managing resources once allocated

**Resources directly contribute to the deliverables**, so they need managing closely. **Four common monitoring methods:**

| Method | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| **Timesheets** | How many hours each person actually put into project work |
| **Monitoring tasks** | Whether **work is completed on time and to quality** |
| **Stakeholder feedback** | How the resource is actually performing |
| **Resource histogram or demand profile** | **Utilisation, visualised** |

Data gets collated into a **resource management report**, setting **performance, availability and utilisation against what the project expected.**

## Resource management governance

**Establish it as early as possible**, so there is a route to **report progress, raise issues, and keep expectations aligned with the resource managers.** It should:

- **report how resources are performing**, with **escalation routes and fallback plans ready for underperformance**
- **monitor constraints affecting resource availability**, feeding into **organisational capacity planning and risk management**
- **track resource utilisation**, giving **transparency on actual utilisation against the project's forecast**

**And the standing reality:** you are **permanently in competition with other projects and programmes for the same people.** That is why levelling and smoothing exist — they are what you do **when constraints cannot be overcome.**
core_content.outcome_title: Categorising and allocating resources across linear and iterative schedules

Second — levelled: peaks cut to sit under the ceiling, with the end date visibly extended to the right and that extension labelled. Third — smoothed: the end date held at the original position with a vertical marker, peaks flattened by adding resource, and the added resource shaded to show the cost impact. Each panel labelled with its question: 'when can it finish?' for levelling, 'what do we need?' for smoothing.

core_content.key_takeaway: Levelling holds resources fixed and lets the timeline move: with what we have, when can this finish? Smoothing holds scope, quality and time and accepts a cost impact: what resource do we need to hit the date?
core_content.body_markdown:
## The two techniques

Both are ways of **making project-level resource capacity go further once the constraint itself cannot be shifted.** They are **the two most common** examples.

The cleanest way to hold them is by the question each one answers — the source frames them exactly this way, and the questions are more reliable than any rule of thumb.

| | **Resource levelling** | **Resource smoothing** |
|---|---|---|
| **The question it answers** | Given the people we actually have, **when does this finish?** | To hit what we promised, **what resource do we need?** |
| **What is held fixed** | **Resource constraints** | **Scope, quality and time** |
| **What is allowed to move** | **The timeline** | **Cost** |
| **Use when** | You cannot get more resource | The date cannot move |

**Levelling: resources are fixed, so the end date flexes.** You work out what the available people can actually deliver and when that finishes.

**Smoothing: the date is fixed, so cost flexes.** You work out what resource is needed to hit the commitments and accept the bill.

**A memory hook worth carrying:** **levelling moves the level of the finish line; smoothing smooths the peaks and troughs and pays for it.**

## What each involves in practice

**Levelling** leans on **critical path or critical chain** to rework the tasks and the schedule, wringing the most out of whoever is available right now. It is scheduling beneath a resource ceiling.

**Smoothing** is more than simply adding people. It is **not simply a matter of hiring more people** — it also means **finding ways to get more out of existing capacity, or rearranging work so the peaks and troughs flatten.**

That second half is the more interesting one for a scenario answer. Reshaping *when* work happens, so demand sits flatter across the same period, is smoothing without buying anything.

## The output

**What project-level optimisation produces is a curve: how resource — and so how spend — is planned to be deployed over time to finish the scope at the quality required.**

That curve is what feeds LO22, because costing works from the resourced schedule. Levelling and smoothing happen before the budget is finalised, not after.

## Optimisation above project level

At **programme, portfolio or organisational level**, optimisation works differently:

- **resequencing or phasing initiatives so their resource demands stop colliding**
- **identifying synergies between initiatives**
- **project and programme phasing** more strategically

So a resource conflict a project cannot solve internally may be solvable by the portfolio deciding which initiative goes first. That is the escalation route, and it connects to LO2 — the decision sits above the project's authority.

## When neither works

**Demand outstrips capacity sometimes, and a trade-off becomes unavoidable.** The answer is not more optimisation: it is **setting out plainly what each initiative is worth, where it ranks and what it depends on, so stakeholders can make the priority call on the facts.**

And where the project's own resource requirement must change, **work out what that does to quality and cost**, then **take a formal change request to the baseline** through **change control**.

misconceptions.wrong: Resource management means managing people.

misconceptions.right: They are identified once the high-level scope is established, because scope is what provides clarity on the work to be completed. And allocation continues to change as the project progresses.
misconceptions.wrong: Resource requirements are identified at the start of the project.

misconceptions.right: Responsible means conducting the work. Accountable means owning it and approving it when complete. They can be the same person, but accountability does not transfer when work is delegated.
misconceptions.wrong: In a RAM, responsible and accountable are the same thing.

misconceptions.right: Accountability shared is accountability absent. One A per work item — the same principle that separates sponsor from project manager, applied at task level.
misconceptions.wrong: A work item can have several accountable people if it spans teams.

misconceptions.right: Linear work tends to concentrate design and planning specialisms at the front; comparable iterative work needs them present in every iteration. Same skills, different demand curve.
misconceptions.wrong: Linear and iterative projects need the same resources at the same times.

misconceptions.right: Levelling optimises the timeline when resources are fixed — with what we have, when can it finish. Smoothing achieves scope, quality and time while accepting an impact on cost — what resource is needed to hit the date.
misconceptions.wrong: Resource levelling and smoothing are two names for flattening the resource histogram.

misconceptions.right: It does not necessarily mean just adding resources. It also identifies ways to increase current capacity, or to better manage the work to avoid peaks and troughs — reshaping when work happens rather than buying more.
misconceptions.wrong: Resource smoothing means adding more people.

misconceptions.right: Demand outstrips capacity sometimes and a trade-off becomes unavoidable. What you do is set out what each initiative is worth, where it ranks and what it depends on, so stakeholders can make the call on the facts.
misconceptions.wrong: If the project cannot get the resource it needs, escalate for more.

misconceptions.right: Costing works from the resourced schedule. Levelling and smoothing produce the deployment curve the budget is then built on.
misconceptions.wrong: Resource optimisation happens after the budget is set.

misconceptions.right: Impacts should be assessed against factors such as quality and cost, then a change to the baseline formally requested through the organisation's change control process.

key_definitions.plain_english: Anything the work consumes. In practice, usually people.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Anything that is needed to complete a project, though the emphasis falls on people resources and how best to leverage their skills and experience.

key_definitions.plain_english: The project's people, broken down into a hierarchy. One half of what makes a RAM.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The structure created by the choice of organisational structure, visualising the project hierarchy and enabling identification of resource requirements.

key_definitions.plain_english: Work down one axis, people across the other, roles in the cells. The grid that stops 'I thought you were doing that'.

key_definitions.plain_english: Four letters, four relationships to a task. Only one person should be accountable for any one item.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The coding used within a RAM to define who is Responsible for conducting each piece of work, Accountable for owning and approving it, Consulted during decision-making, and Informed about progress.

key_definitions.plain_english: Resources are what they are — so the end date moves to fit them.

key_definitions.plain_english: The date holds — so you find the resource to make it happen, and pay for it.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A technique that ensures scope, quality and time are achieved while accepting an impact on cost, answering the question: what resources are required to deliver the expectations?

key_definitions.plain_english: A bar chart of demand over time. Peaks and troughs are what levelling and smoothing attack.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A visualisation of resource utilisation over time, used to show performance, availability and utilisation against the project's expectations.

key_definitions.plain_english: Working out what all the projects need against what the organisation actually has.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The process, typically managed at programme, portfolio or organisational level, of establishing resource requirements, assessing total capacity, and optimising capacity to create maximum benefit.

key_definitions.plain_english: How much of someone's time the project is really getting, against how much it planned for.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The proportion of a resource's available capacity actually used on project work, tracked to provide transparency on actual utilisation against the project's forecast.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Where budgeting sits

Budgeting and cost control has **four elements**:

1. **estimating what it will cost**
2. **agreeing a budget**
3. **tracking actual and forecast spend against that budget**
4. **shutting the finances down properly at the end**

The first two are 22a; the third is 22b; the fourth closes the LO.

**Cost planning runs alongside resource planning and scheduling**, and takes **the resource-optimised schedule as one of its inputs.** That ordering matters and is worth stating in an answer: you cannot cost a schedule you have not built, or a resource plan you have not levelled.

## The cost breakdown structure

The **CBS** defines scope in terms of **the project budget** — the fourth of the breakdown structures from LO17 and LO20.

| Structure | Defines |
|---|---|
| PBS | The things to create |
| WBS | The activities to complete |
| OBS | The allocation of people |
| **CBS** | **The project budget** |

Building the budget through a CBS means every cost traces to a work package and a deliverable. That is what makes variance analysis possible later — an overspend can be located, not just observed.

## The cost types to know

**All types of cost** get considered:

| Category | Covers |
|---|---|
| **Labour** | People, **both internal and contracted** |
| **Services** | Software development, legal advice |
| **Materials and consumables** | **Both finished and raw materials** |
| **Assets** | Equipment, vehicles, infrastructure — **bought, leased or rented** |

And the behavioural distinctions the syllabus names:

| Pair | Distinction |
|---|---|
| **Fixed vs variable** | A **fixed cost is unaffected by scale or quantity; a variable cost moves with how much you use or make** |
| **One-off vs recurring** | **Pay it once** — buying a computer — or **pay it again and again**, like a software licence renewal |
| **Capital vs revenue** | **How each is treated follows the organisation's accounting rules**, and **capital spend is often controlled tightly, especially in the public sector** |
| **Direct vs indirect** | Direct costs attach to a specific work package or deliverable; indirect costs support the project without being traceable to one item |

**The fixed/variable distinction behaves differently in an iterative life cycle.** In linear work, fixed cost sits as a baseline with variable cost rising by quantity. In iterative work, **each iteration carries its own fixed cost**, and total cost rises in steps by released scope rather than smoothly by units made. That is why **a client or sponsor can cap future commitment simply by cutting how many iterations are funded** — each one being a discrete, largely fixed cost.

## Scheduling the money, not just totalling it

**Beyond totalling the budget, costs get profiled across the initiative's life — a cash flow forecast.** In earned value terms this cost profile is the **budgeted cost of work scheduled (BCWS)** — which is the same thing as planned value.

So the budget is not a number, it is a curve. That curve becomes the baseline everything in 22b is measured against.

**Timing of funding release** matters too: **money may only be released once products ship, certification passes, or a stage gate clears.** On iterative work, **funding release is often tied to iterations.** A budget that exists but cannot be drawn down yet is not available money.

## Estimating the costs

**Approaches differ by cost type.** Material costs come off **published prices, multiplied by estimated volumes**. Subcontractors on **time and materials** need an estimate of the hours they will work; on **fixed price**, the supplier estimates the time and **includes contingency or a risk premium** — the LO5 link, where fixed price transfers risk and the supplier prices it in.

**The bias to watch: optimism bias.** It is **the most prominent**, the tendency to **assume everything will run the ideal course.** Two counters:

- **review and challenge processes**
- **contingency for each cost area**

## Whole-life costing

**Sustainability is important in project-based working**, and **whole-life costing** is one way to ensure long-term impacts are considered — **increasingly, budgets are planned to the end-of-life and decommissioning stages.**

This is the LO3 link made financial. The cheapest option to build is frequently not the cheapest to own, and LO5's lifetime cost of ownership makes the same argument in procurement.

## Contingency and management reserve

**There is no magic purse with unlimited funds**, so experienced professionals ensure budgets include **contingency and a management reserve.**

| Type | Covers | Released by |
|---|---|---|
| **Planned contingency** | **Known risks and anticipated events** | Authority to draw down, once the risk occurs |
| **Management or project reserve** | **Unanticipated issues** | **The governance board** |

**It is not a secret stash that makes problems disappear. It is a management tool, and governance controls it.**

**It can appear as** line items in a budget, **additional timeboxed iterations**, or **a management reserve across the whole project.**

**Different levels can hold contingency** for different kinds of risk. **Handing the whole lot to the project professional takes real trust from sponsor and board** — they need confidence it will **only be spent where genuinely needed**. And **things like currency or interest rate exposure sit better at organisational level.**

## Governance sits over all of it

**Every pound spent falls under governance oversight and decision-making**, which puts **cost planning right at the centre of governance.** **How much detail and rigour is applied depends on the organisation, on how risky and how large the initiative is, and on which workstream or phase you are in** — and **iterative life cycles can control expenditure more easily, so can tolerate reduced rigour at the outset.**
