core_content.body_markdown:
## What cost control does

**Budget set and expenditure scheduled, delivery starts and the money goes out. Managing what actually gets spent against what was budgeted is cost control.**

**The baseline is that same cash flow forecast the project was approved on.** Monitoring happens against that and the approved budget.

**How often to monitor:** **track spend as close to real time as you can manage — and the quicker money is going out, the more often you should be looking.** A useful, specific rule.

**Project systems can hook into enterprise accounting software** and report expenditure in real time — but even those **run behind whatever the project has already committed to.** Committed is not the same as recorded, and **holding an accurate, current picture of budget status is genuinely hard**, which is why **big projects bring in dedicated finance and cost management specialists.**

## Why monitor

| Reason | What it enables |
|---|---|
| **The primary reason** | So that a deviation from plan can be corrected quickly |
| **Recovery or re-forecast** | If expenditure will exceed budget, the team investigates and intervenes. **Where the original budget cannot be recovered, a revised expenditure forecast gets produced** — and that **may need signing off by a client, sponsor or governance structure** |
| **Authorising payment** | Knowing **when contractors have met their obligations**, so payments can be authorised **subject to any outstanding quality control** |
| **Supporting stage gates** | Often what unlocks **the next tranche of budget** |
| **Contingency drawdown** | Where overspends cannot be recovered, seeking authority to **draw down budgeted contingency** — or in extreme cases **additional, unbudgeted funding** |

## What financial reports contain

**Good governance needs good information.** Reports combine three things:

1. **where things stand now, and which way they are trending**
2. **a look backwards at why the plan was missed**
3. **a look forwards — the forecast, and what will be done about it**

All three. A report with status but no reasons cannot be acted on; one with no forecast tells the board nothing about where this ends.

**Who wants them:** the sponsor, project board, PMO or corporate finance function — and **stakeholders beyond the sponsoring organisation**, including **lenders, investors, grant-giving bodies or shareholders**, who **want to know the money they lent, invested or gave is being used wisely.** For substantial programmes, financial reports **may appear in statutory reporting and annual reports.**

## Earned value

Earned value analysis solves a specific problem. Comparing budget to actual spend tells you how much you spent, but not what you got for it — a project that has spent half its budget might be half built or barely started. **Earned value adds the third measure that makes the comparison meaningful.**

### The four base measures

| Measure | Also called | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **PV** — planned value | **BCWS**, budgeted cost of work **scheduled** | What the work planned for this point was budgeted to cost |
| **EV** — earned value | **BCWP**, budgeted cost of work **performed** | What the work actually completed was budgeted to cost |
| **AC** — actual cost | **ACWP**, actual cost of work performed | What has actually been spent |
| **BAC** — budget at completion | | The total approved budget |

**The trick to remembering BCWS and BCWP:** both are *budgeted* costs. **Scheduled** is what you planned to have done; **performed** is what you have done. Only ACWP is a real-money figure.

### The derived measures

| Measure | Formula | Reads as |
|---|---|---|
| **CV** — cost variance | **EV − AC** | Negative = over budget |
| **SV** — schedule variance | **EV − PV** | Negative = behind schedule |
| **CPI** — cost performance index | **EV ÷ AC** | Below 1.0 = over budget |
| **SPI** — schedule performance index | **EV ÷ PV** | Below 1.0 = behind schedule |
| **EAC** — estimate at completion | **BAC ÷ CPI** | Forecast final cost if current efficiency continues |

**Both variances subtract from EV. Both indices divide EV.** Get that and the formulas stop needing memorisation — what changes is whether you compare against actual cost (money) or planned value (progress).

### Worked example

A project with a **budget at completion of £240,000**, reviewed at the end of month 6:

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| PV (BCWS) — work scheduled by now | £120,000 |
| EV (BCWP) — work actually completed | £96,000 |
| AC (ACWP) — actually spent | £128,000 |

**Cost variance:** CV = EV − AC = £96,000 − £128,000 = **−£32,000**. Negative, so **over budget**.

**Schedule variance:** SV = EV − PV = £96,000 − £120,000 = **−£24,000**. Negative, so **behind schedule**.

**Cost performance index:** CPI = EV ÷ AC = 96,000 ÷ 128,000 = **0.75**. For every £1 spent, **75p of budgeted value has been earned**.

**Schedule performance index:** SPI = EV ÷ PV = 96,000 ÷ 120,000 = **0.80**. The project is earning value at **80% of the planned rate**.

**Estimate at completion:** EAC = BAC ÷ CPI = £240,000 ÷ 0.75 = **£320,000**.

**Forecast overspend:** £320,000 − £240,000 = **£80,000**, a third over budget, **if current cost efficiency continues.**

**Reading it in one sentence:** the project has completed less work than planned and spent more than that work was worth, so it is both behind and over — and on current performance will finish about a third above budget.

**The sanity check to apply:** CV and CPI must agree, and SV and SPI must agree. If CV is negative, CPI must be below 1.0. If they disagree, an input is wrong.

### What EVA gives you

CPI shows **how efficiently money is being turned into value**; SPI shows **how productively work is being completed**. Between them they let **schedule and budget performance be judged side by side** — the only technique in the course that does.

**And the exception worth knowing:** **none of this applies under critical chain**, which watches **rate of buffer consumption** instead — buffer used against chain completed. **Where a customer insists on the earned value figures, they can be generated from an unbuffered version of the schedule.**

## Iterative life cycles are easier to control

**Monitoring and controlling an iterative project is usually easier**, because **most of what an iteration costs is fixed**, and **future commitment can be capped by funding fewer iterations.**

But the honest counterweight from the financial reporting section: an iterative approach is often chosen **when there is high uncertainty about the specification or the development process**, which **makes the funding requirement hard to judge at the start** and **forecasting difficult — unless the project runs to a fixed total budget.**

So iterative work is easier to *control* and harder to *forecast*. Both are true, and a scenario answer that says only one of them is half an answer.

## Financial closedown

The fourth element, and the one candidates forget:

| Task | What it involves |
|---|---|
| **Meet outstanding commitments** | **Invoices from contractors, consultants and suppliers all get processed and paid.** A contract is not complete until every bill against it has been settled |
| **Secure transition funding** | Where budgets include transition activities, **secure drawdown of those funds** |
| **Return contingency** | Professionals **aim not to draw down all contingency or management reserves**. These may be **returned to the organisation**, or **held as reserves for other initiatives** within a portfolio or programme |
| **Close out timesheets and expenses** | **The last costs to surface are usually unsubmitted timesheets and expense claims**, so **put a deadline on them** |
| **Assess financial performance** | **Compare actual expenditure against the business case budget**, with a **final financial report** |
| **Close cost centres and archive** | Close project-specific cost centres, **review team access to finance systems**, and **secure and archive financial records per organisational policy** so they are **available for any potential future audit** |

That last row connects to LO6 and LO15: records are retained because someone may need to audit them, and retention is governed by policy and legislation.

key_definitions.apm_definition: Managing actual costs against the budget during delivery — forecasting costs, monitoring spending, controlling variances and reporting on status.

core_content.key_takeaway: Risk and issue management minimises the effects of uncertainty, producing a more robust baseline and plan. Contingency is what converts an identified risk into a funded response — planned contingency for known risks, management reserve for the rest.
core_content.body_markdown:
## The two disciplines

| | Risk management | Issue management |
|---|---|---|
| **What it handles** | Uncertainty that **has not happened yet** — threats and opportunities | Something that **has happened** and exceeded tolerance |
| **Process** | Identify, assess and respond appropriately | React appropriately, including **escalation to the relevant authority** |
| **Who resolves it** | Risk owner, within the plan | **Requires support from the sponsor to agree a resolution** |

**The definition that decides which process applies:** an issue arises **the moment delegated work breaches its tolerances — or is certain to.**

**And the distinction candidates miss:** **issues are different to problems.** A **problem** is dealt with day to day by the project manager and the team. An **issue** needs the sponsor. The dividing line is tolerance, not severity or inconvenience.

**They are related but not the same:**

- **A risk, or a cluster of them, materialising is often what produces an issue.**
- **An issue running now can itself generate fresh risks**, and can **force you to re-score how likely and how damaging risks you had already logged now look.**

So a materialised risk becomes an issue, and that issue seeds new risks. The two registers talk to each other.

## The benefits

Direct answer to 23a:

| Benefit | How it arises |
|---|---|
| **Minimises the effects of uncertainty** | The core purpose. **All projects bring change and therefore uncertainty** |
| **A more robust deployment baseline and PMP** | Stated directly as the result |
| **Confidence to stakeholders** | They can see risk is being got ahead of rather than reacted to |
| **Protects organisational reputation** | Named explicitly |
| **Realistic plans and appropriate contingency** | Analysis sizes the contingency rather than guessing it |
| **Prioritisation** | **It is unrealistic to believe every risk can be managed**, so prioritisation lets **the top risks be addressed** |
| **Better escalation** | Analysis reveals **which risks warrant the sponsor's or the board's attention** |
| **Opportunities captured** | Uncertainty sometimes **helps you hit your objectives rather than hindering** |
| **Decisions at the right level** | Issue management **keeps people inside the authority they were given, and puts each resolution decision at the level that should be taking it** |

That last one is the strongest argument for issue management specifically, and it links straight to LO2.

## A diagnostic worth knowing

**Where issues keep arriving, the plans and the controls themselves are probably the problem.**

A useful scenario answer. Repeated issues are a symptom, not just a run of bad luck — the tolerances, the plan or the controls are probably wrong.

**And a related bias:** **project professionals understandably prioritise issues over risks, because issues are happening now whereas risks are only potential.** Understandable, but it is how a project ends up permanently firefighting.

## Contingency

**Contingency planning means putting resource aside that exists for one purpose only: responding to risk and uncertainty.** It **bridges the gap that risk creates**, covering:

- **known risks**
- **unknown risks**
- **the uncertainty of early-project estimates**

That third category is the one candidates forget: contingency covers estimating uncertainty as well as identified risk events.

**Two types:**

| Type | Covers | Released by |
|---|---|---|
| **Planned contingency** | **Known risks and anticipated events** | Authority to draw down when the risk occurs |
| **Management or project reserve** | **Unanticipated issues** | **The governance board** |

**Contingency is time as well as money** — buffers in the schedule as much as reserve in the budget. **References to budget contingency apply equally to schedule contingency.**

**And the framing that matters:** **contingency is not a secret stash that makes problems disappear. Governance controls it, as a management tool.**

**The drawdown route** (LO22): risk previously identified → planned contingency. Not identified → management reserve, released by the board. Reserve insufficient → **change request for additional funding.**

**Analysis sizes it.** Probabilistic analysis is what lets you **settle how much contingency buys the confidence level you need** — which is why no business case or plan is complete without risk analysis behind it.
core_content.outcome_title: The benefits of risk and issue management, and the role of contingency

core_content.key_takeaway: Risk runs identification, analysis, response, monitoring, escalation and closure — iteratively. Issues run logging and analysis, escalation, assignment of actions, change control and tracking to closure. Iterative life cycles run both far more frequently and at lower ceremony.
core_content.body_markdown:
## The risk management process

| Stage | Purpose and why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Identification** | Surface **every risk to the objectives that can be known about**, using stakeholder expertise to do it. Describe each as **cause, event and impact** so opinions align and group bias is addressed. Assign a **risk owner** — the individual or group **best placed to assess and manage it**. Document in the **risk register** |
| **Analysis** | Assess **probability and impact** to prioritise. **It is unrealistic to believe every risk can be managed**, so this is what makes the top risks visible |
| **Response** | Decide and plan the response — proactive or reactive (23c). If investing time and money is justified, **resources are planned and agreed** and **the deployment baseline and PMP updated** |
| **Monitoring** | **Keeping the risk conversation alive is crucial.** The process **captures and manages emerging risks**; **new knowledge is acted upon and contingency estimates refined** |
| **Escalation** | **Priority risks go up to the sponsor or the governance board**, which is how **expectations get managed and decisions get made on evidence** |
| **Closure** | **Close a risk once it has happened, or once it no longer can** |

**It cycles rather than concludes, because project work itself keeps moving.** Not a stage you complete.

**Closure is the stage most often skipped.** A register full of risks that can no longer happen buries the ones that still can.

## Risk analysis in more detail

**Two techniques:**

| Technique | What it does | When |
|---|---|---|
| **Qualitative** | **Ranks risk events** on **how likely they are** and **how hard they would hit schedule, cost, benefits and any other objective at stake** | **As a minimum**, always. **For many projects a qualitative approach is sufficient** |
| **Quantitative** | **Focuses on specific risk-based decisions** — **decision trees, sensitivity analysis**, or a holistic view of overall project risk | **For large or complex projects**, and to **support the investment decision** |

**Probabilistic analysis** — **Monte Carlo simulation** is the example given — **predicts the probability of a variety of outcomes**. Its outputs help you:

- see **how likely a given end date, final cost or benefit level actually is**
- **put odds on delivering the business case and the plan**, and decide accordingly
- **fix contingency at the level that buys the confidence required**

**Two points about people, not technique:**

- **Focus on the objectives that are at risk**, then **fine-tune project-specific impact scales**. Generic scales produce generic prioritisation.
- **What looks risky, and why, varies from person to person**, so **get a spread of project professionals into the analysis** — their **different perspectives add value and integrity to the process.**

## The issue management process

**Wherever the issue came from, you run the same process:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Log and analyse** | Straight into the **issue register**, then **analysed fast** — what caused it, and what it costs if left |
| **Escalate** | **To the sponsor, who may in turn escalate to the governance board for resolution** |
| **Assign actions** | To whoever is genuinely best placed to own it |
| **Apply change control** | An issue can end up changing scope, and when it does the agreed change control process applies |
| **Track to closure** | **Management is tracked from identification through to resolution** |
| **Update risk analysis** | Because a current issue may cause new risks or change existing assessments |

**Speed is part of the process.** 'Analysis takes place quickly' is stated for issues and not for risks — an unresolved issue is actively consuming the project.

## The two barriers

**Simple enough as a concept — but two things reliably stop it working:**

1. **Reluctance to escalate issues early.** Which connects to LO12 and LO14 — a blame culture guarantees late escalation.
2. **The governance board treating the symptom rather than addressing the root cause.**

Naming either in a scenario answer is worth more than reciting the process steps.

## How the stages differ by life cycle

The syllabus asks this specifically.

| | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| **Identification** | Concentrated **in the early stages**, often through **group workshops**, feeding the initial risk register | Continuous — each iteration surfaces risks as scope is drawn down |
| **Analysis** | Fuller up-front analysis supporting a business case approved once | Lighter, repeated. Detail arrives with the work |
| **Response** | Responses planned into the baseline; changing them means change control | Responses can be absorbed into the next iteration's plan |
| **Monitoring** | At defined review points and gates | **At the end of every iteration**, alongside the value-proposition test |
| **Escalation** | Through the governance structure at gates or by exception | More frequent, lower ceremony — but the same tolerance principle |
| **Closure** | At review points | Each iteration closes risks that can no longer occur |
| **Contingency** | Held as budget and schedule buffers | **Can appear as additional timeboxed iterations** |

**The structural reason for the difference:** an iterative project **re-justifies itself every cycle**, so risk review is built into the rhythm. A linear project reviews at gates, and between them the machinery is change control.

**But the principle holds either way.** No business case and no plan — project or programme, whichever life cycle — is complete without risk analysis behind it. Iterative does not mean less rigorous — it means more often and closer to the work.
core_content.outcome_title: The risk and issue management processes, and how they differ by life cycle

core_content.key_takeaway: Three proactive responses each side — avoid, reduce, transfer for threats; exploit, enhance, share for opportunities. Reactive means planning the response but implementing only if it materialises: accept a threat, reject an opportunity.
core_content.body_markdown:
## The two modes

| Mode | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Proactive** | **A planned and implemented response: 'We do something now.'** |
| **Reactive** | The response gets worked out now and sits unused unless the risk actually happens |

The distinction is *when you act*, not how serious the risk is. A reactive response is still a planned response — the plan simply sits waiting.

## The six proactive responses

| | **Threats** | **Opportunities** |
|---|---|---|
| **Change the scope** | **Avoid** — change the scope to **eliminate the cause** | **Exploit** — change the scope to **make sure the opportunity happens** |
| **Change probability or impact** | **Reduce** how likely the threat is, how much it would hurt, or both | **Enhance** — push up how likely the opportunity is, how much it would gain, or both |
| **Involve another party** | **Transfer** the cost — **insure against it**, or **hand it to someone better equipped to carry it** | **Share** the benefit, **possibly through a joint venture** |

**Learn them as three mirrored pairs, not six items.** Avoid mirrors exploit; reduce mirrors enhance; transfer mirrors share. Each pair uses the same mechanism, pointed in opposite directions.

## The two reactive responses

| Side | Response | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Threat** | **Accept** | The threat is **accepted with a contingent response** — you carry it, with a plan ready |
| **Opportunity** | **Reject** | The opportunity **may not be worthwhile** pursuing |

**Accept is not the same as ignore.** It is a decision, recorded, usually with contingency behind it. **Reject is not pessimism** — it is a judgement that chasing this opportunity costs more than it returns.

## Choosing a response

**Someone has to decide whether spending time and money up front to cut exposure is worth it** — and **how much exposure is tolerable is set by what the investors and wider stakeholders are willing to carry.**

That is the deciding factor, and it is not the project manager's to set. LO1's risk appetite reappears here as the thing that determines how much response is warranted.

**Where investing is justified:**

- **the resources it takes get planned and agreed**
- **the deployment baseline and the PMP both get updated**

A risk response is scheduled, resourced work. It is not free, and it changes the plan.

## Perception shapes response

**People perceive risk in different ways.** **Plenty of factors shape how someone reads risk and what attitude they take to it — some conscious, some not, some purely emotional** — so you have to **talk to a spread of stakeholders to find out where each of them stands.**

**Without that engagement the responses you design will not be ones anybody actually adopts.** Without it you get responses that are technically correct and that nobody will actually implement.

## Opportunity management

The half of risk that gets forgotten. **Uncertainty sometimes helps you hit your objectives — that is risk's positive face.**

**Look for opportunities across the whole life cycle, and run them through exactly the process and tools you use on threats.**

Same identification, same analysis, same register, same owner, same monitoring. The only thing that changes is the direction of the impact and which three responses apply.

**A useful test in a scenario:** if a project's risk register contains only threats, opportunity management is not happening. That is a finding worth stating.
core_content.outcome_title: Proactive and reactive responses to threats and opportunities

core_content.key_takeaway: Tolerances define what the project can absorb and what must escalate. Governance sets risk appetite, receives escalation, releases contingency, and makes the decisions that exceed the project's authority — including cancelling the project.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Tolerances are the mechanism

**Get the tolerance levels agreed, or issue management has nothing to stand on.**

That sentence carries the whole sub-outcome. Tolerance is what converts a judgement call into a rule: inside it, the project manager acts; outside it, someone else decides. It is LO2's delegated limits of authority, applied to uncertainty.

**What escalation buys**, stated directly: an issue goes up to people who:

- **see the organisation more strategically than the project can**
- **can put more resource behind it if that is what it takes**
- **have the authority to change scope**

**And the ultimate power:** where an issue leaves the project unviable, **it can be cancelled.**

That is the strongest single reason governance matters here. No amount of project-level effort can cancel a project that should be cancelled.

## What governance provides

| Governance function | Why risk and issue management needs it |
|---|---|
| **Sets risk appetite** | How much exposure is tolerable comes from **what the investors and wider stakeholders will carry** — not from the project |
| **Sets tolerances** | Defines the boundary between a problem and an issue |
| **Receives escalation** | **Priority risks travel up to the sponsor or the governance board** |
| **Releases contingency** | Planned contingency is drawn down with authority; **management reserve is released by the governance board** |
| **Authorises scope change** | Issues **may result in changes to scope, so change control must be followed** |
| **Decides continuation** | Including cancelling an initiative made unviable |
| **Provides confidence** | Stakeholders can see risk is **being got ahead of rather than reacted to**, which also **protects the organisation's reputation** |

**Three things shape how risk management is set up: the organisation's appetite for risk, the governance already in place, and how big and complicated the change is.** Governance is an explicit input to how risk management is designed, not just a recipient of its outputs.

## Why this keeps decisions at the right level

**Issue management is a genuine project control. Run properly, it keeps people inside the authority they were given and puts each resolution decision at the level that should be taking it.**

Both halves matter:

- **Working within delegated authority** — the project manager does not quietly absorb something they were not authorised to absorb.
- **Decisions at the appropriate level** — the sponsor or board is not asked to adjudicate on day-to-day problems either.

Escalating too little and escalating everything are both governance failures.

## What governance enables in the analysis

**Escalating is what lets expectations be managed and decisions be taken on evidence.** The words doing the work are *on evidence* — which is why analysis, the risk register and clear risk descriptions matter. A board asked to decide on an unanalysed risk is guessing.

And since no business case or plan is complete without risk analysis behind it, governance leans on it at approval as much as during delivery.

## Where governance fails

Be able to name these, because a scenario will describe one:

| Failure | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Reluctance to escalate issues early** | Problems arrive at the board too late to be solved cheaply |
| **The board treating the symptom rather than the root cause** | The same issue recurs |
| **Tolerances not agreed** | No basis for deciding what escalates, so escalation becomes personality-driven |
| **Continual issues** | **May indicate an underlying problem with project plans and controls** |
| **Contingency treated as spare money** | Undermines the control it was meant to provide |

## The connection to the wider governance triangle

From LO7: **governance leans on assurance to make its decisions sound**, **risk analysis points assurance at the greatest vulnerabilities**, and **what assurance finds sharpens the risk picture**. **Weakness in any one compromises the others.**

So risk management is not merely governed — it is one of the three legs holding governance up.
core_content.outcome_title: Why governance matters in risk and issue management

misconceptions.right: A problem gets handled day to day by the project manager and the team. An issue needs the sponsor's support before it can be resolved. Escalating everything is as much a governance failure as escalating nothing.
misconceptions.wrong: Anything that goes wrong is an issue.

misconceptions.right: It covers threats and opportunities. Opportunity management uses the same process and tools, and a register containing only threats means opportunity management is not happening.
misconceptions.wrong: Risk management is about threats.

misconceptions.right: Acceptance is a reactive response — a threat accepted with a contingent response. The response is planned; it is implemented only if the risk materialises.
misconceptions.wrong: Accepting a risk means doing nothing about it.

misconceptions.right: Transfer moves the cost, through insurance or by placing the risk with a better-equipped owner. As with fixed-price contracts in procurement, the risk relocates rather than disappearing.
misconceptions.wrong: Transferring a risk removes it.

misconceptions.right: It is unrealistic to believe every risk can be managed, which is why analysis prioritises them so the top risks can be addressed. Deciding to spend time and money is a decision governed by risk appetite.
misconceptions.wrong: Every risk needs a response.

misconceptions.right: It cycles rather than concludes, because project work keeps moving. New risks get picked up throughout, and fresh knowledge sharpens the contingency estimate.
misconceptions.wrong: Risk identification happens at the start of the project.

misconceptions.right: Close a risk once it has happened, or once it no longer can. A register cluttered with dead risks buries the live ones.
misconceptions.wrong: Closing risks is administrative tidying.

misconceptions.right: No business case or plan is complete without risk analysis, whichever life cycle is in use. Iterative projects review risk more often and closer to the work, not less thoroughly.
misconceptions.wrong: Iterative projects manage risk less rigorously.

misconceptions.right: Where issues keep arriving, the plans and the controls themselves are probably at fault. Recurrence is a symptom worth diagnosing.
misconceptions.wrong: Repeated issues mean the project is unlucky.

key_definitions.plain_english: Working out what might happen, how much it would matter, and what to do about it before it does.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The process that allows project professionals to identify, assess and respond appropriately to risks. It involves deciding which threats to actively minimise and which opportunities to maximise or pursue.

key_definitions.plain_english: Something that has gone beyond what the project manager was authorised to absorb. It needs the sponsor.
key_definitions.apm_definition: What occurs when the tolerances of delegated work have been exceeded, or when the tolerances will definitely be exceeded. Issues require support from the sponsor to agree a resolution.

key_definitions.plain_english: Something inside your tolerances. You just deal with it.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A day-to-day matter dealt with by the project manager and the team, as distinct from an issue.

key_definitions.plain_english: Risk that would help rather than harm. Managed the same way, and routinely forgotten.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Recognition that uncertainty can have a beneficial effect on the achievement of objectives — the positive side of risk — using the same process and tools used for threats.

key_definitions.plain_english: Ranking risks by how likely and how bad. Enough for most projects.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Analysis that allows risk events to be prioritised, based as a minimum on the probability or likelihood of occurrence and the size of impact on schedule, cost, benefits and potentially other objectives.

key_definitions.plain_english: Putting numbers and probabilities on it. For large or complex projects, or to support an investment decision.
key_definitions.apm_definition: Analysis focusing on specific risk-based decisions, using techniques such as decision trees, sensitivity analysis, or a probabilistic approach such as Monte Carlo simulation.

key_definitions.plain_english: The live list of what might go wrong or right, what it would cost, and whose name is against it.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The record used to document risks, analysis and responses, assigning clear ownership of actions.

key_definitions.plain_english: Whoever is actually positioned to do something about it — not automatically the project manager.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The individual or group best placed to assess and manage a risk, assigned as each risk is identified.

key_definitions.plain_english: Acting before the risk materialises, to change its probability or impact.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A planned and implemented response — 'we do something now'. For threats: avoid, reduce, transfer. For opportunities: exploit, enhance, share.

key_definitions.plain_english: Deciding in advance what you would do, then waiting to see whether you need to.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A response that is identified but implemented only if the risk materialises. A threat may be accepted with a contingent response; an opportunity may be rejected.

key_definitions.plain_english: How much risk the people funding this are willing to carry. Not the project manager's call.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The tolerance level for risk exposure, determined by the risk appetite of the investors and wider stakeholders.

body.where_this_fits: Risk is uncertainty that has not happened yet; an issue is uncertainty that has. That single distinction organises the whole LO and decides which process applies. It connects to LO19 (risks are identified during integrated planning), LO22 (contingency is the money side of the response), LO24 (issues and risk responses often become change requests) and LO2 (escalation exists because authority is delegated with limits). The most-missed idea: risk includes opportunity, and the same process handles both.
learning_outcomes: 23a) Understand the benefits of risk and issue management and the role of contingency planning in projects.

23b) Understand the purpose and importance of each stage in a risk management process (such as identification, analysis, monitoring, escalation, response and closure) and an issue management process (such as logging and analysis, escalation, and assignment of actions), and understand why these stages are different for linear and iterative life cycles.
23c) Know proactive and reactive responses to risks (such as avoid, reduce, transfer or accept and exploit, enhance, share or reject).
23d) Understand why governance is important in risk and issue management.

body.apm_learning_objective: Understand risk and issue management as the ability to identify and monitor risks (threats and opportunities); plan responses to those risks and respond to issues.

diagrams.alt: The change control process from raising and logging a request through initial evaluation, detailed impact assessment, sponsor decision, plan updates and implementation, with rejection possible at initial evaluation and approve, reject or defer at the decision point.
diagrams.spec: A left-to-right flow: raise change request → log in change register → initial evaluation → detailed evaluation (impact assessment) → decision → update plans → implement and monitor. Show two exit routes off the main line: rejection at initial evaluation, and approve/reject/defer at the decision point, with defer looping back to the register rather than terminating. Mark the sponsor as the decision owner. The two exits and the defer loop are what the diagram must convey — most change requests do not travel the full path.
diagrams.caption: The six stages of the change control process
diagrams.heading: The six stages

core_content.key_takeaway: Six stages: log, initial evaluation, detailed evaluation, decision, update plans, implement. Each exists to make sure the sponsor understands the impact before deciding — and the sponsor, not the project manager, is accountable for that decision being made.
core_content.body_markdown:
## What change control is

**The governance around a project's baseline, plus the process and controls for spotting a change, weighing it and acting on it.**

**Why it exists:** **every project will change, and handling that badly produces plans that no longer agree, people who no longer know what is true, and consequences nobody intended.** The point is not to prevent change — it is to prevent *uncontrolled* change.

**And the purpose in one line:** with a defined process, **a sponsor knows what a requested change would actually do before deciding — which is what makes the decision a real one.**

## The distinction to get right immediately

| | Change control | Change management |
|---|---|---|
| **What it is** | The process governing changes to one project's baseline | A whole-organisation approach to transformation |
| **Scope** | This project's plan | The organisation and its people |

The source flags this explicitly, which means it is examinable. They share a word and nothing else.

## Where change requests come from

They arrive from all over:

- **issues that surface while delivering** — the LO23 link
- **new stakeholder requirements** — the LO16 link
- **changes in the project's external environment** — PESTLE factors from LO4

**The project manager is usually where a request first lands**, and they then run the process.

## The six stages

| Stage | What happens | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Log change request** | **A change register or log records all requested changes** | Nothing gets assessed informally, and rejected requests stay on record |
| **2. Initial evaluation** | A first look at whether this even merits a full assessment. If it does not, it is rejected here | A cheap filter. Detailed evaluation is expensive, so not everything earns one |
| **3. Detailed evaluation** | **An impact assessment**, covering **how it may alter benefits, scope, quality, schedule and costs.** It takes real analysis and input from a spread of stakeholders | This is where the real work is, and 24c covers it |
| **4. Decision** | The sponsor gets the options, a recommendation, or both. **Making sure a decision actually gets taken — approve, reject or defer — is the sponsor's accountability.** The team is then told what was decided | Three outcomes, not two. And accountability sits with the sponsor |
| **5. Update plans** | **Plans are updated to reflect the change** — and because the project's plans are integrated, that update has to carry through into **scope definition, solutions development and configuration management** too | 24e covers why this cannot be partial |
| **6. Implement** | **Necessary actions are taken, and the impacts are monitored through to completion** | Approval is not implementation, and implementation is not the end |

**Two stages carry more weight than candidates expect.**

**Initial evaluation** exists so that not every idea consumes an impact assessment. Rejecting at this gate is a proper outcome.

**Monitoring after implementation** is stage six's second half. The impact assessment was a forecast; monitoring checks whether it was right.

## What the process enables

Run this way, the sponsor and stakeholders can see **what a change would do to the outcomes the project is forecasting**. Specifically it should:

- keep decisions **consistent with strategic objectives and with how much risk the organisation will carry**
- **handle the knock-on effects on other projects, programmes, portfolios and BAU**

That second point is easy to miss: a change to this project can break another one's plan.

## Two situations worth knowing

**Change implemented without formal approval.** **Run the process after the event.** You do not pretend it did not happen — you run it through the process after the fact so the impact is understood and recorded.

And the framing to carry: this is not red tape for its own sake — it is **the most reliable way to be sure everyone understands what the change actually did.**

**Change freeze.** Sometimes a project **stops considering change requests altogether for a period.** Typically **around exceptional points in its environment** — Christmas, the summer holidays — **so that avoidable risks and issues are not manufactured at the worst moment.**

## Where the stages differ by life cycle

The syllabus asks specifically. **Whatever approach or life cycle a project uses, it needs a defined process** — but how that process operates differs.

| | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| **What is baselined** | **Scope is fixed at the deployment baseline**, so **any change identified in deployment must go through change control** | Scope is held in a **product backlog** and fixed only for the current timebox |
| **What counts as a change** | Any variation from the approved scope | Changing what is **already committed to the current iteration**; new items simply enter the backlog |
| **Frequency and ceremony** | Less frequent, more formal | Frequent, lighter — much of what would be a change request in linear is absorbed by re-prioritising the backlog |
| **Where decisions are made** | Sponsor and governance board, often at gates | **The team may have authority to prioritise and act on new knowledge** within the timebox |
| **What flexes** | Scope and quality drive; **cost and time are calculated from the scope** | **Time and cost are fixed; scope and quality flex** |
| **Unfinished work** | Becomes a variance requiring action | Anything the timebox did not deliver goes back into the backlog |

**The structural reason:** a linear project fixed its scope at approval, so every deviation is an exception. An iterative project only ever fixed the current timebox, so most change is normal operation. **The formal change control process still exists** in iterative work — it applies to the things that were genuinely committed.
core_content.outcome_title: The change control process, stage by stage

core_content.key_takeaway: A change request records what is being asked for, who asked, why, and what it would do to the baseline — enough for someone else to evaluate it without going back to the requester.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Why the record matters

**Every requested change goes into a change register, or log.** All of them — including those rejected at initial evaluation. That record is what stops a rejected idea returning six months later as though it were new, and what lets anyone see how much change pressure the project is under.

## What gets captured

Drawing together what the process needs at each stage:

| Field | Why it is needed |
|---|---|
| **Unique identifier** | So the request can be tracked through the register to closure |
| **Date raised and requester** | Source matters — a change from a regulator is not a change from a preference |
| **Description of the change** | What is actually being asked for |
| **Reason or justification** | Why it is being requested. **Requests arise from issues discovered in delivery, new stakeholder requirements, or changes in the external environment** |
| **Priority or urgency** | Whether it must be decided now or can wait |
| **Initial evaluation outcome** | Whether it is **worth evaluating in detail**, and the rejection reason if not |
| **Impact assessment** | The quantified effect on **scope, objectives and success criteria, benefits, time, cost, resource, quality and risks** |
| **Options considered** | Usually more than one, each carrying a different level of impact |
| **Recommendation** | What the project professional advises, and why |
| **Decision** | Approve, reject or defer — with the sponsor recorded as decision maker |
| **Date of decision and communication** | **The decision is communicated to the project team** |
| **Implementation status** | Tracked, with **impacts monitored through to completion** |

**The test of a good change request:** could someone who was not in the conversation evaluate it from the record alone? If they would have to go back to the requester to understand what is being asked or why, it is incomplete.

## The three characteristics assessed before evaluating

Before committing effort to a detailed assessment, **determine the effort required** by considering three characteristics of the requested change:

| Characteristic | The question |
|---|---|
| **Size and scale** | How large is it, and does it reach across the whole project or only part of the scope? |
| **Complexity** | Will this be technically hard, or is the solution straightforward? |
| **Feasibility** | Given what the project and the organisation can actually do, can this be done at all? |

These are worth capturing on the request itself, because they justify how much assessment effort was applied — and a change judged infeasible at this point can be rejected without further cost.
core_content.outcome_title: What a change request should capture

core_content.key_takeaway: Impact assessment gathers information, works out the effort required, then quantifies the effect across eight named areas of the baseline. Usually several options are assessed, each with a different level of impact.
core_content.body_markdown:
## What an impact assessment is

**A structured way of working out what a change would mean for the baseline.** It is what **the detailed evaluation rests on**, so that **nothing the sponsor needs in order to decide properly is missing.**

**Speed matters:** **quickly and effectively completing a detailed evaluation is crucial for success.** A change held in assessment is a change the project is planning around without a decision.

## The sequence

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1. Size the effort** | Assess the change's **size and scale, complexity and feasibility** to determine how much assessment work is warranted |
| **2. Gather information** | Draw on **subject-matter experts and on data from inside and outside the organisation** to pin down the specifics — the worked example being which technology best suits a software solution |
| **3. Assess work and effort** | Nobody has designed the solution in detail yet, so the experts **work to stated assumptions about how it would be built** |
| **4. Quantify the impact** | Against each area of the baseline |
| **5. Present options** | Usually more than one, each with a different level of impact on the baseline |

**Step 3 is worth noticing.** You are assessing something not yet designed, so the assessment rests on assumptions — which should be recorded, exactly as estimating assumptions are in LO19.

## The eight impact areas

This is the directly examinable list, and each is phrased as a question:

| Area | The question |
|---|---|
| **Scope** | Does this fundamentally alter what the project is delivering? |
| **Objectives and success criteria** | Do the outcomes shift, or does what counts as success? |
| **Benefits** | Does it add new benefits, or disturb the ones already promised? |
| **Time** | Does the schedule move — out, or in? |
| **Cost** | Does it push costs up, or take them out somewhere else? |
| **Resource** | Does this need people we do not have, or can the current profile absorb it? |
| **Quality** | Do the deliverables get better or worse? |
| **Risks** | Does it introduce risk, or retire some? |

**Note how many are two-directional.** Time can shorten. Cost can fall. Quality can improve. Risk can reduce. A change is not automatically a degradation, and an assessment that only looks for damage will miss the case for approving it.

**And note what the list covers:** it is essentially the contents of the integrated PMP from LO19. That is the point — **put numbers on the impact, and look specifically at the rest of the integrated PMP when you do.**

## Assessing options

**Most requests get more than one option worked up**, each landing differently on the baseline.

Ways to frame the options, drawing on the wider course:

| Option type | What it tests |
|---|---|
| **Do nothing** | Always an option (LO17) — what happens if the change is not made? |
| **Full implementation** | The change as requested |
| **Partial or minimum implementation** | The smallest version delivering the essential benefit |
| **Defer to a later phase or iteration** | Same change, different timing |
| **Alternative solution** | A different way of achieving the same outcome |

Each is then assessed against the same eight areas, so the sponsor can compare like with like.

## Presenting it

**Put real effort into presenting the options so the sponsor can follow them — summarised enough to be digestible, detailed enough that the decision is a sound one.**

That balance is the skill. Too much detail and the decision stalls; too little and the sponsor is deciding on a summary that hid the difficulty. It is the same principle as the integrated PMP in LO19 — succinct enough to be used, complete enough to be trusted.
core_content.outcome_title: Assessing options and the impact of a proposed change

core_content.key_takeaway: Three outcomes, and the recommendation must be justified against the impact assessment, the business case and the organisation's risk appetite. The sponsor is accountable for the decision being made.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Three outcomes, not two

**Making sure a decision gets taken — approve, reject or defer — is the sponsor's accountability.**

**Defer is the one candidates forget.** It is not indecision — it means the change may be right but this is the wrong moment: too close to a gate, inside a change freeze, or better handled in a later phase or iteration. Deferring keeps the request alive in the register rather than losing it.

**Accountability sits with the sponsor** for ensuring the decision is made. The project professional's job is the recommendation and the evidence behind it.

## What justifies a recommendation

| Basis | The argument |
|---|---|
| **The impact assessment** | The quantified effect across all eight areas. This is the evidence, and no recommendation is justified without it |
| **Strategic alignment** | Decisions should **be made in line with the strategic objectives** — the LO4 and LO9 link |
| **Risk appetite** | And in line with **the appetite for risk** — LO23 |
| **Effect on the business case** | Does the change strengthen or undermine the justification for the project continuing? |
| **Effect on benefits** | **Would it create new benefits, or impact existing ones?** |
| **Impact beyond this project** | What it does to other projects, programmes, portfolios or to BAU |
| **Feasibility** | Given what the project and the organisation can actually do, is this achievable? |
| **Options comparison** | Why this option rather than the others assessed |

## Shaping the argument

**For approval:** the change delivers benefit or avoids harm that justifies its cost in time, money, quality and risk; it aligns with strategy and sits within risk appetite; the project and organisation can actually do it; and it is better than the alternatives assessed, including doing nothing.

**For rejection:** the impact outweighs the benefit; it takes the project outside risk appetite or away from strategic objectives; it is not feasible with current capability; or the same outcome is available more cheaply another way. Rejection can also happen at **initial evaluation** if the change is **not worth evaluating in detail**.

**For deferral:** the change is sound but the timing is wrong — a change freeze is in force, a gate is imminent, dependencies are unresolved, or the assessment itself is not yet complete enough to decide on.

## Communicating the decision

**Whatever was decided, the project team gets told.** All three outcomes, not only the approvals. A team that never hears what happened to a rejected request stops raising them.

## The connection to decision gates

Change decisions and gate decisions work the same way. A **decision gate** asks whether the business case **is still viable** — whether benefits remain achievable **for an acceptable level of cost and risk** (LO6). A change decision asks the same question about a specific proposed variation.

And the governance board's own remit from LO2 includes **reviewing and determining change requests, escalating them to a higher authority where necessary** — so a change exceeding the sponsor's delegated authority goes up, exactly like any other decision beyond a limit.
core_content.outcome_title: Justifying a recommendation to approve, reject or defer

core_content.key_takeaway: An approved change that only lands in one plan creates the misalignment change control exists to prevent. Because the PMP is integrated, updates must propagate — into scope, schedule, budget, resources, risk and configuration — and then be monitored.
core_content.body_markdown:
## Why partial updating fails

**Approve a change and the plans get rewritten to match it — and because a project's plans are integrated, that rewrite has to carry through into other processes too.** The source names **scope definition, solutions development and configuration management.**

That phrase — *the integrated nature of projects* — is the whole argument for 24e. LO19 established that the constituent plans constrain each other, so moving one of them moves another whether you meant it to or not. Update the schedule but not the budget and you have two plans making different claims about the same project. That is precisely the **misalignment, confusion and unwanted consequences** change control exists to avoid.

## What has to be updated

| Plan or artefact | What changes |
|---|---|
| **Scope definition** | The PBS and WBS, and the in-scope / out-of-scope statement (LO17) |
| **Solutions development** | The specification of the chosen solution (LO17) |
| **Schedule** | Activities, durations, dependencies — and the critical path may move (LO20) |
| **Budget and cash flow forecast** | Cost baseline and drawdown profile (LO22) |
| **Resource plan** | New resources, or reallocation of the existing profile (LO21) |
| **Risk register** | Risks created or reduced by the change (LO23) |
| **Quality plan** | Acceptance criteria affected by altered deliverables (LO18) |
| **Benefits** | New or altered benefits, and the benefit profiles behind them (LO9) |
| **Configuration** | **Approved changes reflected in the latest configuration version**, with **interrelationships between configuration items updated** (LO16) |
| **Business case** | Where the impact is material, reapproval may be needed (LO4) |
| **Deployment baseline** | The amended baseline that delivery is now measured against (LO19) |

**The configuration point is specific and examinable:** **an agreed change has to show up in the configuration itself — whatever it does to how the deliverables function or what they physically are gets written down and passed to everyone on the team.**

Without that step, a change is approved and half the team keeps building to the old specification.

## Implementation is not the end

**Then it gets implemented, and its impacts are watched right through to completion.**

With **controls established to do that watching.** The impact assessment was a forecast made on working assumptions about a solution that was not yet designed — monitoring is how you find out whether it held.

**Communicate it too:** approved changes must be **communicated to stakeholders** (LO17), and **the decision is communicated to the project team** (LO24a). A change nobody was told about is an uncontrolled change with paperwork.

## Why the updated baseline matters

The updated plan becomes **the starting point for progress monitoring**. Everything downstream depends on it:

- **Progress monitoring** needs **a baseline to measure against** (LO20). Measuring against a superseded baseline produces variances that are artefacts of the paperwork rather than the work.
- **Earned value** compares actual and earned against **planned value** — which comes from the cost baseline (LO22).
- **Change control itself** assesses future requests **against the baseline**. An out-of-date baseline corrupts every subsequent impact assessment.

So failing to update plans does not just leave one document stale. It degrades the control system that every remaining decision depends on.

## And where it cannot be recovered

From LO20: **when monitoring surfaces something the project cannot recover from, you replan and set an amended baseline.** Change control is the ordinary route for a variation; replanning is what happens when the accumulated position no longer works at all.

That is the honest closing note for the syllabus. Control does not mean the plan survives — it means the plan only ever moves for a reason, with the impact understood and someone accountable for the decision.
core_content.outcome_title: Updating plans and schedules to reflect approved changes

misconceptions.right: Change control is the process governing changes to one project's baseline. Change management is a whole-organisation approach to transformation. The source distinguishes them explicitly.
misconceptions.wrong: Change control and change management are the same thing.

misconceptions.right: Change is an inevitable part of any project. The purpose is to ensure sponsors understand the impacts of a requested change so they can make an effective decision — controlling change, not preventing it.
misconceptions.wrong: The purpose of change control is to minimise change.

misconceptions.right: Initial evaluation exists to consider whether a change is worth evaluating in detail. If not, it is rejected at that stage, before the expensive assessment is done.
misconceptions.wrong: Every change request gets a full impact assessment.

misconceptions.right: There are three outcomes — approve, reject or defer. Deferral keeps a sound change alive in the register when the timing is wrong.
misconceptions.wrong: The sponsor either approves or rejects a change.

misconceptions.right: The project professional presents options and a recommendation. The sponsor is accountable for ensuring the decision is made, and changes beyond their authority escalate to the governance board.
misconceptions.wrong: The project manager decides whether a change goes ahead.

misconceptions.right: Most of the eight impact areas are two-directional. Time can shorten, cost can fall, quality can improve and risk can reduce. An assessment looking only for harm will miss the case for approval.
misconceptions.wrong: An impact assessment looks for the damage a change would do.

misconceptions.right: The project professional should manage the process retrospectively, so the impacts are still fully understood and recorded.
misconceptions.wrong: If a change was implemented without approval, the process has been bypassed.

misconceptions.right: A clear process is needed regardless of approach or life cycle. What differs is what counts as a change — new items entering a backlog are normal operation, while altering what is already committed to a timebox is not.

key_definitions.plain_english: The route by which a baseline is allowed to move — deliberately, with the impact understood.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The governance, process and controls that identify, evaluate and action changes to a project's baseline.

key_definitions.plain_english: A different discipline entirely. Change control is about the plan; change management is about the organisation.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A holistic approach to organisational transformation, distinct from change control, which is a process to manage changes to an individual project's baseline.

key_definitions.plain_english: Every request goes in, including the ones that get rejected. That record is what stops the same idea coming back unexamined.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The record used to log all requested changes.

key_definitions.plain_english: A cheap filter before an expensive assessment. Rejecting here is a legitimate outcome, not a shortcut.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The stage at which a change is reviewed to consider whether it is worth evaluating in detail. If not, it is rejected at this stage.

key_definitions.plain_english: The work of finding out what this change would actually do to scope, time, cost, quality, benefits, resource and risk.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A structured approach to assessing the implications of a change on the project's baseline, underpinning the detailed evaluation so the sponsor has the information needed for an informed decision.

key_definitions.plain_english: A deliberate window where the baseline is locked — around a go-live, a holiday period, a critical delivery.
key_definitions.apm_definition: A period in which no change requests are considered, usually implemented around exceptional events in the project's environment so as not to create unnecessary risks or issues.

key_definitions.plain_english: Not now. The change may be right but the timing is wrong, so it waits rather than being lost.
key_definitions.apm_definition: One of the three decisions available to the sponsor, alongside approve and reject.

key_definitions.plain_english: Where an approved change lands in the record of what is actually being built.
key_definitions.apm_definition: The technical and administrative activities that manage the creation, maintenance, controlled change and quality control of the project's technical configuration, ensuring approved changes are reflected in the latest configuration version.

body.where_this_fits: The last LO, and the one that protects every baseline the other twenty-three produced. Scope, schedule, budget, quality, requirements and configuration are all baselined somewhere in this course; change control is the single mechanism that lets any of them move deliberately rather than by drift. The distinction worth fixing immediately: change control manages changes to a project's baseline, while change management is organisational transformation. They are not the same discipline.
learning_outcomes: 24a) Understand the purpose and importance of each stage of a typical change control process (such as request, initial evaluation, detailed evaluation, recommendation, update plans and implement), and understand where these stages are different for linear and iterative life cycles.
24b) Know what should be captured and recorded in change requests.
24c) Know ways to assess options related to a proposed change and the high-level impact of the proposed change.
24d) Understand how to justify recommendations about whether to approve, reject or defer changes.
24e) Understand the importance of updating plans and schedules to reflect approved changes.
progress_checkpoint: I can define change control, distinguish it from change management, and say where change requests come from.
I can name the six stages of the change control process and explain the purpose of each, including why initial evaluation exists.
I can explain what a change freeze is and what to do when a change has been implemented without approval.
I can explain how change control differs between linear and iterative life cycles, and why.
I can list what a change request should capture, and name the three characteristics assessed before committing to a detailed evaluation.
I can give the eight impact areas as questions, and explain why several are two-directional.
I can describe ways of framing options for a change, and justify a recommendation to approve, reject or defer.
I can explain why approved changes must propagate across all the plans, and what depends on the baseline being current.
body.apm_learning_objective: Understand change control as the ability to manage variations and change requests in a controlled way.
